f5e9ced9235e.text: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan , flipping another GOP-held seat in a state President Trump carried comfortably in 2024, the AP projects. Why it matters: Peltola becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008, extending a historic blue wave in a race marred by controversy. Her victory comes in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, underscoring the extraordinary reach of the Democratic backlash against his second term. It also delivers another blow to Republicans after sweeping Democratic victories in states including Texas, Ohio, Iowa and South Carolina. State of play: The race drew scrutiny after The New York Times reported allegations that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Dan Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied involvement, but the reporting prompted Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, to order an investigation into whether state laws were broken. The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation and subpoenaed people connected to the alleged effort. No one involved in the race has been charged with a crime. On the campaign trail, the candidates clashed over the cost of living, the Iran war and Alaska's energy industry, with Peltola challenging Sullivan's record in Washington. Peltola campaigned on her signature "fish, family and freedom" message, emphasizing affordability, protecting Alaska's fisheries and putting the state's interests ahead of party politics. Trump traveled to Alaska in October to rally support for Sullivan, whom he praised as one of Washington's most respected senators. Sullivan embraced the president's support , betting it would energize Republican voters despite their party's political headwinds. The big picture: Alaska has long leaned Republican, but Peltola's ability to win crossover support — including votes from Republicans who ranked her above former Gov. Sarah Palin in 2022 — helped put the state in play for Democrats. Peltola made history in that 2022 special election as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She won a full term later that year before losing her House seat to Republican Nick Begich in 2024. Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and Marine Corps veteran, has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2015. The two-term Republican campaigned on his record on energy development and national security. Context: Another candidate named Dan Sullivan — a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — became a factor in the race. The Trump administration sued Alaska on Oct. 22, seeking to delay certification if Sen. Sullivan lost and votes for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, ruling that the administration lacked standing to bring the case and that its proposed remedy was unworkable. The Justice Department appealed the decision. Sen. Sullivan committed to accepting the results even if he didn't win. How it works: Alaska's ranked-choice voting system added another wrinkle. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the last-place candidate is eliminated and votes for that candidate are redistributed according to voters' next available choices. The process repeats until a candidate wins a majority. What's next: Alaska election officials will complete the remaining certification steps, with the Justice Department's appeal potentially affecting the process.

Despite Nvidiaâs proclamation Tuesday that it didnât plan to bring ousted CEO Jensen Huang back to the chipmaker, a faction of board members is pushing for his return, according to people familiar with the matter.
Huang has met with a number of tech executives and spoken with at least one board member about the possibility of his return, the people said.
The conversation with the director took place before the companyâs earnings report and before Huang issued a public statement Tuesday that heâd be willing to return to the company if the board decides it is in the âbest interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.â
Hours later, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the companyâs earnings call that the chipmaker wasnât considering bringing Huang back and that the board had voted unanimously to accept his resignation.
Spokespeople for Huang and Nvidia declined to comment.
Despite the pushback from a minority of directors, other board members are starting to narrow the search for Huangâs replacement, some of the people familiar with the deliberations said.
ARM CEO Rene Haas and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have both been considered, the people said. Haas has spoken to at least some Nvidia directors about taking the job, one of the people said, but heâs said heâs concerned about the optics of taking it over calls to bring Huang back to the helm.
Spokespeople for ARM and Marvell didnât immediately respond to requests for comment. Itâs also unclear whether Marvellâs Murphy would be able to take over as Nvidiaâs CEO given the company is navigating a mega-merger with rival Lumentum.

Europeâs tech scene is still fighting the same battles that have held it back in the global AI race, leaders and CEOs from the continent said at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said the US, and to an extent China, are âradically in a different leagueâ when it comes to scale and capital. Employing a soccer (or football) metaphor, he said those are the only two countries that are in AIâs Premier League, while the UK sits atop the Championship, the tier below. Heâs ânot happy enoughâ with that.
Marco-Alexander Breit, director-general at Germanyâs digital ministry, argued that Europe still needs more âinnovation-friendly regulationâ if it wants to compete. He said he agreed with most of the EUâs AI Act, but argued it âactually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world.â Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak echoed some of the criticism, saying that âtrying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.â
Still, the continent is starting to figure out its niche: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch pointed to a rising need for cheaper, open-source, and sovereign AI â models that companies can run on their own premises, without relying on US models or exposing their data. Germany is leaning on its industrial base, with Breit pointing to the troves of data that manufacturers like Siemens and Bosch sit on. Narayan said the UK is looking to make inroads in inference chips and AI for drug discovery.
âItâs not all doom and gloom in Europe,â Breit said.

266e6fe70b9e.text:
NATO aims to spur space industry, help militaries by joining data marketplace
Easing the sale and sharing of information should increase launch tempo and ward off threats, officials said.
IZMIR, Turkey—NATO allies hope that joining a marketplace for orbital data will nurture Europe’s growing space industry and help militaries keep the satellites they rely on safe from attack.
On Tuesday, alliance officials announced they would begin using the Global Data Marketplace, a platform run by Colorado-based Bluestaq that U.S. Space Force has used for about six years. The platform gives companies a “single-entry point” to sell data about space objects and debris, which military and commercial customers might use to, say, more easily plan satellite launches, or to ward off potential Russian attacks, NATO officials told reporters on Monday, before the opening of the NATO Edge conference here. Like the Space Force, NATO has set up a separate data repository where purchased data can be flowed in and mixed with classified information.
More than 220 companies from 17 Allied nations already participate in the marketplace, and NATO expects to place its first orders by year’s end, according to an alliance press release.
The alliance also announced the opening of STARLIFT, a multinational effort to increase satellite launches.
One NATO official pointed to an incident in October, when a Russian satellite maneuvered within a few hundred meters of a U.S. satellite whose operator, a Finnish company called ICEYE, provides cloud-piercing synthetic aperture radar imagery to Ukraine. The maneuver was “consistent with on-orbit weapons operations,” U.S. officials said at the time.
On Monday, the official said such incidents “illustrate the concern about threats to commercial systems.”
“We've adopted this from the United States Space Force,” a second NATO official said. “They've been working on these technologies for quite some years, and this shows the approach we're able to deliver faster.”
The Space Force began using Bluestaq’s Global Data Marketplace in 2020, when the initiative was known as the “Space Domain Awareness Marketplace.” It enables Space Force and Space Command operators to purchase “indication and warning information, which includes commercial partners, through commercial sources that are inherently shareable,” according to a 2021 award announcement.
In August, the Government Accountability Office reported that the Space Force purchased nearly $124 million worth of data and services via Global Data Marketplace between January 2023 and September 2025.
Bluestaq launched the platform in 2019 with just a handful of vendors, CEO Seth Harvey told Defense One on Tuesday. Since then, he said, it’s picked up the Space Force as a customer and is on track to onboard upwards of 400 vendors by the end of the year.
The idea is for customers — such as the Space Force and now NATO — to quickly order unclassified data from commercial vendors that track space activity, he said. Orders can be placed anonymously to protect the identity of, for example, troops looking to use a commercial satellite constellation for military operations.
Like the U.S. Space Force, NATO can now collect information from commercial partners via the marketplace and catalogue it in an information repository that the alliance controls–dubbed the NATO Unified Data Library. There, commercial information can be compared with more sensitive data to help build a clearer picture of space activity, then quickly shared with allies if desired, the Bluestaq CEO said.
Harvey said one recent demonstration saw a customer place an order to track space activity, which a telescope vendor responded to, downloaded the data into the marketplace which then linked to the NATO repository in 14 minutes. He declined to say which specific entities were involved.
“It really reduces the barrier to be able to leverage commercial data for really meaningful operations,” he said, adding that a decade ago, governments would have to go through a lengthy contracting process with vendors to collect data. “What it does is it creates tremendous agility.”
NATO officials hope that the marketplace will give some space startups an additional revenue stream—selling timely intelligence on space threats—while decreasing satellite risks to other businesses and putting a political price on acts of space sabotage.
Better data sharing might also help European militaries and companies get more satellites into space by making it easier to plan flight paths. The marketplace will help support STARLIFT, a NATO effort to help military users book available slots on commercial rockets, coordinate launch requirements, and find more launch sites. STARLIFT, which has been in the works for two years, was also officially launched on Tuesday.
“I think all of you know that launch remains a critical bottleneck, particularly in Europe,” the NATO official said. “The first challenge is how to acquire the commercial space data and services our forces need faster, and then the second challenge is how to get the satellites they depend on into orbit more reliably.”
Just creating a data marketplace doesn’t automatically fix things. In its August report, GAO said, “Some Space Force officials told GAO about challenges they have faced related to purchasing and using commercial space data such as licensing costs, perceived use restrictions, and concerns over long-term access to the data. These challenges led to hesitation to purchase and use commercial data among these potential users.”
Security researchers, meanwhile, have noted that creating a giant pool of information about satellites gives potential adversaries an immensely valuable target for theft or disruption.
Bradley Peniston contributed to this report.

The world is âprobablyâ going to enter an era of âunprecedented safety of software systems,â AMI (Advanced Machine Intelligence) founder and chair Yann LeCun said on Tuesday at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World.
âIâm worried about very few things when it comes to AI,â LeCun told Semaforâs Shelly Banjo. LeCun predicts a short period âwhere AI tools facilitate cyberattacks and favor the attacker over the defender,â but that will be âjust a short period of transition.â Future software, he suggested, will be âhardenedâ by AI.
LeCun, a winner of the 2018 Turing Award, has long been skeptical that scaling large language models will usher in superintelligence or artificial general intelligence. He left Meta to found his world-model company AMI in 2025, which raised more than $1 billion in seed funding, the largest ever for a European company. He told Banjo that âI think itâs called a coconut when itâs that big.â
He spoke on Tuesday about world modelsâ practical application in physical AI, but acknowledged there is a long way to go in their development. âWeâre going to need a few conceptual breakthroughs in AI to make domestic robots that are useful,â he said. âWe can use humanoid robots for very narrow tasks in well-controlled environments at the moment,â but domestic robots are ânot for tomorrow.â
He said he and his peers working on world models are gravitating toward physical AI because itâs a âcomplete blind spotâ of LLMs.
When asked about open source models, he remarked that âit made a lot of people really sad in the US, including people who are in the current government, that the most powerful open source systems are Chinese.â

95f6450ce969.text: House Democrats aren't unanimous on whether House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) should be speaker, but they pretty much all agree on two things: He probably will be speaker, and they just want this to be over. Why it matters: Their phones and emails are still being blown up by constituents and grassroots activists urging them to do what they can to block Jeffries from securing the speaker gavel. There isn't much Jeffries' skeptics and detractors on Capitol Hill can do: He is set to easily win his caucus' nomination on Wednesday and then be formally elected to the role on Jan. 3. Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who told Axios last week he was undecided, said Tuesday he met with Jeffries and was "assured" votes on his two key issues: Ending the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran. "I'll be voting for Leader Jeffries," Johnson told Axios. State of play: The movement to deny Jeffries the speakership has proliferated online and among the progressive grassroots but has struggled to gain a foothold on Capitol Hill. A handful of members of the progressive "Bloc" — and some other newly elected members in deeply red district — have voiced skepticism of Jeffries, but only in a few cases has that evolved into outright opposition. "As of now, I'm a 'no,'" Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) told Axios on Wednesday. "The people are saying we deserve better, and better is possible." Reality check: Nobody is challenging Jeffries. Some people floated as potential potential challengers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), have firmly ruled it out . Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), the subject of an online petition urging her to seek the role, has privately told colleagues she is not running but been more equivocal in public. "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation," Pressley said at a town hall on Monday. She added that she was "making no declarations or announcements" at that event and does not "need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." What we're hearing: Some of Pressley's fellow Congressional Progressive Caucus members, granted anonymity to speak candidly, expressed frustration that she hasn't more forcefully tamped down the speculation. "She's only playing coy with people online," one CPC member told Axios. "The rest of us know she's not running. But that's generating additional calls and making people … even more pissed off in the end." Said another CPC member: "Many of us feel like she's stringing people along online to make them think that she's running and it's just not reality. " A third CPC member complained that it's "a bit selfish," with an incoming CPC member saying "it's not real" and chalking it up to Congress being an "attention economy." Yes, but: A second incoming CPC member said the grassroots would be "blowing us up regardless" of whether Pressley shut down the speculation or not. "It's true that the percentage of emails that mention her has grown, but the number was large to begin with," the member-elect added. What they're saying: "Everyone's trying to use whatever leverage they have and I think she's probably hoping that maybe this could be a way to make sure her voice is heard," said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.). Gonzales-Torres said she is "fully behind" the policy agenda Pressley has laid out but, asked if she would vote for her for speaker, said, "Where does she stand? What is she doing? Do you know?" Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio), one of Jeffries' most outspoken critics in the freshman class, said in a Breaking Points interview that Pressley "would have my support." Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) said Pressley "would be a great speaker but she's not running, so it's a hypothetical." What's next: House Democrats will meet behind closed-doors Wednesday to vote on their nominee for speaker and other caucus leadership roles. Jeffries plans to request a tallied vote, rather than being nominated by acclamation. He needs a simple majority among Democrats to secure the nomination but at least 218 votes on the House floor to formally win the gavel on Jan. 3. Democrats are expected to have a majority of at least 260 seats, giving Jeffries a wide margin for error. The bottom line: "The whole thing has been a stupid clusterfuck," the senior CPC member told Axios. "This is such a distraction from reality."

The UK is likely to miss legally binding climate targets if the government reduces electric vehicle (EV) targets, independent adviser the Climate Change Committee (CCC) has warned.
In a letter to Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander, the CCC argues that weakening the targets would result in "economic and energy security costs" and leave households "more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices".
The CCC says that switching to an electric vehicle can save a typical household around Â£800 a year, with fewer people benefiting if the targets were watered down.
The warning comes after weeks of speculation that the government plans to announce changes to the EV targets. Government sources insist no decision has been made.
Under the current rules, a "zero emission vehicle" (ZEV) mandate requires 80% of new cars sold in the UK to be zero emission by 2030 and all new cars to meet that standard by 2035. Companies that fail to meet their ZEV mandate face a potential fine of Â£12,000 per car, although there are exemptions.
Industry groups have long complained the current rules impose too heavy a burden, calling instead for a "sustainable transition".
Latest data from trade body the Society of Motor Manufacturing and Traders (SMMT) shows that EVs, as well as plug-in hybrids, are driving growth in new car sales.
In the year so far, 26.6% of all new car registrations have been fully electric, the SMMT says, which is below the headline target of 33% for 2026.
But the industry as a whole appears on course to comply with this year's mandate once flexibilities are accounted for, according to analysis by New AutoMotive, a transport research organisation which supports the transition to electric cars
SMMT Chief Executive Mike Hawes accused the CCC of ignoring the costs of the targets it was defending.
"The industry cannot subsidise the transition indefinitely, which is why it is unified in seeking change," he said.
Carbon budget
The CCC analysis also argued that weakening the targets would lead to a hole in the government's carbon savings that need to be made in order to meet its legally binding climate targets.
The CCC said the ZEV mandate "underpins the largest share of emissions reduction to 2037" in the government's net-zero plan. The climate targets set for 2033-2037 will be missed "without alternative action at the same scale", the CCC argued.
CCC analysis shows surface transport - which includes cars, vans and trucks - remains the country's highest carbon-emitting sector and one of the slowest to decarbonise.
Lord Deben, former CCC chairman, said going against CCC advice would "not be sensible" as it would "cost people money".
He said climate targets were "not random targets" and "if you don't reach them then you put yourselves in really serious danger of having climate change, which we can't handle".
A government spokesperson said: "We remain committed to the phase out of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets. Our consultation on the Mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition."

3859b6ecab1c.text:
OpenAI gives NATO access to most advanced cybersecurity AI
NATO operators this month built and deployed AI agents in an exercise, with help from OpenAI.
IZMIR, Turkey—NATO governments will now have access to OpenAI’s most powerful AI models to find and patch cyber vulnerabilities, company executives said Tuesday at an alliance conference here.
The announcement follows new NATO efforts to allow operators to work with new cyber tools, including AI agents, in key exercises such as Crossed Swords, a cyber wargame that took place in Tallinn, Estonia, earlier this month. Participants designed and deployed AI agents to achieve missions, “working alongside them as operators. The technical environment also uses on-premises AI and, for the first time in the exercise, OpenAI Daybreak,” according to a NATO announcement.
The move marks an international expansion of the company’s Daybreak effort, launched in May, which gives accredited institutions and the U.S. government access to the company’s most advanced models to find vulnerabilities in key pieces of software. Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, launched in April, is similar.
OpenAI made the announcement during NATO Edge, the alliance's largest annual technology business event. This year, more than 3,500 attendees and more than 270 exhibitors came to discuss security, tech, and business opportunities resulting from NATO’s growing defense commitments. A NATO official said the NATO Communications and Information Agency, orNCIA, will award more than $3 billion in contracts to industry by the end of 2027, with a heavy focus on cloud computing, space services, and artificial intelligence. That $3 billion is on top of whatever NATO allies each spend on AI. Not surprisingly, many of the exhibitors offered AI tools or AI-powered products.
This event also comes as Russia increases its cyber attacks on NATO allies. Cybersecurity experts and officials have warned for years that AI would enable actors like Russian criminal groups to multiply their efforts, exposing more vulnerabilities in software and helping attackers write more effective malware. That could fuel Russian efforts to cause havoc and disruption in Western populations and drive public frustration with their governments. A growing number of cybersecurity experts, along with executives from AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic, have said that the best defense is to use AI in new ways to find and fix vulnerabilities first.
That philosophy drove the emphasis on agentic AI cyber defense at this year’s Crossed Swords.
In Izmir, OpenAI national security and policy head Sasha Baker said what tech companies and NATO need to focus on is “collapsing that time window from when a vulnerability is discovered to when it is patched…from months to weeks to hours to minutes? That's the outcome that we want to achieve. And so I encourage you all to hold us accountable for that.”

e00aed0633cb.text:
Countless manure lagoons on dairy farms across California’s San Joaquin Valley will be vulnerable to serious flooding during what is likely to be a fierce and historic El Niño this winter.
These pools of cow feces and urine are commonly how dairies store waste on-site. When the lagoons overflow, any number of contaminants in the solid and liquid slurry—which contains high concentrations of chloride and nitrogen as well as pathogens—can pollute the environment and communities nearby.
The San Joaquin Valley has upwards of 1,000 dairy farms, the most in any part of the state. The total number of waste lagoons in the valley and statewide—dairies can have more than one—is unknown.
The current El Niño, which will ramp up heading into December, could bring devastating flooding to waste lagoons, leading to environmental problems like contamination of drinking water and the spread of manure sludge through rural neighborhoods, experts warned.
It wouldn’t be the first time the weather phenomenon has battered the state. Along the coast and throughout Southern California, families and farmers saw record-breaking storms in the El Niños of 1982-83 and 1997-98. The current El Niño is likely the strongest in over a millennium, a recent study in Science found.
Three years ago, the San Joaquin Valley was pummeled by atmospheric rivers that forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of cows from dairy farms. How overflow from manure lagoons impacted the many rural communities that sit beside dairies is impossible to know, as a true accounting of the effects has never been completed.
“Much of what we saw [in 2023] focused on protecting the cows … which certainly helps save the animals’ lives. However, I feel we saw very little regarding the issue of manure and the pollution that originates from all those farms,” said J. Pablo Ortiz-Partida, director of innovation and collaboration at the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists.
Ortiz-Partida, who has a degree in environmental engineering from Instituto Tecnológico y de Estudios Superiores de Occidente in Mexico, is concerned about families who live in proximity to dairy lagoons. Communities in central California, many majority Hispanic, are known to bear a disproportionate amount of the negative health harms from concentrated animal feeding operations.
He said that even without flooding, pools of manure from CAFOs have contaminated the groundwater and air in some areas and pose health risks to people nearby.
Typically, cow waste from lagoons is applied to land, converted into biogas or trucked away.
Learning from Experience
Justin Leyendekker, a 36-year-old dairy farmer in the San Joaquin Valley, counted himself lucky for not having had significant damage when the region flooded in 2023.
“I know one dairy was as deep underwater as like 15 or 20 feet,” said Leyendekker, whose family—back to his grandfather in the 1960s—runs eleven other dairy farms in California.
The experience three years ago was instructive for Leyendekker when considering what extreme rain could bring.
“That gave us an idea of some I guess you could call them ‘weak points’ or ‘maintenance points’ that we needed to take care of. So once I heard the news that we’d potentially be getting another El Niño, those gave me some nice focus points to work on,” Leyendekker said, of Hoppy Cows Dairy, which he’s been running for about a decade and is named for his love of home brewing.
The dairy in Kingsburg, which has about 2,000 cows, has a sizable waste lagoon that fills up to roughly 15 feet deep.
“Each year we try and drain it down to as low as we can go,” said Leyendekker, who noted that El Niño has been extra motivation to keep the lagoon as empty as possible.
Ortiz-Partida said he remains worried that residents in areas adjacent to waste lagoons don’t truly know what’s in store for this winter.
Besides nitrates, he said bacteria, heavy metals and other water contaminants could escape from lagoons at dairies facing more stormy weather and rainfall.
The unknowns—what makes up these pools of waste and where runoff could flow as weather patterns worsen—also concern him. “We don’t know where all that will end up,” he said.
Lewis Bernier, an advocate with Direct Action Everywhere, said the impacts of the winter of 2022-23 have led the grassroots group to prepare for the current El Niño, which should peak over the coming months.
“We’re looking to this winter as well, trying to have response plans ready in advance,” Bernier said. “These open pits of waste are like ticking time bombs of massive amounts of pollutants.”
Dairies in California have been getting ready for El Niño, said Scott Hatton, supervising water resource control engineer for the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board.
The water board, which is providing online resources for dairy farmers, requires them to submit a report in the event any waste discharge could threaten human health or the environment. They are also required to inform the board if cattle need to be moved to higher ground, Hatton said.
“The Water Boards are preparing for a very heavy rainfall year, with significant flood concerns,” Hatton said in an email to Inside Climate News. “We are encouraging all dischargers to review their storm and flood preparedness … The dairy industry, in particular, has sent out suggested guidelines in a recent newsletter.”

d0d3c1b9bf0c.text: The White House is dropping Heidi Overton 's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA as HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks to advance his Make America Healthy Again agenda. "FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation," a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday. Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August. She had drawn criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine Kennedy agenda. Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone. The backstory: Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee. Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying." What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said. The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation. What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday. The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

7450cf1497b4.text: A string of major technology failures is raising new questions about the reliability and security of systems millions of Americans depend on every day. The incidents are said to be unrelated, but their timing has fueled concerns about whether something more is at work. Geoff Bennett discussed the wave of disruptions with Eric O'Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative. Amna Nawaz: A string of major technology failures is raising new questions about the reliability and security of systems that millions of Americans depend on every day. The latest incident involved the NSA, or National Security Agency, which said its own internal systems were affected by an outage today. The NSA said it happened as part of routine maintenance and did not affect security operations. But several news reports said the outage involved a classified internal network. Geoff Bennett: And this was the latest in a series of high-profile problems. In just the past week, a Microsoft outage last Thursday disrupted services around the world. On Friday, a nationwide ground stop by the FAA brought air travel to a halt. And, yesterday, United Airlines experienced a separate outage, while customers of several major banks, including Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, reported problems accessing their accounts. The incidents are said to be unrelated, but their timing has fueled concerns about whether something more is at work. Homeland security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in an interview last night dismissed suggestions of a coordinated cyberattack, instead blamed artificial intelligence. Markwayne Mullin: So I started talking to the tech industry, and one guy that's very smart with tech -- he asked not to mention his name -- no, it's not, Elon, so let me just put that out. But I said, what could be causing all these separate allergies? And he says, I believe that it's the SI. He said, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is. And so when they contribute -- or when they put in a program that's able to write codes and it goes in itself fixes itself, that's a ripple effect. And it causes a systems to be overrun that weren't designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today. Geoff Bennett: But that is far from conclusive. For more on this wave of disruptions, we turn to Eric O'Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative, who's now a cybersecurity executive specializing in cyber threats and national security. Thank for being with us. Eric O'Neill: It's great to be here. Geoff Bennett: So we have seen a remarkable series of technology failures in just the past week. Understanding that, as we sit here and speak, there are more questions than answers still, what do we know about what's behind these disruptions? And is there any evidence that these are connected in any way? Eric O'Neill: Right. So, so far, no evidence that they are connected, other than there is a massive coincidence behind this, and I'll get into that as a second. And, unfortunately, we don't know a lot because each of the different organizations and the government agencies that have been brought down by this are being very not forthcoming. So we start with Microsoft, who called it a technical glitch. And then, of course, we have the ATC system, the air traffic control communications system, where one of the 21 nodes suddenly has all of these issues and is communicating erratically, which causes the FAA to ground all flights, which was extraordinary, but probably because they, I would bet they thought it was a cyber attack. They did that under an abundance of caution. Then, the banks -- right after that, on the heels of that, banks start to fail and people can't log in. And then, of course, United comes back and says, we're having problems. I'm really glad I'm not flying this week. And then, finally, the NSA has a problem with one of their classified systems. You put that all together in this string of events -- and there are other companies that, by the way, in all of this have gone down -- and it's too much of a coincidence to say that there might not -- there might be some external factor causing all of these. How confident can investigators be in ruling that out at this stage? How long might it take to determine whether there was a sophisticated intrusion? Eric O'Neill: They can't be confident at all. And, three -- and this might actually be the more likely one -- they will be looking at whether there is a common application, networking tool or technology that these companies in these similar industries use that broke down, went bad, or was attacked by an external threat actor. On Wednesday, the president heads to China for meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. 01fef5d8b5b8.text: In our news wrap Tuesday, international health officials say the United States is no longer considered a measles-free nation, a Harvard study shows cellphone bans in some schools are leading to modest improvements in academic growth among students and maritime monitors say a gas tanker went up in flames in the Strait of Hormuz after it was hit by multiple projectiles. Amna Nawaz: In the day's other headlines: International health officials say the United States is no longer considered a measles-free nation. In a virtual briefing today, the Pan American Health Organization said endemic measles outbreaks in the U.S., along with Mexico and Bolivia, signaled the reemergence of a disease that was once seen as controlled. Dr. Jarbas Barbosa (through interpreter): Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world. Measles' elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf. It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community. Amna Nawaz: The measles elimination status is largely symbolic. Still, the Pan American Health Organization said it expects the three nations to submit plans in the coming weeks on how they will try to stop transmission for at least a year. Measles have been spreading in the U.S. at the highest rate in more than 30 years, mostly among the unvaccinated. Today, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz stressed the importance of vaccination. Cell phone bans in some U.S. schools are leading to -- quote -- "modest improvements" in academic growth among students. That's according to a new study led by Harvard University. The report says strict cell phone bans, like using lockable pouches, restore the equivalent of one to two weeks of learning each year. But that's only about half the annual decline in test scores we have seen over the past decade or so. The study is the first nationwide assessment of its kind, analyzing math and reading scores of more than three million students at some 4,600 schools. Turning now to the war in Iran, maritime monitors say a gas tanker went up in flames today in the Strait of Hormuz after it was hit by multiple projectiles. The crew had to abandon ship after it was engulfed by an inferno off the coast of Oman. Separately, Bahrain says it intercepted a flurry of Iranian drones that were headed toward a U.S. radar facility. U.S. Central Command reported no damage or injuries. In the meantime, a third carrier group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is now in the region, even as concerns linger over long deployments. Appearing in front of the Senate Armed Services Committee today, President Trump's pick to lead the Navy, current Acting Secretary Hung Cao, addressed a prior deployment, the USS Lincoln, which saw a number of suicide attempts during its record-setting time at sea. Hung Cao: I did answer those inquiries right away, especially with the mental health issues. You see it as eight suicide attempts. I see it as eight suicide mitigations because of the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists. Amna Nawaz: Cao also acknowledged the Iran war's strain on Navy resources, but insisted that joint operations with other U.S. military branches have sent a message to adversaries like China. In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his country's drones and missiles hit a bridge linking Russia with the occupied Crimean Peninsula, calling the attack unprecedented. The 12-mile Kerch Bridge is a vital artery for moving Russian military supplies to the front line. Video released by Ukraine's security service shows drones hitting the bridge. Military officials say part of its road link was severed, though a railway line remains intact. A Kremlin spokesperson says the bridge will be restored. In the meantime, Russia fired missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two bridges there and killing at least two people. In corporate news, Nvidia beat expectations in its first earnings report since CEO Jensen Huang stepped down. The AI giant reported revenues of nearly $116 billion in the last quarter, more than double what it made a year earlier. And the company's expecting even higher revenues in the current quarter. Those results came after the closing bell on Wall Street. Before that, stocks struggled once again, with the Dow Jones industrial average dropping by nearly 850 points. The Nasdaq fell by almost three-quarters-of-a-percent. The S&P 500 posted its lowest close since July. And on Australia's Christmas Island, tens of millions of red crabs have begun their annual migration in one of nature's most unique and stunning sites. Dubbed the Ruby Red Rush Hour, the crabs make their way from the forest to the ocean to breed. Local authorities say the exact timing and speed of the migration is determined by the phases of the moon. Officials clear roads and even build bridges to help ensure a smooth journey. Naturalist David Attenborough has described it as a -- quote -- "great scarlet curtain, moving down the cliffs and rocks towards the sea." Couldn't have said it better of ourselves.

41201adbe721.text: The Trump administration is seeking $50 billion to modernize the nation's air traffic control system following last week's massive nationwide ground stop. But the proposal could face resistance in Congress, where lawmakers are raising questions about the cost and how the money would be spent. Congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins breaks down the price tag and the political hurdles ahead. Geoff Bennett: The Trump administration is seeking $50 billion to modernize the nation's air traffic control system following last week's massive nationwide ground stop. But the proposal could face resistance in Congress, where lawmakers are raising questions about the cost and how that money would be spent. Our congressional correspondent, Lisa Desjardins, joins us now to break down the price tag and the political hurdles ahead. So, Lisa, how did Secretary Duffy, how is he explaining this $50 billion he's seeking and his decision-making over the weekend with this ground stop? Lisa Desjardins: He has been calling some congressional leaders and he had lunch today with Senate Republicans. He again reiterated that it is was a faulty router made by Juniper Networks that was to blame. However, he and the FAA administrator told the press today they're not sure exactly why that router misfired. They have taken this report, and they have gone forward and shut down all of the Juniper Network routers in the system so far. As to that ground stop, he defended that decision. He said it was critical for safety. Sean Duffy: I get like it was hard for people. But I would rather have that story than the other story that we didn't do our job, and we let risk into the system, but we kept flying, because then all of you would say, why didn't you shut it down? Why didn't you make that decision? Lisa Desjardins: Now he is trying to encourage Congress to make a different decision, which, as you say, is fund $50 billion. We were one of the first outlets to get a copy of that proposal for Congress. It's just two pages, look at that, but $50 billion. Here's what the secretary wants, $20 billion, first of all, for new terminals and upgrades at some airports around the country, $10 billion for air traffic control towers, and some computing needs. Some of that is needed for that fiber copper wire switch, $10 billion for five air route traffic centers. Those are the centers that handle flights as they are overhead at high altitudes. This is a large ask. This is $50 billion, and it is also a late ask, because this Congress is getting ready to close down for its session. Geoff Bennett: So what's been the response from lawmakers so far? Lisa Desjardins: Yes. Talking to Republicans coming out of that luncheon, they all said universally that they actually do trust Secretary Duffy. I didn't sense that he has a threat from them. He still has their trust. However, they all have a lot of skepticism about this request. One senator told me he thought airlines should be paying for all of this. Another, Senator Kennedy of Louisiana, said he thinks that airports should not be something that the federal government is paying to improve. Geoff Bennett: Meantime, this Congress is in its final weeks. It's a lame-duck session. What remains on their to-do list? Lisa Desjardins: Oh, boy, it's a pretty hefty lift. And as you and I speak, Congress is getting ready to leave this week and won't be back until December. Then they will just have a few weeks left. Let's look at what's on that list, some big-time stuff, including, oh, keeping government funded. The deadline for that is December 10. And I have to tell you, Geoff, there are some real red flags going up that we could be in a situation for a potential shutdown. So we will be watching this very carefully. In addition to that, Congress needs to pass the next defense authorization bill. That usually is done each year, usually bipartisan. We will see. Then, after that, Republicans have a big wish list, another reconciliation bill, where they will hopefully get some agenda items in before they're out of power. But I have to tell you, I just don't see the serious discussions happening yet for them to get all that done, especially that reconciliation bill, in time. Geoff Bennett: And, Lisa, while we have you, what is the latest with the midterms? Lisa Desjardins: Right. Geoff Bennett: What races remain to be called at this hour? Lisa Desjardins: Such a fascinating election. Let's start with the House of Representatives. There was even a new race called today. And where Democrats stand right now, you can see 257 seats. They have picked up a seat in North Carolina today. You see those seven yellow dots? Those are the races that remain to be called. Of those, three of them right now are looking like they will be Democratic flips. So we're talking 260 or above for Democrats. Let's go look at the Senate. And you have just one yellow dot there at the bottom. That, of course, is the state of Alaska, where our friends at Alaska Public Media have had one of the longest election seasons in years. But, Geoff, that could end tomorrow. Mary Peltola has been picking up votes, and she is poised to end this election tomorrow with 50 percent. Tomorrow is the day Alaska will decide whether it needs to go to ranked-choice voting or, if she has 50 percent, she will be the winner. Geoff Bennett: Lisa Desjardins, thanks, as always. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

543f81bba06a.text: Almost two years after leaving office, former President Joe Biden has penned a memoir about his time in the White House. “Promise Me, America,” is out, but Biden isn’t out doing the typical run of media interviews. Amna Nawaz discussed more with his former counselor, Steve Ricchetti. Amna Nawaz: Almost two years after leaving office, President Joe Biden has penned a memoir about his time in the White House. It's called "Promise Me, America." And it's out today. But the former president isn't doing the typical run of media interviews. Earlier today, I spoke with his former counselor, Steve Ricchetti, and began by asking him why he was here on Biden's behalf. Steve Ricchetti: Well, he's had to limit what he's doing in terms of a book tour and things like that, because, I think as you know and has been widely reported, he has a stage 4 cancer diagnosis. He got that last May. And so he's working his way through the part of this where he still gets pretty heavy doses of medication to help manage the cancer. It's -- it moved into his bones, so there's some pain and discomfort with it, and frankly, even affects his energy level. So he's not going out in the way that I think he would really like to with a kind of traditional book tour, and so a number of us who worked closely with him are going to try to share some of the load and do it. Amna Nawaz: You have known him for so long. You know him so well. He writes in the book, too, about the span of his career. He says: "I was elected to the Senate as a 29-year-old kid. I left the presidency as an 82-year-old man. I have seen the long sweep of history." You say he wants the book to speak for itself. So what is it he hopes to accomplish by putting it out at this time? Steve Ricchetti: He wanted to do this close enough to his presidency, his time in office, that he could speak with -- and remember the events and talk through what he experienced because it was still fresh in his mind. He waited until after the midterms because I think he didn't want the book to be the subject of what the political dialogue was for the midterm elections. He wanted this to be and, as it was, a referendum in many ways on President Trump's first two years in office. So it was timed to follow the midterms, but to be close to his presidency enough that he could talk about it in the ways that he had, very completely and thoroughly. Amna Nawaz: I mean, it is very thorough. It's incredibly comprehensive. Reading through it, I was reminded of all these stories that we covered, the chaos he stepped into in the pandemic, after the January 6 insurrection, all the legislative efforts I know you were deeply involved in, from the American Rescue Plan to the Infrastructure Act, the CHIPS Act, rallying NATO after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. All of these are detailed in the book. And yet, as I'm sure you have seen, it is his decision to run again that's getting a lot of attention as people are making their way through the book. He writes about that in the book. He says: "I believe I was the best person to do it, the only person who'd ever beaten Donald Trump. I felt I was the best person to do it again." I'm sure you have seen, as folks read this, one journalist in particular called his reflection on this "pugnacious, unrepentant, and unreflective." What do you make of that? Steve Ricchetti: I just don't think that's a fair criticism of the book, for the reasons that you just said. I do think it is now hard to remember. Maybe there's even some kind of psychological effect from what we went through during COVID, but that we forget that he really inherited as severe a set of challenges as any president in our lifetime. There really were three crises in our country. There was an international pandemic. Hundreds of thousands of people had died of COVID on January -- by January 20 of 2021. We were in an -- the economy was flat on its back. We were in an economic crisis. And, again, what you just pointed out that people have forgotten, it was two weeks after the January 6 attack on the Capitol. And, really, the heart of our... (CROSSTALK) Amna Nawaz: ... he was sworn into office. Steve Ricchetti: Yes, and the heart of our democracy was on the line, the institution of the presidency, respect for other branches of government. There was so much at stake in that first year of his presidency just to restore a sense of confidence and respect for the presidency itself and to reaffirm our reputation and role in the world. Amna Nawaz: And yet, since then, as you know, the party is still sort of reckoning with that decision of how his candidacy for reelection ended, what happened in the wake of that... Steve Ricchetti: Yes. Amna Nawaz: ... President Trump's reelection. And I have to ask, because I didn't see it in the book, but, in hindsight, as you know him and you speak to him, has there been any reflection on maybe I should not have run again, maybe this should not have taken a disastrous debate or an intraparty feud? Has that ever been part of the conversation? Because it's not in the book. Steve Ricchetti: It's not because, in April of 2023, when he made the decision to run again, it was a pretty straightforward equation in his mind. We believed we were making progress in the country. There was no question that we had, the country had endured real difficulty, real challenge. His leadership through that period of time, in his mind and in my mind and in the mind of those around him, we just believed we were making progress. We knew there were still challenges ahead and work to be done, certainly more work to be done with respect to the economy and prices. And he believed he was healthy and more prepared than anyone to take the next step and to lead the country for four more years. Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.
From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."
Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (Â£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.
This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eï¬ects.
The power grid death spiral
The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".
"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.
Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.
When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
Pakistan's government says the costs are already being felt.
"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [Â£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."
The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.
Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.
Leghari wants the country to run on "up to 90% clean power" by the end of 2036 - including renewables and nuclear - with dependence on imported energy reducing from 26% to 4%.
Solar-powered business
But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.
Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.
When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.
But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.
"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.
"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."
Critics accuse the government of moving the goalposts on solar power. Previously, households could feed excess electricity into the grid and earn credits, which were then used to offset the cost of grid power when the sun wasn't shining. That policy changed earlier this year.
"Initially their policy was very helpful," says Arif Ehsan Malik, president of Faisalabad's chamber of commerce. "But then the policy changed. Now they have started purchasing at a lower rate and selling back at a higher rate."
Malik says that makes a big difference for small and medium businesses. Leghari counters that the costs of the initial model didn't add up; the electricity the solar producers put into the system was much cheaper than the electricity they ended up taking out of it.

283fe6bc74ea.text: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions in one year than the entire nation of Denmark, according to a new report from Harvard University. From May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2% of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of CO2. Amna Nawaz spoke with the study's lead author, Gianluca Guidi. Amna Nawaz: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions into the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark. That's according to a new report from Harvard University. The study found that, from May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2 percent of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, a level two or three times higher than an earlier estimate in 2018. I'm joined now by the lead author of that study, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, welcome to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Gianluca Guidi: Yes, thank you for having me. Hello, everyone. Amna Nawaz: So, what was most surprising to you from this report? What really stood out to you in the way of the findings? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. So think about it, right? So Denmark is an entire country, and with millions of people, homes, hospitals, and industries. And we're talking about, like, comparable annual carbon emissions from just 403 data centers. So those are just like 400 buildings. And that's an extraordinary scale. And those facilities are just only a fraction of the industry and how the industry looks like right now. Amna Nawaz: You point out in the report too you weren't even able to capture all of the information from many data centers. So what do we not yet know about the impact that they could be having? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's a great question. The study dates back like -- it's almost a year-old by now. And since then, there's been, like, an incredible build-out. We have preliminary results of newer studies that tells us there are around 1,000 hyperscale data centers. So that's just more than the double of what we reported in our study. Amna Nawaz: So many more data centers, meaning the numbers in here, in actuality, now the scope of emissions could be much higher than your report suggests. Is that correct? Gianluca Guidi: That is correct. Yes, that is correct. And together with the emissions, you have the water consumption and potentially also public health consequences. So, in a way, we have that a technology that is actually moving faster than our ability to understand its consequences. Amna Nawaz: Tell us more about that, the intersection of the build-out of these data centers and the impact on public health. What are you finding there? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. In this specific study, we haven't addressed yet the public health, but what's happening basically is that, once you have a powered demand and a power that is produced at the power plant level, not only you're producing, we're producing carbon emissions, but we're also producing hazardous pollutants that travel and eventually somebody breathes them, and the effects for the health are pretty dangerous. And there's plenty and ton of scientific research about this. Amna Nawaz: The power pull as well when we talk about the power use in -- of these data centers, there are states you point out, like Virginia, Iowa, Oregon, and Ohio that account for half of the electricity use. Why is that and what kind of downstream impacts does that have for residents in the area? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's correct. So, basically, the states offer the infrastructure, the land and the electricity that large data centers need. But there's a catch. So the benefits of these expansion aren't necessarily felt by the same communities that bear its environmental costs. So, more electricity demands can mean more power plans and, therefore, as we're saying, more pollution and more pressure on local infrastructure. So those consequences don't stop at the data center's fence. Amna Nawaz: There are those who will argue, Gianluca, I'm sure you have heard, that we need to build out these AI data centers, that the country has to do it to remain competitive, that it's necessary for our economy, for national security, and that the impact of that on the environment or for residents in the area is a necessary evil, in other words. Would you agree with that? Is that -- can that argument be made? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, I see that, and there's a big backlash happening right now. I wouldn't call them like a necessary evil. I mean, I am an AI researcher myself, and I have to say I'm really excited about this technology and what it can do. but there are better ways to build it, so -- that might cost more, they might take longer. The question is whether we're willing to prioritize doing it right over doing it first. Amna Nawaz: The report, as you mentioned, is now several months old, almost a year-old. There are a lot of things you don't address in it. For the average citizen to understand how this might impact their lives, what are the questions you think need to be answered next? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, here's what concerns me the most. We're building this AI infrastructure faster than we can independently understand its consequences. So, our study, as you were saying, was just published, like -- but the data are already over a-year-old. So scientific evidence shouldn't arrive after the infrastructure, and neither should, I believe, the public participation. And the main concerns would be the water consumption, the electricity, so such that putting the power grid into like -- in strain and potentially therefore, as I was saying before, the public health consequences. Amna Nawaz: That is Gianluca Guidi of Harvard. He's a postdoctoral research fellow there focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, thank you so much for your time. It's good

Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown visited for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Jeffrey Brown: A late afternoon walk through farmland in rural North Dakota, for artist Christine Kirouac, a chance to get away from the distractions of everyday life and do her work. Christine Kirouac: It forces you to be alone, really alone, and alone with yourself and alone with your thoughts and alone with the corn and alone with the corn and alone with the soybeans. Jeffrey Brown: Alone with the corn. (LAUGHTER) Christine Kirouac: Alone with the corn. Jeffrey Brown: Because there's a lot of it. Christine Kirouac: There's a lot of corn. Jeffrey Brown: Indeed, there is a lot of corn on the endless prairie in this area. But less known, there's also art making in an old house in McCanna set amid a tree-lined oasis. Kirouac was here to work as part of an artists residency program. What are the particular struggles for you in this region? Christine Kirouac: I think visibility is definitely one of them, but the representation of Manitoba or prairie artists can be lacking in terms of exposure. Jeffrey Brown: The residency is run by the North Dakota Museum of Art, some 35 miles east in Grand Forks on the campus of the University of North Dakota. Museum director Matthew Wallace … Matthew Wallace: We're not MoMA. We're not LACMA. We're just a little museum in the eastern side of North Dakota, just doing what we can do. But also I think that gives us some freedom to do whatever we want to. We don't have someone looking down our shoulders, and we just kind of roll with what we want to do. The building was a women's gymnasium, and we moved in here. For Wallace, this is personal. He was raised on a ranch in rural North Dakota, feeling far from any art center. Matthew Wallace: Growing up knowing that I didn't have access to these kinds of opportunities, that it was something that I really wanted to jump on board with and make available to communities that were interested in participating. Jeffrey Brown: He first came to work at the museum on one of its signature programs, creating small art exhibitions and bringing them into near and far rural parts of the state. Matthew Wallace: You know, the conditions are not museum conditions. Jeffrey Brown: Right. Matthew Wallace: So, we could be... Jeffrey Brown: Probably is put it mildly. Matthew Wallace: Yes, yes, I mean, we -- I have installed exhibitions in an empty tire store, a Masonic temple, a church, a community center. Once in a while, we will we would get an actual gallery. Its recent exhibition Material Abstractions featured works by artists using a wide variety of materials from South Africa, Los Angeles, and points all over. Curator Anna Sigridur Arnar … Anna Sigridur Arnar: I kind of like, juxtaposing those different kind of -- think about geographic diversity. Lee, who grew up in Grand Forks and now lives in Seattle. She returned to her home state in 2014 to document the impact of the fracking oil boom. Each column, says Arnar, is a kind of drill core, also with details representing an individual worker. Anna Sigridur Arnar: I think it can be a game changer. Having a solo exhibition in a museum is kind of the creme de la creme. And it will open doors, and I love being a part of that. Micah Bloom, Artist: For the past 15 or so years of being here in North Dakota... Jeffrey Brown: Micah Bloom, who teaches at Minot State University, was the first art maker to have an exhibition featuring work that captured losses in the 2011 catastrophic Minot flood, including books found in the most unlikely places. His 2015 show included large installations and other works that he says he would never otherwise have been able to make an exhibit. Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/china-and-canada-expand-tariff-relief-while-relations-with-the-u-s-are-strained Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China and Canada expand tariff relief while relations with the U.S. are strained World Nov 17, 2026 6:20 PM EST SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The leaders of China and Canada agreed Tuesday on additional tariff cuts as they pledged for deeper ties and Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States. READ MORE: U.S. and China release product lists for tariff cuts after Trump-Xi meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties. Carney's office said in a statement that the new measures extend and expand an earlier agreement between the countries. Under the agreement, China will provide additional tariff relief on Canadian exports worth around 400 million Canadian dollars ($280 million), including frozen pork cuts, fish and seafood. In return, Canada will extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years. The meeting between the leaders came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry. "Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity," said Xi. "This is the right choice." Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is "greater predictability and stability" in their relationship. "The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems," he said. Carney added that his country is ahead of schedule in its plan to increase exports to China by 50% by the end of the decade. Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 6cf874e5b096.text: What secrets might a 194-year-old tortoise have for humans when it comes to living longer? William Brangham examines the remarkable life of Jonathan. Amna Nawaz: Finally tonight, what secrets might 194-year-old tortoise have for humans when it comes to living longer? Geoff Bennett: William Brangham examines the remarkable life of a much-loved tortoise. William Brangham: It's lunchtime for Jonathan. Man: And he gets the freshest produce. William Brangham: Jonathan is perhaps the most famous resident of the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he's lived for most of his 194 years. Dr. Stephen Clark, Kallel Foundation: And he was born before the telegraph was invented. He was born before the lightbulb was invented. He was born before the telephone was invented. When Abraham Lincoln died, he was 33 years old. William Brangham: Remarkably, after nearly two centuries, Jonathan remains in relatively good health, says neurologist and longevity expert Dr. Stephen Clark. Clark recently led an examination of the earth's oldest living land animal. Dr. Stephen Clark: He is blind. He has cataracts in both eyes, but he's very mobile, and still has a very good appetite, and is very social still. So, we expect he could live quite some more time, for sure. William Brangham: How did you land on the idea of -- that Jonathan would be a useful subject to study? Dr. Stephen Clark: Well, first of all, Jonathan's kind of accessible. So a lot of the long-lived species, like the bowhead whale and the Greenland shark, are kind of difficult to get to. And so knowing Jonathan was on the island was critical, and we could get access to him. And then we wanted to get a blood draw, but the island is very protective of Jonathan because he's very famous on the island. And so they wouldn't allow us to do a blood draw, so we had to do a buckle scrape of his -- of the inside of his mouth. So that's how we got the samples initially is, we actually did a buckle scrape of his mouth. William Brangham: Giant tortoises can live 150 years or more on average, but few reliable historical or medical records about them exist, and many of them outlive the researcher studying them. And what is it, practically speaking, that you're hoping to glean from Jonathan that could be applicable to humans and longevity? Dr. Stephen Clark: Yes, so that what really Jonathan represented is the first time we were able to really look at a difference between two different individuals over 200 years. So we compared him to a 5-year-old tortoise. The secret we have sort of identified with him is, he seems to have somehow been able to keep his mitochondria very young. And the mitochondria are sort of like the powerhouses of the cell. They provide the energy for the cell. They also provide energy for all the repair that's done for the genome. And so by keeping his mitochondria young, we think it's allowed him to repair his genome over 190 years. And so that was really the kind of surprising finding that we found with Jonathan. William Brangham: Do you think that this research and all the other research that is ongoing in this field, do you think we are on the cusp of extending human life in a meaningful way? Dr. Stephen Clark: So there have been predictions about what the maximum lifespan is for humans, and those predictions have ranged from 115 years old to 122 years old. I'm a believer and the nonprofit that I work with is a believer that we can increase current health lifespan at least closer to that. Going beyond that, I think it's going to require a lot more knowledge about the biology of aging. But I think the increasing average health span and lifespan to around 100, I think, is very doable in the near future. William Brangham: In their study published in "Science" this fall, Clark and his colleagues wrote -- quote -- "These investigations have deepened our understanding of gene markers that potentially slow aging and inhibit cancer in these species." In the meantime, one easy lesson from Jonathan... Man: He does love his carrots. William Brangham: ... slow down and enjoy a good meal in the sun. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham. Geoff Bennett: The secret to a long life, taking it slow. Amna Nawaz: Ba-dum-bum.

cd81011a0f9c.text: Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward. Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital . What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said on at the end of conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this." She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added. In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds . Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world." CoreWeave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each ose by more than 10% in after-hours trading. Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly. Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said. The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make." Catch-up quick: Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence. She was also a major Nvidia customer and helped Chinese AI companies gain access to cutting-edge Nvidia technology while the U.S. had banned some chip sales to the country. On the call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones through cold water on the notion of a quick return for Huang . "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said. The company said it wouldn't be taking questions on Huang's departure or its ongoing investigation into his actions.
