Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.
The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.
It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.
It is the ninth Senate seat the Democrats have taken from Republicans in the midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
The Democrats also won back the House of Representatives, the lower chamber.
Peltola defeated the incumbent Republican senator, Dan S Sullivan, who is yet to comment.
In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".
She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.
Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate, and is the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Alaska since 2008.
Donald Trump won the state by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but defeat for the Republicans in this year's US Senate race in the state caps off a string of losses in the midterms for the president's party.
Many voters across the United States cited cost-of-living issues as a factor that affected how they cast their ballots.
Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times, external reported that her team worked with people who tried to recruit so-called spoiler candidates in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.
The alleged scheme led to a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan - a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan - contesting the race.
After legal challenges, state courts ruled that Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.
Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the US justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.
The Trump administration also filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.
A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.
Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could have simply chosen both men, listing them as their first and second choices.
If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would have re-allocated any votes from Daniel J Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to Dan S Sullivan.
Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.
An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for Daniel J Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, Peltola would still have won.
The Democratic win in Alaska cements the party's majority in the US Senate, as the party now has 56 seats to the Republicans' 44.
The most senior Democrat in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, said Peltola had run "a pitch-perfect campaign devoted to the issues Alaskans care most about". Hailing the Democrats' final tally in the Senate, he said: "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago."
The Alaska seat was initially one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the US Senate. But by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50% of the votes, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.
Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.
"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.
"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

ec035efde6d9.text: A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock , breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders. Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime. Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans, allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed. Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks. The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. In a separate report Friday , Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks. Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex. Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector. CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month. Reality check : Cyberattacks are still scary and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks. A litany of popular services — including Microsoft , Apple , Chase , United , Workday , the Federal Aviation Administration , the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last week. An unknown group infected about 178 major websites with crypto-stealing malware through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform in less than a day, according to Report URI . Affected websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, Gitlab and Ikea, and AI doesn't seem to be involved as of now. What they're saying: "We're seeing more active attacks than ever right now," Sam Rubin, senior vice president of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 threat intelligence and consulting unit, told Axios. "The open-weight models are getting close to frontier-level capabilities," and when combined with tools like Artex and Cairn, they are "really hitting organizations hard," he added. Incident response firms worldwide are stretched to capacity, with some turning away cases because they lack resources, John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google's threat intelligence group, told Axios. How it works: Artex and Cairn use AI agents to automate tasks hackers traditionally performed themselves. A hacker gives the framework a target and an objective, such as breaking into a company's network. AI agents develop attack plans, search for vulnerabilities and use hacking tools to test possible entry points. The agents share findings and adjust tactics when something fails, allowing them to operate around the clock without constant human supervision. Between the lines: Hackers are also stealing the computing resources needed to sustain their AI-powered attacks. Amazon's findings show how attackers can steal access to AI models and use that access to find more credentials, expanding their operations without paying for the computing power. The intrigue: These frameworks aren't necessarily good at hiding their activity, but that might not matter. Hultquist said autonomous attacks generate substantial suspicious activity, potentially making them easier to detect. But financially motivated hackers may only need to steal valuable information before defenders stop them. He also warned that state-backed hackers could use these capabilities to disrupt critical systems before defenders can intervene. What to watch: Security teams may need to fundamentally change their defenses to keep pace with automated attacks.

24690346eb13.text: Mary Peltola's path to Senate history ran through four Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide first-choice lead. Why it matters: The Yup'ik Democrat is the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, powered by communities that endured disenfranchisement, forced displacement and federal violence. The win amplifies their voice on tribal sovereignty and subsistence rights after decades of neglect and discrimination — much as Mississippi Delta Black voters powered Democrat Scott Colom to his surprising Senate victory. By the numbers: Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 12,400 first-choice votes statewide in Alaska's Nov. 17 unofficial count . Four western and northern House districts delivered a combined margin of about 6,700 votes. In Bristol Bay/Aleutians , for example, Peltola led by roughly 1,150 votes. In Bethel/Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Western Alaska/Norton Sound , she led by roughly 2,300 votes. In North Slope/Northwest Arctic , she led by approximately 900 votes. Stunning stat: Those four districts accounted for just about 5% of Alaska's first-choice Senate votes, but roughly 55% of Peltola's statewide lead. Alaska's 2021 redistricting report identifies Districts 37–40 as Alaska Native-controlled. Alaska Natives, alone or in combination, accounted for 85.8% of the voting-age population in District 38, 85.1% in 39, 62% in 40 and 43.8% in 37, using 2020 census figures. About 22% of Alaska residents identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or in combination with another race, according to the 2020 census . State of play: Peltola carried the 50% margin needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation , where lower-ranked preferences from other candidates' supporters could have tipped the race toward another candidate. Michelle Sparck of the nonpartisan Get Out the Native Vote effort told KNBA that Native groups mounted aggressive outreach, including in Native languages. Organizers saw gains in some rural communities, though definitive statewide turnout comparisons remain pending. Zoom in: In Kwethluk, the Yup'ik village where Peltola grew up, she outpolled Sullivan 136–9. In Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island , she led 157–5. In Tlingit communities Angoon and Kake , she led 109–22 and 140–30, respectively. The Navy apologized in 2024 for destroying Angoon in 1882 and bombarding and burning Kake in 1869 . Flashback: In 1915, Alaska's territorial lawmakers required Native citizenship applicants to abandon tribal ties and customs. In 1925, after Congress extended citizenship to Native Americans, Alaska imposed an English literacy requirement that disenfranchised many Native voters. During World War II, the U.S. removed 881 Unangax̂ people from nine villages to Southeast Alaska camps plagued by disease and poor shelter. The intrigue: In April 1969, Sen. Ted Kennedy traveled 3,600 miles over three days through Native communities, following a poverty tour his slain brother Robert had planned. TIME documented villages with 60% unemployment and homes without plumbing, comparing the trip to Robert's visits to Appalachia and the Mississippi Delta. Partisan accusations over publicity overshadowed the poverty Kennedy sought to expose. Yes, but: Alaska Native voters today don't vote as a bloc. The Alaska Federation of Natives endorsed no one in the Senate race. And district returns can't establish how individual Native voters voted — or prove a statewide turnout surge. Between the lines: In communities covered by the EPA's Alaska Native Villages data, 1,129 homes lacked drinking water, wastewater service or both in 2025, down from 6,892 in 2005, per an EPA report . Native leaders continue pressing Washington on subsistence rights, infrastructure, education and self-determination.

ST. LOUIS — The teen’s hospital stay began in room 3005.
The room didn’t feel like home at first. Back then, Jaloni didn’t have posters on the wall or snacks on the shelf, and he hadn’t learned about the morgue yet.
He just wanted to survive. Fresh gunshot wounds filled the 14-year-old’s body with unbearable pain. That first night, Jaloni said, he could barely move.
But in his own way, Jaloni could fly. His pain medication was so strong that the teenager said he felt like he was soaring in a dream.
In reality, though, Jaloni was a teenager caught between two worlds. Around his friends he had been a fearless risk-taker who knew how to steal without getting caught. Inside the hospital, Jaloni was now a boy who needed his grandmother to tell him that everything would be OK and that somehow life would get better as soon as he was released from the hospital.
But she couldn’t make that promise. No one could.
He ended up staying in the SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital for more than 475 days over the next three years, his medical records show. Some of that time was not because he needed the hospital’s medical care but because he had no safe place to go. The now-18-year-old asked KFF Health News to use only nicknames or first names to protect his family’s safety.
Like thousands of children throughout the country, Jaloni experienced what is called a social stay. The practice also known as hospital boarding, in which children remain in hospitals “beyond medical necessity,” has become a costly and intractable issue nationwide.
A shortage of suitable foster care homes can mean children with mental health issues, chronic physical conditions, or disabilities that require special accommodations get stuck in hospitals. One study from Minnesota found that boarding a child with a complex medical condition in a hospital cost about $3,932 a day in 2017.
It is not clear how much of Jaloni’s hospitalization was beyond what was medically necessary or how much those extra days in the hospital cost. The hospital system declined to comment on the details of Jaloni’s stay. In a statement, SSM Health spokesperson Liz Sharpe-Taylor said that the health system is committed to its “mission of serving those who are in need” and that when “patients remain hospitalized due to an absence of discharge options, hospitals like ours often bear a burden of extensive uncompensated costs.”
In the past five years, state records show, Missouri has spent more than $64.7 million boarding children in state custody in hospitals because they had nowhere else to go. But Missouri Hospital Association spokesperson Dave Dillon said that’s a substantial undercount of the problem and that hospitals often don’t always have staff to log and request reimbursement for housing children.
And those numbers also don’t account for the toll that living in this limbo takes on the kids.
‘Well, Y’all Almost Killed Him’
Jaloni slept a lot during his first stint at the hospital, starting in June 2023. Bullets had pierced his right arm and the right side of his chest, cutting through his torso. He was glad to be alive.
The teen already knew a lot about death — he had been surrounded by it. An older sister died after getting shot, as did his 17-year-old brother. He’d lost a few cousins to gun violence, as well, in and around St. Louis.
He had continued to walk in the shadow of death for the next few years. “It was a lot of dying going on,” Jaloni recalled. “People were dropping like flies.”
He didn’t want his name added to that list. But he came close one summer evening when the war happening in his community erupted in a gunfight. He was injured, and a 22-year-old died. A 16-year-old was charged in the death.
“I felt like I was Superman with my gun,” Jaloni said. “But when you get older, you realize that it’s just stupid.”
In the hospital, Jaloni tried to focus on healing from the bullet wounds and what his doctors said was a spinal cord injury. After three weeks, he was discharged to a rehabilitation facility, then he was sent home.
There his mother and grandmother struggled with caring for the teen, who now needed a wheelchair.
His grandmother, who had been his legal guardian since he was little, was a double amputee and in a wheelchair herself. His mother was juggling his care and her job as a paid caregiver for another family. Changing Jaloni’s bandages, cooking, cleaning, and turning him every four hours as instructed to prevent bedsores was just too much for anyone to handle, his mother said she repeatedly told hospital officials.
“I just couldn’t take care of him anymore,” said his mother, Quette. “It was something that I was not ready for.”
She said she begged hospital officials for assistance that never arrived. Jaloni was in bad shape with what seemed like an infection on the November day they called 911 for help. He had bedsores. He felt sick and weak.
Jaloni then found himself back at Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital, less than five months after he’d been released.
“They were like, ‘Well, y’all almost killed him,’” his mom recalled officials telling her.
The family was accused of neglect. Because they lived just across the river from St. Louis in Illinois, Jaloni became a ward of that state.
That meant he couldn’t go home to his mother and grandmother. Jaloni’s mother thought about asking her ex-boyfriend to watch over her son. She considered asking other relatives, too. A social worker mentioned the idea of sending Jaloni to a home in Chicago where he could get the kind of attention he needed.
Chicago? “I’m not going,” he recalled thinking.
He wanted to go home, not 300 miles away. So he remained in the hospital while the adults in his life sorted out where he could go.
This time, his hospital stay was longer than anyone could imagine: 250 days.

Trump Administration OKs Native Traditional Healing for Two States’ Medicaid Programs
The Trump administration has approved two states’ requests to expand Medicaid to cover Native American traditional healing practices, even as it prepares to enforce rules that are expected to drop millions of people from the government health insurance program.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced in September that the federal agency had approved traditional healing programs for Utah and Maine. The agency did so through waivers, which give a state permission to pay for certain programs that normally fall outside of Medicaid’s rules.
The move increased to six the number of states with Medicaid waivers for traditional healing, including Arizona, California, New Mexico, and Oregon.
But in California, a sweeping Medicaid waiver that provides federal funding for that state’s traditional healing program, among other things, is set to expire at the end of December. The state’s renewal application was pending with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services as of early November.
In approving Utah’s waiver, CMS wrote that studies have found traditional healthcare practices can reduce symptoms of post-traumatic stress, depression, anxiety, and other mental health issues.
“Emerging evidence supports benefits for physical health functioning and chronic disease symptom management as well,” the approval letter said.
Native health leaders said they are encouraged by the expansion. This way, tribal healthcare can become more aligned with the various Native cultures across the country.
“That’s our goal, to have health within our communities as we define health to be,” said Art Martinez, a commissioner of the Nevada Department of Native American Affairs and member of the Chumash Tribe.
After Kennedy joined the Trump administration in 2025, he pledged to improve Native American access to healthcare through, as a spokesperson put it, “culturally relevant, community-driven solutions.”
Since then, the Trump administration has been limiting Medicaid eligibility. Last year, President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which added work requirements and other eligibility restrictions that are expected to result in approximately 10 million more people than projected going without health coverage, including about 7.5 million in the Medicaid program. Native Americans are exempt from work requirements, though Native health leaders are concerned they will see unmerited disenrollments.
The traditional healing benefit allows Native American health providers to bill Medicaid for practices such as sweat lodge ceremonies and for community events such as canoe journeys.
The canoe journey is used by tribes in the Pacific Northwest to increase community belonging. Since CMS approved Oregon’s traditional healing waiver in 2024, the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde have been eligible for reimbursement for their canoe journeys.
“We’re river people,” said Kelly Rowe, the tribes’ executive director of health services. “We got a lot of our elders out on the water who’d never been in a canoe, and it was like the aha moment, and that’s exactly what good medicine is, you know.”
Though modern Western medicine remains an important part of healthcare, Rowe said, she’s glad to see broader recognition of the importance of tribal cultural traditions as another integral component.
“We’re not just here to give you medicine and exams and Western medicine,” Rowe said. “We’re here to be part of what’s happening in the daily life of the tribe.”
In Utah, the state’s request for traditional healing services included urban Indian health organizations as eligible providers. This helps bring those cultural traditions to people living off-reservation, said Matt Poss, executive director of the Urban Indian Center of Salt Lake.
For those who weren’t born and raised on a reservation, maintaining ties to their culture and traditions can be difficult. Urban Indian health organizations can help fill those gaps.
“Native health is not just going to a clinic and getting a vaccine or seeing your provider,” Poss said. “It’s being connected to community.”
The future of California’s traditional healing program depends on whether CMS renews the Medicaid waiver expiring at the end of December. The waiver covers many areas of health programming besides traditional healing, including programs for people who are homeless or about to leave jail and children with complex medical needs.
CMS sent the state a letter more than 700 pages long directing it to align its Medicaid waiver programs with the federal changes that went into effect in October.
California health officials said the letter clarified that eligibility for Medicaid had been narrowed to certain immigration statuses. In 2024, California opened its Medi-Cal program to all residents, regardless of immigration status, although it has rolled back some coverage benefits amid rising healthcare costs and federal cuts.
Health programs run by tribes have long included what’s considered traditional healing under the federal waivers, Martinez said. However, some tribes have had to scale back their services through the years because they weren’t sustainable without dedicated funding, he said.
Utah didn’t get everything it asked for in its waiver application. CMS rejected the state’s request for the federal government to reimburse 100% of the costs that urban Indian health organizations pay to provide care for Native Americans.
All other tribal health providers, including the Indian Health Service and tribally run health organizations, receive 100% Medicaid reimbursement. According to the National Council of Urban Indian Health, urban Indian health organizations have historically received a minuscule amount of the federal funding allocated for the Indian Health Service. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is facing scrutiny amid the spate of recent technology outages â and his decision to fly to a college football game shortly after last weekâs nationwide ground stop.
This week, Mullin said heâd spoken with an unnamed tech leader who claimed some of the outages were due to issues with AI overloading systems (last week, Mullin also said that the FAA ground stop was due to new technology âoverwhelming the older systemâ).
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Tuesday that thereâs no evidence the issues were the result of a cyberattack or âcoordinated effort by a nation state.â
Mullinâs public comments, coupled with his travel, have prompted quiet criticism from some inside the administration. Mullin is slated to answer questions on Capitol Hill on Wednesday during a House worldwide threats hearing.

House Democrats are all but certain to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker Wednesday morning, setting the stage for a floor vote by the full chamber in January.
Despite some criticism from the left, no formal opposition has emerged to Jeffriesâ bid to become the first Black speaker in US history, and heâs assuaged key constituencies.
Democrats will hold a recorded internal vote â itâs the same procedure used when the House flipped in 2018, but itâs also a way for the leader to force his opponents to go public. The vote will âgive every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned,â Jeffries said.
Democrats will elect a full slate of leaders: the speaker, majority leader, whip, caucus chair, vice chair, and assistant speaker. The only contested race is for vice chair, between Reps. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., and Lauren Underwood, D-Ill.; all other current Democratic leaders are set to jump to their equivalent spots in the majority.
The caucus will elect the rest of its leadership circle on Thursday, including the co-chairs of the caucus messaging arm known as the DPCC. That race is between Reps. Maxwell Frost, D-Fla., Sydney Kamlager-Dove, D-Calif., Eric Sorensen, D-Ill., and Sarah McBride, D-Del.

Capitol Hill is grappling with the prospect of the Food and Drug Administration operating without a Senate-confirmed leader indefinitely, after the White House pulled the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the agency Tuesday night.
Itâd been unclear whether the embattled White House official could get the necessary votes to be confirmed by the Senateâs health committee from lawmakers skeptical of her positions on vaccines, the abortion pill, and flavored vapes.
But Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., asserted after the nomination was dropped that he believed the White House âabandoned a viable confirmation path.â
âPro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administrationâs commitment to life issues,â Cassidy said. âThe Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.â
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, is being weighed as a potential replacement, but there are questions swirling about whether anyone could be confirmed on a compressed timeline before Democrats take power.
Chris Meekins, a Raymond James healthcare analyst who worked at HHS during Trumpâs first term, predicted the FDA will not have a permanent leader anytime soon, a development that âinevitably creates uncertainty.â âHad the White House heeded warnings by many before and after her nomination, they could have avoided this unfortunate outcome,â Meekins said.

A British hacker has been sentenced to six years in a federal prison in the US for conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies via text message phishing, and stealing more than $11.6m (Â£8.8m) in cryptocurrency from individual victims.
Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, started hacking as a teenager and was part of the collective of young hackers known as Scattered Spider, which has been blamed for a string of high profile cyber-crimes.
US prosecutors said the thefts had "severe, life-altering consequences" for victims and showed the growing threat posed by online crime groups.
The sentence brings to an end a years-long international investigation involving authorities in the UK, US, Spain and Canada.
Buchanan admitted taking part in a hacking campaign that began in 2021, when he was 19.
Working from his parents' home, he and other English-speaking hackers in the US and UK targeted employees at major technology and telecommunications companies.
It made them $8m in less than two years, according to US prosecutors.
Buchanan and his hacker gang sent out hundreds of SMS messages to the mobile phones of people who worked for large tech or telecoms companies.
The SMS phishing messages contained links to spoof websites designed to look like legitimate sites of victim companies.
The group used messages like "Hi, your account is due to expire - you need to log in to your work account here immediately or you will lose access to work apps".
The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), and account usernames and passwords.
The boys and young men did it on an industrial scale with Buchanan setting up a Telegram bot to collect all the victims' credentials as the duped workers unwittingly handed over their login details.
For some victim companies, subsequently stolen information included confidential work information, intellectual property, plus account access credentials, names, email addresses, and telephone numbers.
The group then used stolen information and SIM-swapping techniques to target cryptocurrency investors in the United States.
In the largest single theft, prosecutors said one victim lost $1.67m in December 2022.
Overall, authorities calculated that Buchanan and his co-conspirators stole more than $11.6m from victims.
Threatened with a blowtorch
Buchanan was also a victim of cyber-criminals.
In early 2023 his online identity and home address were leaked by rival hackers seeking access to his cryptocurrency.
Cyber security researchers and journalists reported that he was assaulted at his home and threatened with a blowtorch.
"TylerB and his group were highly sophisticated and organised but the violence he and others experienced was a sign of the troubling direction of these online communities of young hackers" says cyber security researcher Allison Nixon from Unit221B.
Buchanan then reportedly fled to Canada to escape further threats before returning home.
In April 2023, officers from Police Scotland searched Buchanan's bedroom after receiving a request from the FBI.
Investigators recovered a device containing the names and addresses of hacking victims, along with cryptocurrency seed phrases and account credentials belonging to at least one victim.
The following month, Buchanan left the UK again.
He was arrested on 31 May 2024 at Palma de Mallorca Airport in Spain while attempting to board a private flight to Naples.
After being extradited to the United States, he remained in custody before being sentenced this week.
In his November 2023 charge, Buchanan was named along with four American men and boys in their twenties and teens for alleged activity linked to the notorious cyber-criminal collective Scattered Spider.
They have all pleaded guilty too and are now serving time in jail.
Two other members of the Scattered Spider group were jailed in the UK in July for various cyber attacks including a disruptive one against Transport for London that caused Â£39m of damage.

Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.
The $60m (Â£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked a political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.
But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.
The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.
Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.
Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.
The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.
While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.
Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.
"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.
He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.
Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.
"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.
But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.
Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.
Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.
"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.
He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.
"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.
Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.
Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.
He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.
"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (Â£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.
The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.
But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".
"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.
He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.
The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.
The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.
Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.
Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin, an economist at the University of Ghana said that while the president's safety was paramount, the timing of the purchase was difficult to justify amid severe austerity measures, high unemployment and widespread infrastructure challenges.
"The timing makes it a bit difficult to understand," he told the BBC, adding that the government should provide a cost-benefit analysis explaining why buying the jet was preferable to leasing one and how the decision serves Ghana's interests.
Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

There are six old oil wells within 150 feet of Brittany and Ryan Mahoney’s first house in the South Fayette neighborhood known as The Berkshires. They didn’t know about any of them.
Why would they?
The thousands of oil and gas wells that still linger underground in this region are often long forgotten up on the surface. Some wells were drilled more than a century ago, and many haven’t produced oil or gas in decades. Some have been plugged with tree trunks. Some are still cavities.
Many don’t pose any immediate health or safety risks, but there’s no easy way for residents to know if a nearby well is leaking gas, fouling groundwater, or otherwise reacting to all the other extraction activities going on underground. It’s especially hard to monitor any of those hazards if you don’t know where the wells are.
That’s why Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette built an interactive map to bring these old ghosts to light. The tool allows you to search any location in the state and look up information about nearby wells, many of which were long since abandoned.
More than a hundred years ago, The Berkshires neighborhood was part of the most prolific oil play in the world, the McDonald Oil Field—so productive that its output was reported in gallons per minute.
Over time, farms have yielded to branching, tree-lined streets that spoke into cul-de-sacs, with names like Windsor Court and Walnut Ridge.
When the Mahoneys started to look for a new, bigger house, they wanted to stay in the neighborhood. In 2012, they learned that a piece of undeveloped land just up the street from where they lived would be going up for sale. It was their chance to build their own home—one that would eventually house their four young children and a restless chocolate lab.

They were told that before they could start building there, someone would come and “cap” an abandoned well just behind the backyard. Brittany Mahoney’s recollection is that someone did. She remembers a truck pulling up and workers clearing a path. That’s all she knows.
The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, which oversees oil and gas wells and is supposed to be called to inspect well plugging activities to ensure they are done right, was never notified of any work being done behind the Mahoneys’ house. Historic maps show two oil wells were drilled less than 50 feet from where a trampoline now stands in the backyard. During a recent visit, a wade through the bushes and trees just past the property line showed no evidence of a well.
“Should I be worried?” Mahoney asked when she saw the dots on a map.
In some ways, she’s ahead of the pack.
“We don’t have any wells here,” a neighbor who answered the door two houses down said, although the interactive map that pulls well locations from DEP data and historical documents shows otherwise.
When Agnes Warner moved to The Berkshires 19 years ago, she could still see horses milling about on farmland across the street.
Abandoned wells? “That was one of the problems that never came up,” she said.
Dots indicating old wells mark six homes on her street, including her own.
If you’re in Pennsylvania, you too might have a dot near your home. In southwestern Pennsylvania, you could have dozens of them. So, what should you do?

Abandoned: The aging oil and gas wells haunting Pennsylvania. This project is a collaboration between Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.
Thanks to its long history of oil and gas exploration, the geology of Western Pennsylvania resembles a huge block of Swiss cheese. From the industry’s beginnings in 1859, when Edwin Drake struck oil less than 70 feet beneath the surface just south of Titusville, to the modern-day fracking boom that launched in 2004, hundreds of thousands of wells have been drilled into the landscape—adding to a labyrinth of shafts and tunnels from the region’s coal mines.
Many of these wells have long since been abandoned. Their operators may have gone out of business, if they are even known. Some old wells are still obvious from rusting wellheads and pipes. But in many cases, there’s little sign of them at the surface.
These wells are hidden in forests, shopping centers, even the Pittsburgh Botanic Garden. Others lie beneath the terminal and runways of the Pittsburgh International Airport. There could even be a hidden well in your backyard or beneath your home.
And while many of these wells pose little hazard beyond tripping over a protruding pipe, some may be leaking explosive methane, toxic carbon monoxide or carcinogens like benzene. Oil and gas wells can create air and water pollution. Exercise great care if you think a well may be nearby.
The state’s Department of Environmental Protection does provide an oil and gas well mapping tool. But it can be slow and difficult to use, especially if you’re not an expert.
Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette teamed up to develop a streamlined and responsive tool that would help state residents identify the locations of wells near their homes, schools, workplaces and parks, grouping them into a small number of meaningful categories and providing easy-to-digest information about each well.
We have simplified the state’s system for classifying wells into four categories:
Active/Other. These are mostly wells that are still producing oil or gas. regulatory inactive status,” which allows an operator to shut down production for up to five years without having to seal a well.
Plugged wells are recorded as sealed. Most were plugged by contractors hired by their former operators, but some were sealed by the state. Plugging may fail because materials like metal pipe and cement deteriorate over time, so some of these wells may still leak gases.
Abandoned/Orphaned includes abandoned wells, which have been out of production for more than 12 months. Orphaned wells are abandoned wells for which no responsible operator or owner exists.
Historical. In addition to its oil and gas wells inventory, which is regularly updated, the Department of Environmental Protection is in the process of digitizing historical maps showing older wells. These maps are not comprehensive—so far they only cover the southwest of the state—and have largely not been verified by modern inspections. Treat this information with extra caution.
We have excluded wells that appear in the state’s data as proposed but never actually drilled.
Explore the map below. You can type an address and hit the search button or accept suggestions. On a search, the map will zoom to the location and display information about the well, including the distance from the searched location. You can then click on other wells in the map view to see information for them.
If photos taken during government inspections are available, you can click on the “See photos” button in the information window to view them.
We used the interactive map to locate relatively new suburban neighborhoods built on top of hundreds of old oil wells in Allegheny County. This brought us to South Fayette Township and, specifically, to the Berkshires neighborhood, where homeowner after homeowner told us they weren’t aware of the wells from historical maps marked by purple dots in the interactive tool.
What the Data Can and Can’t Tell You
The Department of Environmental Protection is responsible for the accuracy of the data. If you have concerns about any wells shown on the map, contact the agency directly through this form or by calling the agency’s oil and gas office in your area.
The agency warns that an individual well may appear in both historical maps and its actively maintained inventory. Wells may also be duplicated, possibly with slightly different locations, across the two digitized historical map collections used for our Historical category.
Wells may be misclassified in the state data. For example, Jane McGill #1, an old well on the property of the Pittsburgh Botanic Garden, was at the time of publication listed as “active” by the Department of Environmental Protection, but it is actually an abandoned well.
Send Us Your Tips
We have only been able to include wells mapped by the agency. Many older wells—possibly several hundred thousand—are missing from the records. In addition, we were unable to map more than 29,000 wells for which the Department of Environmental Protection’s inventory gave no coordinates. About half of these are Plugged wells, almost 6,000 fall into our Abandoned/Orphaned category, the remainder are Active/Other.
So even if our map shows no nearby wells, they may still be present. Signs may include dead vegetation, bubbling in water, rusted metal equipment, unexplained sinkholes and unidentified petroleum smells.
When reporting concerns about wells, you will need GPS coordinates for the well. The more information you can share about environmental or safety risks, the more your report will be prioritized. Wells that the state deems “direct threats” to homes, schools or public spaces can be plugged immediately under emergency contracts.
If you’d like to test your well water, Penn State University offers testing for oil and gas drilling pollution.

The property that became the Pittsburgh Botanic Garden has led many lives: coal mine, farmland, resurrected forest. Inside the southern boundary, in acres of dense woods off-limits to visitors, the relics of a less-remembered chapter litter the landscape.
Past the back gate is a jumble of overturned tanks, stained sheds and tangled, broken pipes. The creek gurgles strangely, a sulfurous smell hanging in the air. High on the ridge, rusted pumpjacks stand like quiet sentries. One wears a metal tag stamped with the name of a woman who lived here more than a century ago.
Jane McGill #1 is an abandoned oil well, drilled at the height of what was then the biggest oil rush in the world, and this is an oil field graveyard. The well is one of hundreds of thousands of oil and gas wells left unplugged by operators and scattered across the state, from Washington County in the southwest to Susquehanna in the northeast.
Some of them are fouling the air with methane, the highly flammable gas and potent climate pollutant, and other chemicals like cancer-causing benzene. In some cases, abandoned wells have been linked to home explosions. Others are implicated in water contamination, acting as accidental conduits between present-day drilling and private water wells.
For decades these lost wells went largely unnoticed. But dealing with them has become more urgent as suburbia sprawls into what used to be open space. Forgotten oil and gas wells now lurk near and even beneath shopping centers, schools, homes, backyards and public parks. They may no longer be marked, their metal casing stripped for scrap, the only sign a patch of dead grass, bubbles surfacing in a pond or an unassuming hole in the ground.
Inside Climate News and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette set out to help make residents more aware of the wells in their midst. Using data from the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, we built an interactive tool that allows users to input an address anywhere in the state and immediately see if active, abandoned or orphaned wells are nearby.
In Pennsylvania, a well is considered abandoned if it has not produced oil or gas in the past 12 months or if it’s no longer equipped for production. An “orphaned” well was abandoned before 1985 and has not created economic benefit for its current operator or owner. Our map includes data from digitized historical sources that is missing from other tools—a critical source of information because many of the state’s orphaned wells are more than 100 years old.
Because recordkeeping was not required until the 1950s, no one knows for sure where the majority of Pennsylvania’s oldest wells are. This is why we’ve included historical data in our tool. These wells’ locations have largely not yet been verified by the state. But they are a valuable resource for finding wells that may no longer be visible at the surface.
“It’s not a situation that we want to leave unchecked,” said Seth Pelepko, deputy secretary for the Department of Environmental Protection’s Office of Oil and Gas Management. Plugging these wells “is a critical first line of defense for ensuring that the environment’s protected and public health and safety is protected.”

People affected by a pollution incident that turned a brook bright blue are being asked to share their experiences as part of an ongoing investigation.
The Environment Agency has launched a survey following the contamination of Littleham Brook in Exmouth, Devon between 11 and 25 September.
It prompted warnings against swimming and other water activities at Exmouth beach while officials investigated the cause.
The survey, external closes on 18 December.
Clarissa Newell, regulatory manager at the Environment Agency, said: "We want information from people, businesses and organisations who may have been affected by this incident.
"This could be specifically during this period or you may still be experiencing ongoing impacts."
The Environment Agency said the anonymous feedback could help investigators understand the wider effects of the pollution and may lead to witness statements supporting the inquiry.
It said possible impacts included illness, cancelled water activities, disrupted visits and reduced income for businesses.
No information could be shared at this stage on the source of the pollution as it could affect any future legal action, it added.
Paper copies of the survey are available from Exmouth Town Hall.

Former three-weight world champion Jorge Linares remains in the custody of US immigration authorities in Texas and is facing deportation.
The 41-year-old Venezuelan was detained on Sunday when US Border Force and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested him at El Paso International Airport.
"On October 26, 2023, he entered the country with permission to stay for a temporary period, but in defiance of our nation's laws, he overstayed his welcome. He will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings," said an ICE spokesperson.
"To be clear, a pending application or work authorisation does not confer legal status in the United States."
Linares is based in Miami and has fought more than 10 times in America.
The immigration law firm Wilner & O'Reilly are representing Linares and they denied their client was in the US illegally.
"Mr Linares is authorised to be in the United States and he has cooperated fully with immigration authorities," said a Wilner & O'Reilly statement.
"We are in communication with ICE and are working to resolve this matter as quickly as possible. Immigration matters follow established procedures, and those procedures take time.
"We are confident in Mr. Linares's position and ask his fans, the press and the public for patience in the meantime."
Linares posted a message on social media on Sunday saying that "ICE has me at the Texas border crossing. This is crazy".
He won 47 of his 56 bouts and claimed world titles at featherweight, super-featherweight and lightweight in a distinguished career which started in 2002.
He retired after being beaten by Britain's Jack Catterall in a light-welterweight bout in October 2023 in his last fight.

Conservationists have spent summer and autumn searching for critically endangered eels to tag as they begin their downstream migration.
The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment.
The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs).
Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch".
The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda.
Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase.
"We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year."
'Mystery' species
The Eels of Steel project is funded by Natural England and the Tees Rivers Trust has been conducting the research alongside Hull University.
Each eel has a tag which emits a unique ping, which provides information about their movements while migrating.
The project aims to discover if the critically endangered animal is successfully leaving the river and making it through river barriers such as sluices and weirs.
Since 2008, European eels have been listed as critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Numbers have declined by between 90-95% since the 1980s due to a range of factors including habitat loss, climate change and overfishing.
Ward said: "It is incredible to think about the journey these eels are embarking on, back to their spawning grounds in the Sargasso Sea.
"No-one has ever witnessed European eels spawning, they are a species that hold so much mystery."
The team say they are always open to suggestions for netting locations, particularly lakes and ponds, and ask people to contact them.

The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim.
But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together.
"People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge.
People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years.
But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA).
Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor.
"There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. We don't swim with cuts or anything."
"This summer I got quite poorly," Jenny says, explaining that she'd had diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle cramps.
"I'd swum and then within six hours I was unwell. I was poorly for probably about seven to 10 days and it was not nice. I think it was the river that day."
So why is she back swimming in it?
"There are germs everywhere, all over the place. You can catch Covid in Tesco," she says.
This summer French Weir Park failed its tests on 13 of the 19 days it was sampled. The BBC analysed data from all four regulators across the UK for 2026 and found French Weir Park's failure rate of 68% was the highest of all the bathing sites
The regulators look for two types of faecal bacteria â E. coli and intestinal enterococci â that originate either in human or animal guts and can make people ill if ingested.
So where's it coming from at French Weir Park? The local water company Wessex Water says it could have come from wildlife, agriculture, private septic tanks as well as its sewerage works.
We decided to take a closer look to see if we could work out where the truth lies.
The testing regime
Our wastewater treatment system is built on the assumption that faecal bacteria - from our poo - once discharged into nature will be rapidly diluted and perish.
The bacteria are known to have little impact on wildlife but they can make humans sick if ingested â so the rise in popularity of wild-swimming and testing of bathing sites have increased awareness.
As part of a BBC investigation we analysed the water sampling results from this summer across all the UK's 700 official bathing sites on the coast, in lakes and rivers.
We found that more than 10% of the UK's coastal sites and 37% of its inland sites failed to meet regulators' minimum standards across the summer.
That difference is likely to be because the sea acts as a more effective dispersant and can dilute and kill faecal bacteria quicker than a lake or river.
Of the 11 worst bathing sites in England in 2026, seven were on inland rivers or lakes.
Why are our rivers so dirty?
Poor water quality has historically been linked to raw sewage spills. These are much more likely after it has rained. So why, in a summer that was extremely dry, did bacteria levels remain high in so many rivers?
In Taunton the official testing data suggests there has been a constant flow of bacteria entering the river.
So the BBC carried out its own sampling near three wastewater treatment works upstream of the Taunton site. We found the treated liquid coming out of the nearest sewage works at Bradford-on-Tone had about 240,000 colony forming units (CFU) of E. coli per 100ml - that's a level about 250 times higher than that considered safe for swimming.
"The counts from just outside the treatment works in my experience were high for treated effluent", Dr Rob Morley from Index Microbiology told us at his laboratory near Bristol as he peered down at small dots of E. coli bacteria on a transparent plastic plate.
What was of particular interest to Morley were the results of the test on water samples we'd taken above and below the point where the treated wastewater enters the River Tone.
It showed 199 CFU of E. coli above, which is fine for swimming and 7,701 CFU just below, more than eight times the regulators limit.
"You can see where it's seeding the river with pollution," Morley says.
"If we were to look further down the river, we would expect the levels to get lower with the dilution effect. But that does quite clearly show the impact that treated effluent can have on the river."
We shared our findings with Dr Andrew Thompson, a fellow at the Institute of Chemical Engineers. He was involved in a 2024 report that warned high concentrations of bacteria and viruses were common, external, particularly in the summer when river levels are lower and could cause serious diseases if ingested.
Thompson told the BBC the levels of E. coli we found in the River Tone were not illegal, or even particularly unusual, because there are currently no laws or regulations about how much bacteria water companies are allowed to discharge in what the industry calls treated effluent.
Animal or human?
We also wanted to know whether analysing the E. coli samples from the bathing site could give us clues to where it came from.
With assistance from researchers at the University of Bristol, Morley arranged for e-DNA analysis to be carried out to identify whether the E. coli bacteria were more likely to be from a human or animal gut.
The answer, as is often the case with water quality, is complex. There were lots of different types of E.coli in the samples.
"Some were from humans, some were from animals and some were just generic from the environment," Morley says. "It definitely suggests that some of the E. coli is definitely coming from human origins, therefore potentially from that treatment works."
As with all of our testing, more needs to be done to reach firm conclusions.

Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.
No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.
The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (Â£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.
Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.
"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.
Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.
Spider's web of financing
That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".
Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.
The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning.
Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.
When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.
"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.
'No CEO is irreplaceable'
The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.
Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.
The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.
Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.
And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.

As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (Â£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says KÃ¡tila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman AdÃ©rito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed widespread concerns online that the series of recent tech outages in the past week are connected, telling reporters there was "zero evidence" of any link.
Rubio acknowledged that "people are fearful" the spate of outages, which included all flights being grounded in the US and widespread disruptions to banking, Apple and Microsoft services, could be linked or part of a plot.
"We are not under systemic attack," he said. "These events, one has nothing to do with the other, they are not inter-related."
Cyber-security experts have agreed that there is no evidence linking the outages, and many of the issues appear due to updates to old infrastructure.
In the past week, there has been a massive Microsoft outage, an apparent tech glitch which grounded all US flights for hours, and issues for the National Security Agency, outages affecting the biggest US banks and Apple.
Every affected company or agency has said the issue was not cyber-related and not the work of an outside actor.
Rubio's comments came hours after US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also addressed the issue, telling Fox News the outages were not the product of a cyber-attack. He explained "lots of institutions" are patching or upgrading systems, which has caused some disruption.
Rubio was asked whether the Trump administration was concerned public fears could lead to stockpiling or a run on the banks.
He said the best way to combat such fears was for the US government to share everything they know with the American people.
"Every indicator we have is that every single one of these events has an explanation or a cause that has nothing to do with a cyber-criminal, has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country," he said.
Technology-related disruptions have happened almost daily since Thursday, when a Microsoft outage disrupted many of its services, including email.
The next day, the US Federal Aviation Administration halted flights across the US for more than four hours with a rare national ground stop. It was the longest halting of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US.
The US transport secretary said the issue was technical and caused by a copper wire upgrade and outdated equipment.
On Monday, a United Airlines technology failure delayed about 150 flights and a JPMorgan Chase software problem disrupted service at the biggest and most utilised banks in the US.
Both United and Chase said a software issue was behind the glitch.
Apple users were impacted by outages affecting iCloud and Apple Pay on Tuesday. The company said the cause was not a cyber-attack but the outage was triggered by an an internal update.
The same day, a highly classified network used by the US National Security Agency (NSA) for internal communications also went offline for a period of time.
Tech experts weigh in: 'No conspiracy here'
Cybersecurity experts say there is no evidence connecting the Microsoft, airline, and bank disruptions from the last five days.
Kris Beevers, CEO and co-founder of the network and infrastructure management company NetBox Labs, acknowledged the circulating theories on social media linking the barrage of outages.
"There is no conspiracy here," he told the BBC.
"There is something more ordinary, and more important to understand: the infrastructure that runs the world is changing faster than ever, and change is risk. Much of it is 30 to 40 years old, with decades of technical debt, and it's now being asked to change very quickly."
Beevers said AI is only part of the story.
"It's putting more strain on these legacy networks, and it's also creating real urgency around security," he said.
"Our customers are the amazing teams behind these networks at airlines, banking, energy, and retail who are essentially doing heart surgery on a global scale to get these networks back up and running quickly."
Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Sherrod DeGrippo, said: "What this week really underscores is how tightly coupled, and fragile, our core digital infrastructure is, where a single software bug or router failure can cascade nationwide."
