1be8a1348363.text: By — Robert Yoon, Associated Press Robert Yoon, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-flipped-9-us-senate-seats-the-most-in-almost-70-years Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats flipped 9 U.S. Senate seats — the most in almost 70 years Politics Nov 18, 2026 5:11 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Former Rep. Mary Peltola's victory over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's competitive U.S. Senate race has flipped a ninth Republican-held seat to the Democrats, giving Peltola's party its biggest midterm gain in nearly 70 years. Democrats last gained nine or more Senate seats in a midterm election in 1958, during Republican President Dwight Eisenhower's second term. That year, Democrats wrested away 13 Republican-held seats and also won both of Alaska's newly created seats, for a total gain of 15 seats. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Peltola's victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party's largest advantage in the Senate in 16 years. Democrats held 58 Senate seats in the waning days of the 111th Congress, which concluded on Jan. 3, 2011. "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said in statement posted on social media. "Most people didn't think 51 Democratic Senate seats was a possibility at the beginning of this cycle." READ MORE: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate seat, beating Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan Even without Alaska, Democrats would have secured their largest majority since January 2015, when Republicans took control after flipping nine Democratic seats in the 2014 midterms during President Barack Obama's second term. Democrat Scott Colom's U.S. Senate victory Wednesday in Mississippi's U.S. Senate race gave his party its eighth Republican-held seat. That win delivered Democrats their most midterm pickups since President Ronald Reagan's second midterm election 40 years ago. WATCH: How Scott Colom won his longshot bid to flip Mississippi's Senate seat Democrats also reclaimed the House, picking up 42 seats as of Tuesday. The gains continued a historical trend of midterm losses for the president's party. The Senate has tended to be less susceptible to the midterm effect than the House. In seven of the last 16 midterms prior to 2026, the president's party either held its ground or gained seats in the Senate, though all but one of those midterms occurred in the president's first term. A president's second midterm tends to be more punishing. By comparison, the president's party had gained House seats in only two midterms since the end of World War II. 558ecf00060e.text: High school students across the U.S. have a new reason to vie for the top spot in their class: a custom pair of Nike Air Force 1 sneakers, thanks to a request from Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom . Why it matters: Colom is putting a fresh spin on academic achievement, turning his historic election into a nationwide incentive for students to hit the books — with a little help from Nike and no taxpayer dollars. What they're saying: Colom initially asked if Nike would celebrate the historic milestone by giving a custom-made version of his favorite sneakers to every Mississippi valedictorian for the 2026-2027 school year. "It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year! #justdoit," he wrote on X . Nike then upped the ante, extending the offer to valedictorians nationwide. "The athlete mindset makes things possible, including this idea," Nike said. Colom praised Nike for "stepping up to motivate students across the country in this historic moment," and suggested the design honor Hiram Revels, the first Black member of Congress who represented Mississippi. Context: There were more than 23,000 public high schools in the U.S. during the 2020-2021 school year and more than 3,600 private high schools during the 2019-2020 school year, according to the National Center for Education Statistics . A classic pair of Nike Air Force 1s retails for about $115 on Nike's website . Zoom in: In January, Colom will become Mississippi's first Democratic senator in nearly four decades and its first Black senator in almost 150 years. The senator-elect pulled off a stunning upset of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the ruby-red state, which hadn't elected a Black senator since Reconstruction. His victory was fueled in part by voters in the Mississippi Delta, where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. What we're watching: What Nike cooks up for the nation's brightest students.

It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.
So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival â Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.
It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (Â£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.
Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.
Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
A benchmark valuation
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".
The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.
It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.
"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.
Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?
"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."
So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.
But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.
It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.
There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.
Public doubts
It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.
With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.
Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.
Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.
If Anthropic â and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.
The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (Â£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.
Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".
The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.
Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.
A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Marnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.
Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.
The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.
There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.
Marnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."
The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.
The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.
Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.
Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.
The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.
Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.
Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

âNo end in sightâ
Increasing numbers of foreign executives are leaving Riyadh as the city continues to suffer Houthi attacks that have forced the closure of the cityâs main business district and schools.
Offices in Riyadhâs King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) have already been closed for several weeks and some businesses are not expecting it to reopen until next year, according to people familiar with the matter. That was before the Public Investment Fundâs head office in the district was hit on Thursday morning, which is likely to further delay any reopening of the area. As a result, staff are increasingly deciding to work from other countries, Semafor was told.
The destinations vary. Some have headed back to homes in Europe, others have joined families that are based in the UAE and normally only visited on weekends, while another group has upped sticks temporarily to third countries.
âThe office is closed and schools are online. Thereâs no end in sight, so thereâs no point in us staying,â said one executive of a Saudi company, who decamped with his family to Thailand because he was at risk of crossing a UK tax threshold if he spent any more time in his home country.
To be sure, the numbers leaving the city are limited and in many ways life carries on as normal. Other parts of the city remain active and business continues as usual in areas so far unaffected by the Houthi attacks. If the security situation improves those that have left are expected to return.
Yet the sense of insecurity is a blow to ambitions to make the Saudi capital a regional business and finance hub. The kingdom had aimed to grow Riyadhâs population to 10 million by 2030, up from 7 million in the 2022 census. A significant portion of that growth was based on a rising number of expatriates moving to the city.
Some staff at Saudi companies had already made the decision to leave several weeks ago after KAFD offices shut and schools shifted to online learning in the wake of the deadly attack on Riyadh airport in early October. Many businesses based in Riyadhâs other tower blocks have also advised staff to work from home until further notice. That has added to the numbers of people who are no longer required to be in the country to continue working. People have been driving to airports in Bahrain or Qatar to fly out.
A recent uptick in attacks on the city, combined with the upcoming Christmas holiday season, is leading more people to decide to move if their jobs do not require them to be in the country. âWe were already planning to leave for the holidays in a few weeks, so now we have just bought that forward,â said one executive in Riyadh who planned to drive to Doha. âI really donât know when we will come back.â
KAFD is now almost deserted. Baristas in the areaâs coffee shops, many of which have remained open, say they have had few customers for weeks. The attack on the PIF tower comes just over a week after Aramcoâs building in the area was also damaged in a Houthi attack.
The decision by the cityâs expatriates to go is a reversal of the situation in the early months of the Iran war, when Riyadh suffered far fewer direct attacks than other Gulf cities and its airspace mostly remained open. That made the city a key channel for people in Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and the UAE to leave the Arabian peninsula.
Notable
Saudi Arabian officials foresee the war against Yemenâs Houthis to stretch well into next year, despite setbacks on the battlefield in Yemen and attacks disrupting life at home, according to two Western officials briefed by Saudis on the plans.

A Florida pastor has been found guilty of a number of charges relating to the assassination of the Haitian President Jovenel MoÃ¯se.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon, a dual US-Haitian national, was convicted of all eight charges against him, including conspiracy to kill or kidnap a person. He faces a potential sentence of life in prison.
The 67-year-old was accused of being involved in a plot to replace MoÃ¯se as Haiti's president with himself in 2021, allegedly so he could award lucrative contracts to a Florida-based security outfit once in place.
The murder of MoÃ¯se has left Haiti without a leader for five years. That political vacuum has intensified gang violence in the impoverished Caribbean nation.
A presidential election is scheduled for next year and MoÃ¯se's wife, Martine, who was injured in the attack that killed her husband, announced this week that she intended to stand.
Sanon was found guilty on Wednesday following an eight-week trial in federal court in Miami, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. His lawyer said he maintains his innocence and that he intends to appeal against the verdict, it reports.
Prosecutors said Sanon had "political aspirations" in Haiti and, in April 2021, met several other co-conspirators to devise a plan to oust MoÃ¯se in an armed raid on the presidential palace in the capital, Port-au-Prince.
Among them were the heads of the companies Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security - collectively referred to as CTU - who would finance the coup in exchange for government contracts for infrastructure projects, and to provide security forces and equipment.
A few months later, the other conspirators realised that Sanon had "neither the constitutional qualifications nor the popular support" to become Haiti's president and so shifted to another candidate, the US Department of Justice said.
At the same time, the plot had developed from one to forcibly remove MoÃ¯se from office to assassinating him, investigators said.
Dozens of people have been implicated in the conspiracy, which prosecutors said involved co-ordinating funding for and delivering weapons and mercenaries to Haiti to carry out the attack.
On 6 July that year, a group of Colombian mercenaries entered the presidential palace and killed MoÃ¯se. His wife, who was also injured in the attack, said at the time that the assailants had "riddled" her husband with bullets.
The successful assassination plot raised questions in Haiti about the relative ease with which the mercenaries were able to gain access to the president.
The country - the poorest in the Americas - has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but MoÃ¯se's assassination ushered in a period of worsening instability that emboldened gangs and prompted the deployment of a multinational force.
However, this has struggled to penetrate areas where gangs hold sway and more than 5,700 people have been killed or injured in the year to 11 September, the UN said last month.
Sanon and several other co-conspirators were arrested by Haitian authorities, while three mercenaries were killed in a gun battle with police. Eighteen people were transferred to Florida in September to stand trial over the plot.
Four men, including the heads of the CTU, were convicted of their role earlier this year. Sanon had been scheduled to be tried with them, but his case was delayed due to health reasons, according to CBS.
Sanon was born in Haiti but moved to the US as a teenager. He told the court he had worked in churches in Haitian immigrant communities in several parts of the US including Florida, US media report.

When James Talarico - who recently became the first Democrat to win election to the US Senate for Texas since 1988 - appeared onstage at a Democratic political conference, he was greeted by a chorus of cheers and a standing ovation.
But the audience's enthusiasm dimmed when he suggested working in tandem with the Republican Trump administration.
"We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history," said Talarico, who at 37 will become the youngest member of the Senate when he takes his oath of office in January. "Because this moment is so much bigger and so much more important than the red team or the blue team."
He was just one of many rising stars speaking last week during a political conference in Denver, titled "What's Next: investigating strategies and priorities for the future of the Democratic Party".
And the answer to what's next? No one's sure.
Those present, who included activists and political organisers, were invigorated and celebratory the week after a "blue tsunami" saw Democrats win in Republican heartlands in the midterm elections.
The party took control of both chambers of Congress, winning a majority in the House by over 80 seats and gaining nine seats in the Senate.
But the atmosphere in Denver was also introspective and forward-looking, as discussions focused on how those victories were won, which issues did not resonate, and what would be needed to continue the party's seat-winning momentum.
Some, like Talarico, suggested working alongside Republicans to push forward an economic agenda that would resonate with Americans, such as extending health coverage and reducing inflation.
Alabama Congressman Shomari Figures - who surprised many pollsters when he held his seat despite Republicans redrawing his district months before the election - cautioned against going after Trump, when there were more pressing concerns for Americans.
Previous Democratic-led efforts to impeach Trump both ended in Senate acquittals.
"We impeached him twice and got him back - with a Republican majority," Figures said.
Yet others, like Maryland Congresswoman Angela Alsobrooks, insisted that voters wanted to see accountability.
Voters "realised the smash-and-grab that occurred, and they want people to account for it", she said, pushing for transparent investigations into the Trump administration.
The two-day event was staged by Majority Democrats, a political action committee launched last year to address tensions between the left and centrist factions of the party, with some of the biggest divisions forming over how to deliver health care and the war in Gaza.
Prominent left-wing members of the party - such as Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed - were not in attendance.
In Denver, it was clear those tensions weren't going away, as protesters waving Palestinian flags shouted as people walked past and armed police looked on.
Some in attendance made a point to criticise Chuck Schumer, the long-time Democratic Senate minority leader who is seen as a part of the party's centrist establishment.
He has been challenged for the role of Senate majority leader by Chris Van Hollen, a senator from Maryland who is considered a left-wing populist.
Democrats have not been "strong enough in their displeasure with what's been happening with Trump, and I think that's one of the reasons that people are asking for new leadership," said Vicki Saxe, holding a sign criticising Schumer.
"I'm frustrated with the lack of urgency that I feel coming from the party leadership," said Tami Butters, 65, standing beside her with a "Vote Yes for Chris Van Hollen" sign. She cited the absence of 11 Democrats last week, when the House voted on whether to consider impeaching US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The effort failed.
Hakeem Jeffries, a centrist Democrat who is poised to become the country's first black speaker of the House, faced similar pushback, as protesters heckled his speech.
One of the biggest issues of division is the war in Gaza, with both Schumer and Jeffries backing continued military assistance for Israel, while some new members of Congress, like El-Sayed, support ending unconditional US military aid to Israel.
Non-profit founder Shiva Saram, who also chairs the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund, travelled from Connecticut to the conference despite having "almost left my party over Gaza and the Iran War".
Saram has been newly encouraged, however, by the "real depth in our bench of new and young leaders".
"What my party has done wrong for too long is we did not listen," she said.
Many speakers and guests stressed that the Democrats won because they focused on real policies that would impact their constituents' daily lives - and that failing to do so in previous years might have been why they lost on those occasions.
Delaware Senator Chris Coons told BBC News that he had advised newly elected members to "under-promise and over-deliver".
"We got hired because the average American wants us to help make their lives better - lower their costs, end the cruelty and the corruption and give them more reason for hope," he said. "That's going to require hard work, and it isn't going to be easy to get done."
Michigan Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet agreed, saying she did not care "if we have to put Donald Trump's name" on legislation to gain the president's support for efforts to help her district.
Tahra Hoops, the 28-year-old senior director of economic analysis at the Chamber of Progress, a "left-of-centre" tech think tank, suggested that the party's divisions be embraced, not paved over.
"I think Democrats can look different wherever they are," she said.
While "very progressive" candidates can win in her home town of New York City, she said it made sense that Talarico held more centrist views because running in Texas "is not going to be the same".

South African DJ Lag says it is a "dream come true" to have his music featured on Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), the hugely popular video game released on Thursday.
DJ lag, one of South Africa's best-known electronic music producers, is among several African stars to feature, alongside Nigerian singers Burna Boy and Asake.
"I can't explain the feeling. I started playing the game last night and it's amazing," DJ Lag told the BBC's Newsday programme, adding that he had been playing GTA since he was about 10 years old and could hardly believe he was now part of the latest edition.
Many players have already had a chance to play the game following its worldwide launch.
The game, which lets players explore a fictional American city, features a dedicated African music radio station playing Afrobeats, amapiano and other sounds from across the continent.
The release of GTA 6 ends a 13-year wait for a new edition of the game.
Rockstar Games, the developer behind the franchise, has revealed details of the game's soundtrack and some in-game radio stations, but has yet to release a complete list of songs featured in the game.
Rockstar says AfroBank FM features everything from 20th Century African classics to contemporary amapiano and 3-step, giving the continent's music a prominent place in the latest edition.
Burna Boy co-hosts the station alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax, while Asake's hit song Joha is among the tracks players can listen to as they drive around the game's virtual world.
DJ Lag, whose real name is Lwazi Asanda Gwala, is regarded as one of the pioneers of gqom, a genre of electronic dance music that emerged in the port city of Durban in the early 2010s.
He posted on Instagram: "God did."
Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor also feature, alongside South African artists Robot Boii and Kamo Mphela, bringing a mix of classic and contemporary African music to one of gaming's biggest franchises.
Rockstar has also announced a 34-track official soundtrack album, released in partnership with Atlantic Records, featuring an original Burna Boy song titled Bigger.
For African fans, the inclusion of familiar music adds another dimension to the experience, allowing players to hear some of the continent's biggest sounds while exploring the American setting.
The series allows players to roam through sprawling fictional cities, drive vehicles and complete missions involving crime, police pursuits and other adventures.
The latest instalment takes players to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami, and the surrounding US state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.
Its story follows two criminals, Jason and Lucia, who become caught up in a wider conspiracy after a robbery goes wrong.
The launch has generated enormous excitement among gamers around the world.
Some fans downloaded it in advance so they could begin playing as soon as it became available, while others have booked leave from work.
The previous edition, GTA 5, was one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 200 million copies worldwide.
The new release is expected to be another major commercial success, although it remains to be seen whether it will match its predecessor's extraordinary sales.

bc80716f0fe4.text: China is intensifying efforts to control the entire drug supply chain, putting the U.S. at risk of being cut off from future lifesaving treatments, the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology warns in a new analysis out Thursday. Why it matters: Western drug giants have invested huge sums in Chinese biotechs to boost their product pipelines. But sharing capital and expertise could give Beijing more control over critical pharmaceutical technologies. Concerns about the U.S. getting boxed out have intensified after the Chinese government proposed new restrictions last month on the export of certain technologies, including cell and gene therapy platforms. Driving the news: Western drug giants are increasingly entering into licensing agreements with Chinese firms that redirect U.S. capital away from U.S. innovation and toward the Chinese pharmaceutical industry, the commission found in its analysis of 57 deals from the beginning of 2023 through last month. The deals are being made earlier in the drug discovery process, allowing the Chinese partners to gain not just capital but know-how in developing and commercializing treatments. This kind of knowledge transfer in automobiles, semiconductors and industrial chemicals gave Chinese industry a competitive edge and leverage to control global markets for the products, according to the commission, which was established by Congress to examine how emerging biotech intersects with national security. "The end game is the same for the [Chinese Communist Party] in the pharmaceutical industry," the commission warns, saying the goal is increased U.S. dependence on Chinese innovation and enrichment of the Chinese pharmaceutical industry. Between the lines: Drugmakers including AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb and Pfizer have been drawn by China's surge of investment in the life sciences and the promise of faster clinical trials and product approvals. Typically a Chinese biotechnology company sells the license to develop or commercialize a treatment it developed to a multinational pharmaceutical company. The Western companies see the arrangements as a way to outsource the burden of drug discovery and verify early results. But the commission found that the deals are increasingly based on preclinical data and that upfront payments are coming earlier in the R&D cycle. The commission says this can result in a "flywheel effect" that sees royalties and equity in joint ventures flow back to China, fueling new research and infrastructure and attracting global talent. What they're saying: "The CCP seeks dominance in biotechnology as a source of economic power and geopolitical advantage, and Beijing has spent decades pursuing a deliberate strategy to achieve that at all levels of the value chain," said commission executive director Caitlin Frazer. "U.S.-China pharma deals are starting to favor the Chinese startups, which risks eroding biotech R&D in the U.S. This trend should be alarming for policymakers." Threat level: The concern is what happens if China scales up and corners a market, establishing a stranglehold on supplies of key products and ingredients. That's especially critical in pharma. While a chip shortage may result in delays replacing a car or phone, a drug shortage delays treatments for controlling seizures, treating infections or managing severe pain, Brookings Institution senior fellow Marta Wosińska has noted . In a report last year to Congress, the commission posed a hypothetical scenario in which Beijing withheld a breakthrough treatment from American patients in the event of a conflict in Taiwan. State of play: Last month, the Trump administration proposed subjecting certain deals with Chinese life sciences companies to new screening requirements or prohibiting them altogether. The administration cited the risk of "outbound investments" being used to create biological weapons or brain-computer interfaces for surveillance, or to make U.S. supply chains overly dependent on a country. Cash-based deals that bring royalties and milestone payments are still permitted, but equity investments in Chinese firms would be prohibited and certain joint ventures could also be targeted, per a Sidley analysis . The commission, in its new analysis, calls the proposal "a prudent step to curtail China's biotechnology ambitions" but adds policymakers "must act now to empower the United States to out-innovate strategic competitors before it's too late." Pharma and biotech interests have been pressing Congress and the administration to take steps to update and streamline U.S. drug development, improve patient access to clinical trials and pass stronger patent protections. What we're watching: Whether this week's meetings between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping yield new agreements on strategic technologies like biotech or lead to tighter export controls.

68413ff47444.text: Republican voters in four early 2028 primary states have favorable views of Israel by wide margins and have negative opinions of three leading right-wing critics of the Jewish state, according to a new poll by a national GOP consulting firm. Why it matters: The poll challenges the notion that Republican opinion toward Israel is fracturing significantly, and points to a potential disconnect between GOP voters' attitudes and the sentiments of those who often draw the most attention online. The survey, conducted by OnMessage Inc . for the Combat Antisemitism Movement 's political arm, essentially provides a roadmap for pro-Israel Republicans' messaging ahead of the 2028 presidential campaign. It seeks to cast the right's leading critics of Israel — Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens and Nick Fuentes — as liabilities in the GOP primary. Zoom in: After the midterms, Vice President Vance called on the U.S. and the GOP to "change our relationship to Israel," elevating the nations' longtime partnership as a 2028 campaign issue at a time when Vance is eyeing a presidential bid. Israel is supported by 68% of Republican voters in Iowa, New Hampshire, Nevada and South Carolina, according to the survey, a result similar to findings by Gallup and Pew . 17% disfavored Israel. 78% said the GOP's "relationship with Israel" makes them more likely to vote Republican. Large majorities also agreed with pro-Israel messages. In contrast , 53% of those surveyed said they disapprove of Carlson, and 30% approve. But among voters under 45 years old, Carlson's approval/disproval ratings were tied at 46%. 49% of the Republicans surveyed disapproved of Owens, while 23% approved. Fuentes, the least-known of the three media figures, was viewed unfavorably by 25% and favored by 13%. Among self-described MAGA Republicans, 22% approved and 23% disapproved of him, however. "The fringe messengers are underwater," says a slide deck for the poll, which was conducted ahead of the Combat Antisemitism Movement's national conference Thursday in Charleston, S.C. Stunning stat: Vance is more popular in the GOP than President Trump. 75% view Trump favorably and 23% disfavor him, a net of +52 points. Vance: 80% favorable and 19% unfavorable, a net of +61. The intrigue: Vance is friends with Carlson, whose son used to work in the vice president's office. The two have resisted speaking ill of each other even as Carlson has grown more critical of the president and the war in Iran. 46% of the GOP voters surveyed said a Carlson endorsement of a presidential candidate would make them less likely to support that person; 16% said it would make them more likely and 39% said it wouldn't matter. Yes, but : The poll is conducted for an advocacy group and seeks to provide messaging guidance for candidates and surrogates. So some of its questions are leading. By 83%-5%, Republicans said they viewed Carlson less favorably when told "he endorsed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a radical Muslim socialist recently elected to the U.S. Senate in Michigan whose political associates include someone that said, 'America deserved 9/11.' " The survey tested ways to attack Owens and Fuentes on the campaign trail by describing extreme comments from both and found that outsized majorities of Republican voters would call on a candidate to denounce them. By 86%-7%, respondents agreed with the statement, "There is no place for antisemitism in the Republican Party." And 66% said there's no place in the party for antisemites, while 15% said they should be welcomed under a "big tent." What they're saying: Fuentes declined to comment, Owens couldn't be reached and Carlson questioned the financiers of the poll. "The poll was commissioned by the 'Combat Antisemitism Movement'? Seriously? Pretty funny. Where does their funding come from?" Carlson asked via text. (The donors are primarily Jewish and Zionist contributors, according to Influence Watch ). "If the point is to convince Republican candidates that American voters love [Israeli leader Benjamin] Netanyahu and want more wars for Israel, good luck in the next election," he said. "It's so absurd. But I'm sure you'll have Republican senators waving around the poll results like they mean something." Former Virginia Attorney General Jason Miyares, a U.S. Advisory Board Member of the Combat Antisemitism Movement, dismissed the criticism: "For a Republican presidential candidate, standing up against antisemitism is not a political risk — it is the price of admission and good politics. Most importantly, it is simply the right thing to do." The poll of 1,000 respondents (250 from each of the four early states) was conducted Nov. 7-10. The margin of error: +/- 3.1%.

6f70168f6a21.text: Axios chief technology officer Dan Cox, who's spent 25 years at some of the world's biggest tech companies, puts the recent spate of high-profile failures in perspective: My parents, my siblings and plenty of other people are asking the same question: How worried should we be? The big picture: I've been in technology a long time. I take these threats seriously , but I'm not in panic mode. When something breaks, we need to understand what happened, how far it reaches and what we can do about it. A frightening headline doesn't answer those questions. Zoom out: The way I think about it, we've put powerful tools in more hands, and people are taking potshots to see what they can hit. Those shots can do real damage, and we need to protect ourselves. But hearing gunfire doesn't, by itself, mean an army is coming over the hill. We need to understand who's firing, what they can actually do and whether the threat is changing. Zoom in: Over the past few weeks, we've identified bad actors snooping around our own website, too. Our talented engineers have investigated threats and put mitigations in place. There may still be attempts on our site, but each incident gives us an opportunity to strengthen our systems. Between the lines: There are thousands of smart, resourceful and dedicated engineers working to protect the systems we all rely on. I see that commitment in our own team. I believe that if the threat grows, more people with those skills will step up. That's part of why I have confidence in our ability to respond, even as the threats evolve. The bottom line: Fred Rogers shared his mother's advice for frightening news: "Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping." I think about that here. There are a lot of capable people working on these problems. I have confidence in them, even while we have real work to do. I want people to feel informed enough to act, rather than frightened enough to assume the worst.

5ce699bc856d.text: The internet has caught the emergency preparation bug , fueled by fears of AI-led cyberattacks , power grid vulnerabilities, transportation standstills and international threats . The big picture: The "prepper" mindset is resonating with larger slices of society — who are packing emergency bags, stocking up on water and taking inventory of non-perishables. Michael Mills, a University of Greenwich senior lecturer who studies doomsday preparation, says some people are turning to "lightweight versions" of traditional prepping amid doubts about global stability. By the numbers: Sales at Survival Frog, a survival retailer that sells gear like emergency food and radios, saw sales jump 450% between Oct. 27 and Nov. 16, compared to prior weeks, CEO and founder Byron Walker tells Axios. Competitors saw similar trends, he says. And most recent buyers at Survival Frog were new customers. Food, including canned meats, leads demand, Walker says, followed by products like radios, solar generators, battery packs and water filters. State of play: Systems the world relies on for travel , communications , business , food, health care and more have been disrupted in recent weeks — whether because of tech shortfalls or malicious acts. While officials assure the incidents aren't broadly connected, fears of critical infrastructure failing are growing, and more people considering how to prepare for crises. "It does seem much more mainstream now," Walker says of preppers. "You can't turn on the news without hearing about a new cyber attack or a tech meltdown." Many of the emergency preparation skills people are using have long been observed in disaster-prone areas. And as many Americans learned during COVID, supply chain disruptions mean having extra water, radios and shelf-stable foods around the house isn't a bad thing. Krystal, known online as the "Queen of Doomsday," spends about five hours daily coaching new preppers and told Axios that recent online engagement with her content, which she says has more than doubled across platforms, has been "mind-blowing." "Families are generally concerned —...people who would have normally turned their nose away from it and thought, 'No, nothing could ever happen.' We've seen lockdowns. We've seen supply chains be crippled. We've seen oil crises, inflation," she says. Between the lines: Overlapping tech oddities boosted "a sense of anxiety about social stability around us, knowing that planes can be grounded, or fridges can all of a sudden become heaters," Mills says. Costco has become an apparent cornucopia for concerned consumers, with sales on goods like rice, canned goods and water reportedly surging. Walker attributes the Survival Frog sales boom to the U.K. government and EU urging households to prepare three days of supplies, as well as the Pentagon readiness plan for military bases to operate at least 90 days, per Fox reporting , if civilian systems fail. That plan fueled rumors about a 90-day "blackout" across the U.S. Worth noting: Asked about the outages and Pentagon preparations, Vice President JD Vance told Fox News' Laura Ingraham that friends have asked whether they should be "preparing to build a bunker" or stock up on food and water. "And my answer to that is no," he continued. "We do not see some crisis coming down." The bottom line: But Krystal said in a video response to Vance, "Yes, we should be preparing." She's not here to fear-monger, but she tells Axios, "one more person prepared is one less person to worry about if there's a crisis." Go deeper: The internet's latest obsession: The end of the world

f7d36e06473d.text: Anthropic will make its Wall Street debut Thursday at a moment of profound contradiction in the history of AI: The humans are embattled — bogged down by scandal, financial turmoil and political revolt. But the machines are ascendant — accelerating toward an "intelligence explosion" they expect will transform civilization. Why it matters: The industry's recent chaos has obscured a breathtaking surge in technological progress, forcing some of the world's leading researchers to reconsider just how soon AI could surpass human intelligence. Zoom in: Inside Anthropic, soon to be valued north of $1 trillion, independent researchers at METR found that AI models are advancing at nearly twice their historical pace — largely fueled, they believe, by AI itself. Anthropic's own data shows Claude went from leading fewer than 1% of the company's AI research tasks in February to more than a quarter by August, with humans still supervising. METR found no clear obstacles to sustaining this pace over the next year, and reviewed confidential evidence suggesting the acceleration itself may be gathering speed. Zoom out: Across the frontier, leading companies are racing up what Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calls "the exponential." OpenAI disclosed Tuesday that Astra 6.2 is its first publicly released model to reach the "High" threshold for AI self-improvement — equivalent, the company says, to giving every researcher another highly capable engineer. The advances span both software and silicon: OpenAI says its models helped AMD compress a year of chip-design progress into less than five months, while Google's Gemini is reducing weeks of chip-layout work to hours. The big picture: These breakthroughs are pushing some of AI's top forecasters to shorten their timelines for the fabled "intelligence explosion" — a runaway cascade of self-improving AI that could propel machine intelligence far beyond human comprehension. The influential AI Futures Project now expects machines to surpass the world's best human AI researchers next year, a dramatic revision driven largely by METR's findings at Anthropic. Paul Christiano, an AI safety pioneer who recently joined OpenAI's board, puts the odds of superintelligence emerging within a year at one in three if development continues at its current pace. Between the lines: For all their extraordinary capabilities, the machines remain at the mercy of a fallible human race. Take Nvidia: Jensen Huang's sex scandal has plunged the chipmaker into crisis at the very height of its technological and financial power, endangering virtually the entire AI ecosystem. AI leaders' disastrous messaging , veering between promises of utopia and warnings of mass unemployment, has poisoned public trust and helped fuel a revolt against data centers. Meanwhile, the industry's enormous capital requirements, increasingly tangled financial arrangements and intensifying U.S.–China chip war threaten to impose limits that the technology itself has yet to encounter. Then there's the question of control: Months after OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face, the company acknowledged Wednesday that it still cannot fully rely on AI behaving as intended to prevent harm. One of the industry's biggest gambles is that AI itself will help solve the problem of controlling future superintelligence. "You're building the plane as you fly it," Christiano told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel this week. The bottom line: Anthropic's historic IPO captures the central contradiction: Investors are betting on nearly limitless technological progress, while the industry's future remains hostage to distinctly human failures.

254b01190ebf.text: Bot accounts have helped spread conspiracy theories about a wave of major tech outages over the last week, according to new research shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: Purveyors of disinformation appear to be exploiting public anxiety over the cyberattacks and fragile infrastructure, amplifying suspicions of coordinated cyberattacks and government cover-ups. While it's unclear who's behind these accounts, the pattern shows that when technology failures lack substantive explanations, bot networks will fill the void to manufacture panic. Catch up quick: Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, United, Workday, the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Security Agency each faced outages over the last week. Then came the conspiracy theories: When the FAA grounded flights for four hours Friday, people were quick to assume it was tied to the rollout of an AI tool at the agency. Some also tried linking the widespread Microsoft outage to recent company layoffs. Yes, but : There's no publicly established evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack, despite the theories circulating online. Several companies have attributed their disruptions to technical problems, rather than malicious activity, including efforts to patch vulnerabilities in order to make software more resilient. Downdetector data show that while the seven days through Monday saw the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, longer-term patterns are far from unprecedented, as Axios previously reported . By the numbers: Suspected bots accounted for roughly 30% of posts promoting conspiracy theories about several recent tech outages, according to data from social media monitoring firm PeakMetrics. During Microsoft's outage, bots accounted for 26% of conspiratorial posts. Bots accounted for 34% of conspiracy-related posts during Friday's Workday outage, compared with 27% of other posts. Likely bot accounts also made up 31% of conspiracy-related posts about Bank of America's outage and 28% of posts linking Chase's outage to other disruptions. PeakMetrics analyzed social media discussions surrounding six recent outages and automatically classification accounts that were likely to be bots and conspiracy-related posts. Threat level : Jessica Pratt, a spokesperson for PeakMetrics, told Axios that most of the bot activity is aimed at "gaming the platforms' algorithms" and that they see some foreign influence within that — although the company could not detail precisely how many of the bots are tied to foreign state media and governments. PeakMetrics also observed a "small number of foreign state media and state-aligned accounts in the conversation," Pratt added. Zoom in: The most popular theory being pushed was that each of these incidents must be connected. More than half of posts about Chase's outage linked it to other recent disruptions, including the FAA ground stop and Microsoft's outage. A fabricated statement attributed to JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon fueled speculation that North Korean and Russian hackers were behind the banking outages. During Microsoft's outage, suspected bots circulated identical posts linking the disruption to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure and banking outages in Japan and Paraguay. The big picture: Foreign influence operations have historically used bots to amplify political grievances and spread false narratives, but it's unclear who's operating the accounts pushing theories about the latest outages. Between the lines: The longer outages dragged on without clear explanations, the more room conspiracy theories had to spread. During Microsoft's outage, speculative posts nearly tripled on the second day, when the disruption had stretched beyond 12 hours. By then, nearly one in five posts offered an alternative explanation for the outage, according to PeakMetrics. The intrigue: Questions about whether the outages are connected have also reached Washington, where senior officials and lawmakers are raising concerns about what might be causing the disruptions. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters Tuesday that "it's unclear if (the outages are) all infrastructure related or whether there's some malignant activity." Jeffries said he wants briefings for lawmakers in both chambers. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) told reporters that it would be "the greatest coincidence in the history of the world" if these outages aren't connected, according to NBC News. What to watch: Outages are about to become the new normal as organizations race to patch critical vulnerabilities discovered by AI before hackers can use AI to weaponize them. Go deeper : Why the internet suddenly broke all at once

Until recently, economic researchers were cheering an encouraging trend: Older Americans were staying in the labor force longer and waiting longer to claim their Social Security benefits, aiming to enhance their financial stability in retirement.
Not everyone, of course. Despite financial advisers’ counsel and economists’ hopes, most people still claim their benefits before reaching their designated full retirement age, though that usually means lower monthly payments for life.
Early claimers might hit an unexpected financial crunch, as Alan Turner did when he lost his job as a museum exhibit designer in 2022. “I haphazardly looked for work, but my prospects weren’t very good,” he said.
For a while, Turner, 69, who lives in New Castle, Delaware, got by on unemployment benefits and savings, hoping to reach his full retirement age — 66 and a half — before claiming. “It was doable, but it was bleak,” he said. He took his benefits at 64, reducing his Social Security income by about $5,000 a year.
Or people might feel the need to retire earlier than planned. Nancy Mansson, a nuclear medicine technologist in West Hebron, New York, found last year that “I was just fried,” she said. “I had to step away,” though she was more than a year short of her full retirement age.
People can claim Social Security retirement benefits as early as 62, but their payments will be substantially lower than if they wait until full retirement age, now 67 for those born in 1960 or later.
Mansson, 67, sacrificed about $300 a month by claiming early and works at a hospital one day a week to compensate.
Still, economists had documented that Americans were both retiring later and claiming their benefits later — until last year, when “all hell broke loose,” said Alicia Munnell, former director of the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College. In an unprecedented surge, hundreds of thousands more people than usual suddenly filed for retirement benefits.
Why? Understanding what’s happening with older Americans and Social Security requires looking both backward and ahead.
For decades, workers had been retiring at increasingly younger ages; that trend reversed in the 1980s, and the change accelerated in the 1990s. Changes in the Social Security law, which Congress amended in 1983 (“The last time we did anything to Social Security,” Munnell said, pointedly) provided incentives to work longer.
Most employers shifted from defined pensions to 401(k) plans and discontinued retiree health insurance, additional reasons to stay on the job. Plus, work had become less physically demanding overall, and “health and longevity were increasing,” Munnell said.
In an analysis the center published last year, the proportion of men who were filing at 62 fell to 26% in 2023 from 31% in 2019; among women, claiming at 62 dropped to 27% from 34%. Over the same period, claiming at 67 or later rose to 26% from 19% for men and to 25% from 20% for women, a trend that persisted into 2024.
By waiting, “they have more income,” Munnell said. “They can contribute to their 401(k)s. They have higher Social Security benefits and fewer years to support themselves without income.” Waiting also increases spouses’ eventual survivor benefits. Plus, most beneficiaries pay taxes on their benefits, bolstering both the Social Security system and the federal budget in general.
Delaying until 70, the age for receiving maximum benefits, brings particular rewards. Beyond full retirement age, benefits rise by 8% annually.
“It’s an inflation-protected annuity the private sector can’t compete with,” said Jack Smalligan, a senior policy fellow at the Urban Institute, a nonprofit research organization. “If you’re healthy and can afford it, it’s the smartest choice.”
But in 2025, he and a colleague noticed an unusual influx of new retirement claims and sounded the alarm. From October 2024 to April 2025, they found, claims jumped by 267,000 compared with the previous year, a 13% surge. Typically, “the fluctuations were more in the 2 to 3% range,” Smalligan said.
Population growth and adjustments for a small group of public employees couldn’t explain the size of that leap. “It was really a reaction to the turmoil at Social Security during that period,” Smalligan said.
The Trump administration, with its ad hoc Department of Government Efficiency, was circulating false claims of widespread fraud, slashing thousands of Social Security Administration staff members, and threatening to close field offices. “A whole mixture of negative signals about Social Security were coming from the White House,” Smalligan said.
“Having people go at the government with a chain saw was not helpful,” Munnell agreed, referring to a much-publicized stunt in which DOGE chief Elon Musk appeared onstage brandishing the tool at a conservative conference. He has called Social Security “the biggest Ponzi scheme of all time.”
Perhaps it shouldn’t have been surprising that last year so many older Americans decided they’d better grab their benefits while they could.
(Something beneficiaries may not know: Those who regret claiming at full retirement age but before age 70 can direct Social Security to suspend their benefits, then reclaim them later when the payments are higher, with adjustments for money already received. “It’s not irrevocable,” Smalligan said.)
In a 2021 study by the Boston College center, researchers showed more than 3,100 participants headlines about Social Security. One headline referred fairly neutrally to “a long-term financing shortfall,” while others contained scarier phrases like “deplete its reserves” and “headed toward insolvency.” The accompanying short text stayed the same.
“With the headlines that were more fear-inducing, people tended to say they would claim earlier, about a year earlier,” than the control group reading the neutral headline, said Gal Wettstein, associate director of health and insurance at the center and co-author of the study.

Letters to the Editor is a periodic feature. We welcome all comments and will publish a selection. We edit for length and clarity and require full names.
Reader Recipe Exchange
Just saw Rachana Pradhan’s Nov. 13 “The Week in Brief” newsletter (“He Was Diagnosed With Cancer. Then His Medicaid Was Thrown Into Question”). Nice reporting out of Nebraska! Tongue-in-cheek, she asked for Thanksgiving Day recipe submissions. So, below is my recipe for roasted carrots and green sauce. A tasty, veggie-forward side:
Roasted Rainbow Carrots with Green Sauce
Ingredients
For the carrots:
- Rainbow carrots, with about 1 inch of green tops left attached
- Extra-virgin olive oil, for coating
- Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
For the green sauce:
- 1 small bunch cilantro, tough stems trimmed
- 1 small bunch parsley, tough stems trimmed
- 3 oil-packed anchovy fillets
- 1 small garlic clove, crushed
- ⅔ cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 5 Tbs. fresh lemon juice
- 2 tsps. Dijon mustard
- Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
Instructions
- Prepare the oven and carrots. Heat the oven to 425°F. Line a rimmed sheet pan with parchment paper. Trim the carrot greens, leaving about 1 inch attached. I like keeping this little bit of green because it crisps up deliciously in the oven. Scrub the carrots, leaving the skins on, and wash carefully around the tops. Pat dry. Halve any thick carrots lengthwise so they cook evenly.
- Season and roast. Place the carrots on the prepared pan. Drizzle with olive oil, lightly coating the attached greens as well. Sprinkle with salt and pepper. Toss to coat. Arrange in a single layer with space between them. Roast for 20–30 minutes, turning halfway through, until deeply caramelized and fork-tender. Larger carrots may need additional time.
- Make the green sauce. Combine the cilantro, parsley, anchovies, garlic, olive oil, lemon juice, and Dijon mustard in a blender or food processor. Purée until nearly smooth. Taste and season with salt and pepper, keeping in mind that the anchovies already add salt.
- Serve. Transfer the warm carrots to a serving platter and spoon some of the green sauce over them, leaving the crisp tops exposed. Serve the remaining sauce on the side.
— Andy DiAntonio, director of communications for the National Health Law Program; Washington, D.C.
Voices Across the Political Spectrum
I’m writing about Bram Sable-Smith’s Oct. 29 article, “The Campaign To Defend Trans Healthcare in Missouri Is Slow Going, on Purpose,” which NPR and its member stations carried as a top story five days before Missouri voted to reject Amendment 3.
In the interest of disclosure: I’m the executive director of LGB Courage Coalition, a lesbian, and a former case manager at Washington University’s pediatric gender center, and I supported the measure’s restrictions on pediatric gender medicine. I’m not asking you to take my side. I only expect you to hold such articles to the highest standards.
First, an unchallenged medical claim. The story fact-checked the canvasser’s remark about surgeries with insurance claims data. A few paragraphs later, the canvasser told a voter that puberty blockers are reversible. Voters are persuaded on the page, and that claim had no context. The United Kingdom’s systematic reviews that led to bipartisan restrictions, the Swedish review, and a report from the Department of Health and Human Services titled “Treatment for Pediatric Gender Dysphoria: Review of Evidence and Best Practices” all have rated the evidence for these interventions as low certainty and identified unresolved questions about long-term effects, including bone density and fertility. Whether blockers are fully reversible is contested. A story about persuading undecided voters shouldn’t let a contested claim do the persuading without noting the dispute.
Second, balance. The only voice on the other side was a voter whose view was summarized in one sentence. Across this cycle’s Amendment 3 coverage, supporters of the gender-medicine provisions appeared almost entirely as Republican officials and religious leaders. Missing were the gay, lesbian, and left-leaning clinicians, whistleblowers, and detransitioners who supported restrictions on evidence grounds. Their absence told readers the debate is faith against science, when the systematic reviews say otherwise.
— Jamie Reed, executive director of the LGB Courage Coalition; St. Louis
A Referendum Rerun
I appreciate your coverage of this issue (“Midterm Voters Split on Abortion and Trans Healthcare Ballot Questions,” Nov. 5). I just wanted to point out something that was not mentioned in your article. In Missouri, the state legislature banned gender-affirming care for minors in 2023. When the ballot measure to restrict abortion and ban gender-affirming care for minors was presented to the public, it was pointed out that you would be voting to ban something that was already banned. I believe this may have influenced those who voted against the measure. Just thought this should be mentioned for context.
— Jeffrey Best; St. Louis

Katheryn Houghton’s article “Hospital Beds for the Nation’s Sickest Kids Are Disappearing” (Oct. 28) discusses the closures of pediatric units at rural hospitals. A series of consecutive federal emergency orders that have kept a Florida coal plant running beyond its scheduled retirement have come at a cost to ratepayers of some $25.6 million, according to a new analysis.
The Stanton Energy Center in Orlando is one of six power-generating facilities nationwide where the Trump administration ordered the reversal of plans to wind down coal plants. Together the orders have cost ratepayers some $593 million, according to the analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund.
The group said the orders were issued under a law designed for temporary emergencies such as weather events, but the Trump administration repeatedly has renewed the orders. In Florida, the Orlando Utilities Commission had planned to move one of two coal-fired plants at Stanton into a state of “extended cold shutdown” by the end of May 2026, as part of a plan to transition to renewable energy and achieve net zero emissions by 2050.
The Department of Energy issued an initial order to keep the plant running in June and another in September that expires Nov. 30. OUC is the state’s second-largest municipal utility, serving more than 288,000 customers in Orange and Osceola counties in central Florida.
“If they stay true to form then they’re going to issue another order,” said Bradley Marshall, senior attorney at Earthjustice, which filed a legal challenge against the Trump administration over the situation at Stanton.
“We know that a lot of these coal plants were due to be retired for a reason. They simply weren’t economic to run anymore,” he said. “When you unexpectedly have to keep a plant running that you were planning to retire, and you don’t need to keep it running for any kind of reliability purpose but because the Trump administration has told you to keep it running, it shouldn’t be surprising there are a lot of economic costs associated with that.”
The Department of Energy has attributed an energy emergency in Florida to a shortage of facilities and anticipated growing demand related to a burgeoning data center industry in the state. The agency also noted a February cold snap that strained OUC’s resources.
“Radical climate activists will say anything to further their anti-energy agenda. The Trump Administration’s actions—including saving six coal-fired plants, preserving more than 17 gigawatts of coal power from retirement, and unleashing backup power generation—likely saved hundreds of American lives during peak demand periods,” a Department of Energy spokesperson told Inside Climate News.
“The Energy Department remains committed to ensuring reliable power generation is available for American families and businesses, unlike past Democrat leaders, whose energy subtraction policies threatened grid reliability, especially during periods of peak demand.”
The Environmental Defense Fund said the coal plant at Stanton, along with the others under emergency orders, are not cost-competitive with clean energy sources. OUC’s financial reports show coal in recent years has been its most expensive fuel per megawatt-hour. The group, which is involved in the same legal challenge with Earthjustice, estimated that keeping the plant running would cost about $6.2 million a month.
Ted Kelly, director and lead counsel specializing in clean energy at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the Trump administration has been issuing the emergency orders as the coal plants are scheduled to retire, and that Stanton was next on the list, so to speak. He said one reason for the higher costs was that all of the coal plants under emergency orders are older.
“They’re all more than 20 years old, and so in general as plants get older they have more problems,” he said. “Coal just is a costly resource.”

Donate Now
OUC noted, in response to an inquiry from Inside Climate News, that its board in December will consider a proposed fuel rate decrease that would save customers about $5 each monthly, or $3.3 million total. If approved, the new rate would take effect in April 2027.
“Claims regarding the operating costs of Stanton Unit 1 are based on assumptions that do not reflect the comprehensive analysis OUC regularly undergoes to balance reliability, affordability, and sustainability,” a representative for the utility said in a statement provided to Inside Climate News.
The utility said its own analysis found that “adding new solar and energy storage while enhancing fuel flexibility at Stanton Units 1 and 2 is a more cost-effective option than building new fossil-based generation resources in the near term and/or converting the units strictly to 100% natural gas. This fuel flexibility also helps maintain affordable and reliable electric service while protecting customers from fuel market volatility. The recommended portfolio balances affordability, reliability, sustainability, and resiliency while achieving OUC’s CO2 reduction goals of 50% by 2030 and 75% by 2040.”
The Environmental Defense Fund, Sierra Club and Earthjustice, on behalf of Florida Rising, a grassroots group representing communities of color, filed the legal challenge in July asking the Department of Energy to reconsider the order in Florida. The groups argued the order failed to show that an emergency actually exists, exceeded the agency’s statutory authority and violated the National Environmental Policy Act.
The groups also said continuing to operate the coal plant would increase air pollution that is harmful to those living around the facility. It also would lead to higher energy costs for Floridians, further burdening underserved communities that especially are vulnerable to hotter temperatures, rising seas and more damaging storms as the global climate warms. Survivors of a 2019 landslide in eastern Uganda that killed more than 50 people have taken their fight for relocation and compensation to the United Nations.
The 48 complainants accuse the government of violating Uganda's constitution by failing to put effective disaster management measures in Bududa, a mountainous district prone to landslides.
Their case comes as heavy rains raise the risk of further landslides. They say the government relocation programme ignores their safety, land rights and livelihoods.
The UN Human Rights Committee is considering what is believed to be the first case seeking climate adaptation measures, one that could set a global precedent.
At least 33 of the 53 people who died in the 2019 landslide were children. Years later, survivors say every spell of heavy rain brings back fears of another tragedy.
William Tsama, one of the claimants, lost four members of his family.
"My quest should be a lesson," he said.
"Victims in such situations, ignored by governments, can take them to court to compel them to help their citizens."
Uganda introduced a resettlement plan for landslide-prone areas in 2011, but progress has been limited, with relatively few people relocated.
Last month, it launched a new resettlement programme offering affected households 18m Ugandan shillings ($4,300; Â£3,300) to help them move to safer areas.
But some survivors have questioned whether the amount is enough to cover the cost of relocating and rebuilding their lives.
Under the programme, families can choose between receiving two acres of land, valued at 8m shillings, plus 10m shillings towards building a house, or taking the equivalent land allowance in cash, alongside the same housing grant.
The scheme is expected to benefit 1,410 households identified as living in high-risk areas.
The government has now given residents of designated high-risk areas two months, from November to December, to leave or face forced eviction.
The threat extends beyond landslides. The complainants say changing rainfall patterns and declining soil fertility have also affected farming, leaving many families struggling to secure their livelihoods.
"I want to get a new good place for my people, so even if I die, they will be okay. I am an old man, but I am doing it for my children," Tsama said.
The survivors first launched legal action in 2020 in Uganda, and received support from Ugandan environmental organisation Greenwatch three years later.
They are seeking compensation for lost family members and livelihoods, as well as emergency measures, including accessible early-warning systems in high-risk areas.
Greenwatch Executive Director Samantha Atukunda Kakuru Mwesigwa said the case is about changing how governments prepare and respond to climate-related disasters.
"Justice for claimants is not just about winning in court. It is about forcing government policy to keep pace with a changing climate, and ensuring loss and damage is no longer an afterthought in disaster management," she said.
The threat of climate-related disasters extends across East Africa.
In Kenya, floods and landslides killed at least 181 people between March and May 2024, according to the Kenya Red Cross. In Rwanda, floods and landslides killed 135 people in May 2023.
The dangers are also being felt further afield. In October 2026, a flash flood swept through Nepal's Gorkha district after a landslide blocked a river, washing away homes and infrastructure, and killing over 1,500 people.
"Disasters like the one in Bududa are only getting worse because of climate change â and they are happening all around the world, as we've seen recently and tragically in Nepal," ClientEarth lawyer Vesselina Newman said.
She said poorer countries, which have contributed relatively little to global emissions, are bearing some of the heaviest consequences of climate change and need greater financial support.
"High income countries must provide financial assistance and ensure that sufficient money goes directly to countries like Uganda, so they can roll out life-saving adaptation measures," she said.
The complainants say relocation must involve more than moving people out of danger.
They want the government to protect their livelihoods, respect their land rights, and take account of individual needs.
The case is now before the United Nations Human Rights Committee, which will ask the Ugandan government to respond within six months.

Senegalese authorities are continuing search operations after a boat reportedly carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast.
Initial reports said that one person had died, but some local media have reported that at least four bodies have been recovered. Dozens of people are still missing.
Personal belongings were found on the badly damaged boat, which washed ashore near the village of Yenne, south of Dakar. Search operations continued throughout Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday.
This comes less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the coast of the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters.
Oumar Sow, a representative of the village chief, said the latest tragedy happened around 02:00 local time (02:00 GMT).
"Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," the AFP news agency quoted him as saying.
A survivor questioned by the police said there were about 100 people on the boat, including five women, AFP reported.
Police recovered identity documents, several mobile phones and personal belongings from the wreckage, including a school enrolment document.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about a renewed increase in irregular departure by migrants hoping to reach Europe.
He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem.
Following last month's tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the dangerous sea crossings.
Many thousands of people from West Africa have died or gone missing trying to flee conflict, authoritarian rule or poverty in recent years.
The UN's migration agency IOM said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone.
It warned the figures were likely to be an underestimate, as many boats disappear without leaving survivors or a trace.
As it has become more difficult to reach Europe through North Africa, due to tighter controls and increased co-operation with European countries, migrants are increasingly targeting Spain's Canary Islands.
They often travel in wooden boats known as pirogues that are frequently overloaded and not suited to such long voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
Most migrants arriving in the Canary Islands this year are from Senegal, according to the UN.
They are driven to leave home by limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks, according to the IOM.
On 7 November, El Hierro, one of the Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency following a surge in migrant arrivals.
It said more than 3,300 people had reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. This amounts to almost a third of the island's population.
