When refinery operators went on strike to demand safer conditions at a renewable fuels facility northeast of San Francisco in April, they worried that workers brought in to replace them hadn’t been adequately trained to run their potentially explosive processing units. The strikers’ concerns grew as they saw unusually frequent and intense flaring, giant flames shooting up from stacks that burn flammable gases to prevent explosions—a sign of problems inside the plant.
California inspectors confirmed workers’ concerns last month. The state’s Division of Occupational Safety and Health, known as Cal/OSHA, cited Marathon for several violations. Among the most serious was the failure “to train each employee before starting work in a newly assigned process” and “provide the training curriculum … and training certification for newly assigned employees,” documents reviewed by Inside Climate News reveal.
Marathon USW Local 5 members raised their safety concerns during months of contract negotiations with the company, which rejected workers’ proposals to address fatigue from relentless overtime shifts resulting from chronic understaffing. The strike turned into a lockout in June, when Marathon rebuffed the union’s unconditional return-to-work offer.
Operators’ fears about safety emerged as soon as they left the plant to go on strike at midnight on April 27. They realized the people who were taking over their shift had not been trained on their units, said Nick Plurkowski, United Steelworkers Local 5 president. “We had safety concerns with the way the shift turnovers went,” he said.
Plurkowski called Cal/OSHA the next day to outline the workers’ concerns.
Now the workers are even more concerned about inadequate operator training and oversight of the plant’s volatile operations, which they blamed for the catastrophic accident that nearly killed their co-worker Jerome Serrano three years ago on Nov. 19.
The federal agency that investigates the causes of industrial accidents agreed with the workers.
Marathon Martinez’s failure to identify problems with the furnace that processes flammable materials or properly label equipment led to the explosion that enveloped Serrano in a fireball, the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board concluded in March 2025.
“Inadequate operating procedures and operator training for safe burner operation and inadequate engineering controls for operators to identify combustion issues inside the fired heater also contributed to the incident,” the board concluded in its final report.
Workers decided to walk out a year later, saying Marathon rejected their proposals to address safety concerns and refused to offer them the same terms it had negotiated with the national bargaining units that covered more than 30,000 workers across the petroleum and renewables industry.
Cal/OSHA found many of the same problems identified by the Chemical Safety Board over the course of several inspections between April and October. Inspectors determined that at least a dozen employees hadn’t received proper training, including two shift supervisors and 10 operators.
Martinez Renewables has appealed the citations to the state Occupational Safety and Health Appeals Board, said Marathon Petroleum Corp. spokesperson Jamal Kheiry. “We continue to staff the Martinez Renewables facility with highly qualified Marathon personnel, including supervisors, engineers and technical experts with extensive experience and training in safe, reliable plant operations,” Kheiry said. The company looks forward to working with state officials “to resolve the alleged violations,” he said.
Denisse Gómez, a Cal/OSHA spokesperson, confirmed that Marathon appealed the citations. She said the agency is unable to comment on the findings while the appeal is pending.
Altogether, Cal/OSHA cited Marathon for 10 violations, including three classified as serious: inadequate training, uninsulated high-temperature equipment and faulty emergency eyewash stations.

Other violations include failures to provide warning labels on fuel-storage containers; inaccessible fire extinguishers; potential tripping and electrocution hazards; and lack of a heat-illness prevention plan that provides adequate shade, breaks and water for employees loading railcars outside or performing strenuous tasks in rubber suits in high-heat areas. Inspectors spoke with employees who did not know how to acclimate to hot working conditions, as required by California’s heat-illness prevention standard.
Those precautions are critical in refineries, which rely on high heat for processing fuels. California requires pipes or other surfaces that reach 140 degrees Fahrenheit to be insulated to limit harm from accidental contact. Inspectors found uninsulated equipment with average heat readings exceeding 550 degrees F.
That finding outraged Plurkowski, who wondered how workers are supposed to stay safe while doing hour-long tasks while sweating nonstop and standing a foot away from a surface that will melt their skin if they touch it.
While those types of safety issues must be corrected, he said, it’s the lack of training that’s most troubling.
Cal/OSHA “yellow tagged” the unit that burned Serrano, which prohibited anyone from running it until the agency could confirm that employees were sufficiently qualified to operate it safely. Violating a yellow tag results in fines, jail or both.
But the units were tagged only because of “Jerome’s horrific accident,” Plurkowski said. “I just asked OSHA today if they would yellow tag a unit due to lack of training, and they said probably not.”
He asked because he believes the amount of flaring coming from the plant means things are not running smoothly.

4e1f7d6a2cb4.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/kushner-says-russia-is-comfortable-with-nato-like-security-guarantees-for-ukraine-to-end-war-after-trump-talks-with-putin Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Kushner says Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end war after Trump talks with Putin World Nov 19, 2026 1:32 PM EST BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark. Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S. President Donald Trump discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday. READ MORE: For Putin, sharing a spotlight with Trump and Xi boosts his profile on the global stage Kushner and Witkoff met with European allies in Berlin to discuss their support for Ukraine after a third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Russian-held Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, officials said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion. Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable. The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between Kushner, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump's direct talks with Putin. The American leader called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said. Putin acknowledges the damage and vows to strike back "We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that," Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China. He insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered the bridge closed to the transport of military hardware or ammunition. Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been "seriously damaged" but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section is believed to be stronger than the road side, to bear the greater weight of cargo wagons. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine. A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Zelenskyy, and the train track was damaged by domestically produced Neptune missiles, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said. Now Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where "our drones are waiting for the cargo," the ministry said. A Ukrainian attack on Russia's Saratov region killed three people and wounded two others, local Gov. Roman Busargin said, and a drone killed a woman traveling by bicycle with her 8-year-old grandson in the Bryansk region, Gov. Egor Kovalchuk said. Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations. Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said. Two people, including a 44-year-old woman, were killed and at least 23 people, including a 12-year-old boy, were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions. But Kyiv's defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances. Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine's resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv's domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries. Kyiv fears Trump and Putin may try to decide Ukraine's fate In China, Trump called Putin "my friend." The American president's relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured. European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy. Ukrainian officials fear their country's fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments are alarmed by Moscow's aggression. The question of U.S. support for Ukraine, severely curtailed under Trump, could be raised by Democrats in Congress after their wins in the midterm elections. 9eac88092d30.text: President Trump said in a brief phone interview Thursday that he won't make a determination on his next step in the Iran war until the new year. "I am not rushing into any decision [on Iran]. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," Trump told Axios from Air Force One, on his way back to the U.S. from China. Why it matters: The president's comments come as he faces heavy pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to unleash a decisive bombing campaign soon. Yes, but: Trump could change his mind at any moment. And he wouldn't telegraph plans for an imminent attack even if that's what he was intending to do. A day before the war began in February, Trump said he hadn't made a decision, when in fact he had already ordered strikes. Between the lines: Trump's stated timing could mean he's giving more time for the naval blockade and the economic pressure campaign to play out, as many of his advisers and leaders of Gulf countries are urging. But it could also indicate that if Iran doesn't make concessions by the end of the year, Trump wants to leave himself enough time for military action before the new Democratic-controlled Congress settles in. Driving the news: While stating last week that a major new round of strikes on Iran was " quite unlikely ," Trump is still considering a joint attack with Israel, Axios reported on Wednesday. The president's deliberations are likely to pick up when he returns from Asia. Any U.S. operation would involve Israel and could include strikes on suspected Iranian nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain. Bridges and power plants could also be targeted, as well as Iranian military and civilian leaders. Behind the scenes: The White House has asked the Pentagon and intelligence experts for their assessments of how Iran would respond to each of the strike scenarios the U.S. military has prepared, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. The White House has asked whether any of the options would avoid triggering a devastating Iranian retaliation against Gulf countries' oil and gas facilities. The intrigue: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad, Roman Gofman, visited Washington and Miami last week for talks with CIA Director John Ratcliffe and White House envoy Steve Witkoff. Gofman, one of Netanyahu's closest confidants, was sent by the Israeli prime minister to press for resuming the war against Iran, an Israeli source said. The Mossad director relayed Israel's concerns about Iranian activities related to chemical weapons development, U.S. and Israeli sources said. Israel claims it has intelligence showing that Iran has stepped up its research and development of chemical weapons as well as conducted tests. Trump was briefed about this new intelligence, a U.S. official said.

7feba83eae79.text: By — Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press By — Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Kelvin Chan, Associated Press By — Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/are-tech-disruptions-and-and-outages-the-new-normal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Are tech disruptions and and outages the new normal? Nation Nov 19, 2026 1:21 PM EST Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions. In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal. READ MORE: Duffy keeps blaming L3Harris after FAA ground stop, even as cause remains unknown Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government's Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was "zero" indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals. The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches. Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. "To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it's made them realize how many parts of their lives they've handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don't fully understand," Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. "I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way." What's gone offline recently Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors. Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a "latent defect" in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday. Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved. WATCH: What a string of tech problems reveals about America's digital vulnerabilities And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app. Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday "during scheduled routine maintenance." The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there's no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack. Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from "AI / agents." It didn't specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. A press contact for Microsoft didn't immediately have further information to share when reached by The Associated Press. The other companies also did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email. AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps. For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays. President Donald Trump's director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA's outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month's PHP alert has caused some systems to "not come back up" as expected. "That is what has happened at the NSA today," he said. Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world's most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it. At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions. READ MORE: Could everything be broken? Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks â and it appears that he left with little in return.
In the end, the visuals of the meeting â the "optics", as political wags like to say â may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as an historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.
In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" â as evidence that the trip already was a success.
That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.
So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.
While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.
On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.
For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique, released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".
That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric.
"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.
A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court â a recent target of American ire.
If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.
While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.
But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism.
"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday.
"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."
Democrats, for their part, did not mince words.
"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.
Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.
In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.
Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

fe24389dd74d.text: President Trump still considers Elon Musk an ally despite the world's richest man saying he's "not MAGA," the president told NBC News on Thursday. Why it matters: Musk's latest break from Trump's political movement comes after he spent millions backing Republicans in the midterms, only to see Democrats win control of Congress and many state governments. Trump and Musk have weathered public feuds before, repeatedly reconciling despite disagreements. Driving the news: "He's a friend of mine," Trump told NBC News of Musk. "There are lots of definitions out there. MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don't do very well," Trump said. "Elon's got very good intentions," he said. "I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me." Catch up quick: Musk said at the The New York Times' DealBook Summit Wednesday that he considers himself politically moderate. "I'm not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that," Musk told the New York Times. Musk said he felt "pretty foolish" about spending millions in the midterms. "If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money," he said. Yes, but: Musk reportedly accompanied Trump to China this week, underscoring how their personal relationship has endured despite their political differences. Between the lines: Musk may reject the MAGA label, but he has spent years championing its culture wars, bankrolling Republicans and turning X, the social media platform he bought for $44 billion, into a megaphone for far-right voices. He has attacked diversity initiatives, amplified anti-immigration rhetoric and promoted an antisemitic conspiracy theory for which he later apologized . He has also railed against what he calls the "woke mind virus" and backed far-right political movements abroad. Flashback: Musk has clashed with Trump over government spending, tariffs, climate policy and the investigation into Jeffrey Epstein . In October 2024, Musk joked at a Trump rally , "I'm not just MAGA, I'm dark MAGA." Despite their disagreements, Musk has repeatedly reentered Trump's orbit. What we're watching: Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) and Rep. Yassamin Ansari ( D-Ariz.) suggested the tech mogul could still face Congressional probes once Democrats take office next year regardless of whether he breaks with MAGA.

US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.
The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.
In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.
Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".
Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.
In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.
While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".
He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".
Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.
The opening remarks of the trilateral gave some indication about what was to be discussed during the closed-door meeting.
Before giving the floor to his fellow leaders, Xi said that "positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement".
Putin followed this by highlighting a shared interest in ending the Ukraine war and said the conversation would also touch on food and energy security.
China has officially remained neutral since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, rejecting accusations from Kyiv and its allies that it has been tacitly supporting Moscow, including by exporting dual-use technology used by the Russian military.
Beijing has also repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Meanwhile, Trump closed by saying the presidents of three of the world's largest countries have a "special responsibility" to maintain productive dialogue.
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," he said, adding: "We feel the opposite."
Trump referenced the three countries' nuclear capabilities and said they are "uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth".
It is "vital" that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world", he said, adding: "That's what we're doing in Iran."
"We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon".
Trump then turned to Ukraine and said he and Putin have had a "long discussion" on the conflict there already.
He added that Putin "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".
Putin addressed the media following the trilateral meeting and described it as an "important chapter in the history of diplomacy".
He said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine - but he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.
As the talks were under way in China, and even as Putin was holding his press conference claiming to be ready for peace, Ukraine's capital Kyiv was under attack from Russian drones.
Putin has repeatedly rejected all ceasefire offers from Ukraine, insisting on his maximalist demands which Kyiv and its European allies say are tantamount to de facto capitulation of Ukraine.
In Shenzhen, the Kremlin leader also vowed a "far more painful" retaliation in response to Ukrainian attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea. A missile and drone attack on Tuesday destroyed its central road section.
There was no mention from Putin of almost five years of Russian attacks on power plants, bridges and residential buildings in Ukraine.
The Russian president also directly addressed comparisons between his meeting with Trump and Xi and the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the Soviet Union, Britain and the US met towards the end of World War Two.
"Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after WW2.
"And when it comes to today's conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted."
The Kremlin released a video showing Putin leaving the summit venue and saying goodbye to Xi.
"Thank you for organising this," Putin said. "I don't think anyone even expected everything to go so well."
Meanwhile, China's president described his meeting with Putin and Trump as "positive, constructive, and highly productive", according to the country's state broadcaster CCTV.
It added that Xi recalled "the history of fighting side-by-side during WW2", as the three leaders emphasised the importance of "cherishing the hard-won peace".
Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Putin.
Some Russian newspapers called it a "diplomatic victory" as after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine many Western leaders were trying to isolate him.
The summit also marked the first time since Russia's war in Ukraine began that Putin took part in an international gathering attended by leaders from countries including Canada, Japan and Australia.
US lawmakers responded with frustration to Trump's warmth towards America's geopolitical adversaries.

Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The BBC's Anna Holligan is in the Hague and reports on what the ICJ's ruling means.
More on this story: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules

- Published
A South Carolina woman who admitted to drowning her two sons 32 years ago has been denied parole for a second time.
Susan Smith, 55, was convicted of killing her boys by strapping them into their car seats and rolling her vehicle into a lake in 1994.
"I got to my lowest when I let that car go into that lake," Smith said during a hearing on Thursday with the state board that decides whether to release those in prison on parole.
The seven-member board later unanimously turned down her request to be freed. The father of the two boys has vowed to continue to oppose her release, and several people spoke against her in the hearing.
Smith, whose lawyers had argued she suffered a mental breakdown during the crime, can apply to the South Carolina Board of Probation, Parole and Pardon Services for parole every two years.
She told the board that she had changed and matured since killing three-year-old Michael and one-year-old Alex, and that "I am not the same person I was 32 years ago".
She also said she was "very, very sorry" and that she would go back and change the circumstances if she could.
"They were innocent children," Smith said. "They did not deserve to die."
Her children's father, David Smith, attended the hearing so he could advocate for their sons, he said.
The 32 years, he said, do not take away what Smith "deliberately" did.
"I know in my heart granting her parole would be a huge injustice to Michael and Alex," said David Smith, who had pinned a photo of both his sons to his lapel.
Prosecutors argued during the trial that Smith killed the boys after a man with whom she was having an affair told her that her sons were the reason that the pair did not have a future together.
At Thursday's hearing, Smith said: "This did not happen because of a man. That's just not true."
When the boys first disappeared, Smith said she was carjacked late at night and a man drove away with her car. While she pleaded publicly for their safe return, her sons were at the bottom of a nearby lake.
But ultimately she confessed to the crime.
Defence lawyers said she had wanted to die with her children but left the car at the last minute.
Smith was convicted of murder. Under South Carolina law at the time, she was allowed to request parole every two years after serving 30 years in prison.
In the US, some people convicted of crimes are eligible for parole, which means they can be released from incarceration.
She would have needed two-thirds of the board members present to vote in her favour to be freed.

8c347b4e95bc.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/im-not-maga-elon-musk-says-after-republicans-midterm-thrashing Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 'I'm not MAGA,' Elon Musk says after Republicans' midterm thrashing Politics Nov 19, 2026 12:09 PM EST ATLANTA (AP) — Elon Musk was on the front row at Donald Trump's second inauguration and has spent hundreds of millions of dollars trying to help the Republican president and his "Make America Great Again" allies win elections. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Now, after Republicans' midterm thrashing by Democrats, the world's richest man insists he's not a MAGA acolyte after all and feels "pretty foolish" for spending so much money on the cause. "I mean, I'm not MAGA," Musk told The New York Times on Wednesday during the newspaper's DealBook Summit. "I'm not sure what MAGA means," the Tesla and SpaceX CEO continued, "but I, I don't think I'm, like, if, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that. I think there are, there, there are positives and negatives in both parties." Musk, who has based himself and several of his companies in Texas, spent more than $400 million on Trump-aligned Republicans running in November. That included around $200 million backing Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico. Democrats scored sweeping victories after making Musk, other tech titans and the proliferation of artificial intelligence and AI data centers a feature of the midterm campaigns. Their party will take control of Congress and many more U.S. statehouses in January, with a promise of a regulatory crackdown and congressional investigations into tech firms' dealings with the Trump administration. That leaves Musk and others scrambling to rebrand themselves after spending years aligning closely with Trump and his fellow Republicans as they sought government contracts and favorable policies on everything from taxation to AI regulation. WATCH: How Elon Musk gained so much power over U.S. security interests Palantir co-founder and CEO Alex Karp, whose software is used by the Pentagon, among his lucrative government portfolio, earlier this month raised eyebrows when he insisted to Politico that he's always been a progressive. "I've been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment," he said. "I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir — all of our products are essentially progressive." Karp, a donor to Trump's White House ballroom project who has adopted the president's rhetoric to describe his own business as "anti-woke," said he's willing to support a Democrat for president in 2028. At the Times' event, Musk said if he had a do-over, he "probably" would have "spent less money" on the midterms. "I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," Musk told columnist Andrew Sorkin. "Or maybe it would've been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money." Musk sat alongside other Big Tech billionaires at Trump's inauguration and led the president's Department of Government Efficiency, a post that for months made him the most high-profile figure in the administration other than Trump himself. Hours after Trump was sworn in on Jan. 20, 2025, Musk appeared at a Trump rally in Washington, where he enthusiastically embraced the president's agenda and his supporters. "This was no ordinary victory," he said. "This was a fork in the road of human civilization. OK? There are elections that come and go. Some elections are important, some are not. But this one really mattered. ... It is thanks to you that the future of civilization is assured." Some Democrats were unimpressed with Musk's change in tenor. Responding to Musk's turnabout on X, the social media platform that Musk owns, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona was concise: "You are still getting a subpoena." d5890408f66d.text: Meta's greenhouse gas emissions surged 45% last year amid its AI infrastructure boom, prompting the tech giant to reconsider its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2030. Why it matters : Other tech giants have reported rising emissions as they race to build data centers, but Meta is going a step further by explicitly reconsidering its climate deadline. Driving the news : The just-released sustainability report of the tech giant, one of North America's largest data centers operators , shows just how much growth in the AI industry is outpacing any efficiency gains. Meta executives said they were "re-evaluating" the 2030 goal, first announced in 2020 when the company was still known as Facebook and before the generative AI boom. They didn't specify what changes they're considering or when they'll make a decision. By the numbers : Meta's electricity use jumped 35%, comparable to other tech giants. But Meta's emissions increase of 45% is far higher than its peers, Google (18%), Amazon (16%) and Microsoft (25%). What they're saying: "When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned," wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability. "The reality has been far more complex." Zoom out : The race among tech giants to dominate AI is pushing their climate goals into the backseat, even as they continue investing heavily in clean energy. State of play : Meta says it has contracted more than 30 gigawatts of clean energy, including nuclear, solar and geothermal, though less than half that capacity is generating electricity so far. The intrigue : Meta's report says it may turn to natural gas plants to power data centers when utilities can't deliver electricity fast enough — even though such projects are already underway. It's also seeking to offset some of the methane emissions associated with its natural gas use by paying for cleaner gas production elsewhere. Reality check : Meta's 45% emissions increase doesn't yet reflect the full impact of some of its biggest planned natural gas projects, suggesting its footprint could grow considerably more. In Louisiana, utility Entergy is pursuing seven new gas-fired generating units totaling more than 5,200 megawatts to serve Meta's data centers. Separately, Ohio regulators approved a 200-megawatt gas plant built specifically to power Meta's data centers, while research firm Cleanview identifies a 521-megawatt gas project under construction for Meta in Utah. Friction point : Meta's report was also revealing about water, a more immediate concern for many communities near data centers. The company's direct water consumption fell 4%, but consumption in highly water-stressed regions rose 24%. The estimated water consumption associated with generating its electricity — an often-overlooked environmental impact — rose 37% before accounting for its clean-energy purchases. How it works : Natural gas plants typically use substantial amounts of water for cooling, meaning Meta's growing reliance on gas could increase its indirect water footprint even as its data centers become more water-efficient. Yes, but : Meta is the only tech giant to disclose the water consumption associated with electricity, earning it high marks for transparency from Alex de Vries-Gao, a researcher at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam who has studied AI's environmental footprint. What we're watching : Meta's reconsideration of its climate deadline raises the question of whether other tech giants will eventually follow suit as the AI boom continues to strain their environmental commitments.

da9e2752fd11.text: By — Vladimir Isachenkov, Associated Press Vladimir Isachenkov, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/for-putin-sharing-a-spotlight-with-trump-and-xi-boosts-his-profile-on-the-global-stage Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter For Putin, sharing a spotlight with Trump and Xi boosts his profile on the global stage World Nov 19, 2026 11:51 AM EST For Russian President Vladimir Putin, Thursday's three-way meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping offered a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to demonstrate that he heads a superpower on a par with the United States and China. READ MORE: No breakthroughs from Trump, Xi and Putin's 3-way talks on nuclear risks While dealing another blow to Western efforts to isolate Putin, it also gave him an opportunity to try to persuade Trump to lean into Moscow's demands for a settlement in Ukraine at a time when Washington wants to broker a peace deal. Putin said afterward that the meeting showed that the three-way format was "useful and substantive" and marked "serious joint work," including discussions on Ukraine. Earlier Thursday, Trump and Putin also met separately. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Kyiv and its European allies viewed the meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, with deep suspicion. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Europeans feared another "Anchorage moment," a reference to a Putin-Trump meeting in Alaska in August 2025 that produced proposals that were rejected by Ukraine and its partners. READ MORE: 'The symbol of the occupation': Ukraine destroys span of Kerch Bridge linking Russia with Crimea Putin said Thursday that Russia accepted what he described as a U.S.-proposed compromise in Anchorage, declaring that Ukraine and its European allies would better accept it now or face tougher demands. The 3-way meeting reminded some of the 1945 Yalta conference The three-way meeting raised comparisons to the 1945 Yalta conference, where the wartime leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union divided Germany and Berlin, carved out zones of influence in Europe, and agreed to establish the United Nations. The Kremlin, which long has courted the concept of a "multipolar world" offering an equal say to all nations, plays down the Yalta parallels, which also are unwelcome to China for similar reasons. Asked about the analogies, Putin responded that just as Yalta conference cemented the "realities" at the time, "they will have to accept the realities in today's conflicts," an apparent reference to Moscow's demands to Kyiv and its allies. Fyodor Lukyanov, a Moscow-based foreign policy expert, noted that the Kremlin seems to believe the leaders could "reach agreements and make decisions that will determine global developments." Of the three nations, "it seems that only Russia really believes in the possibility of global control," he told a recent roundtable. Chatham House director Bronwen Maddox said in a commentary ahead of the three-way meeting that "standing with Xi and Trump, Putin will look like one of the three main leaders of the world," even though "Russia is no superpower" and its economy, overloaded with military spending, is dwindling. She warned that "the danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force." The meeting followed U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine held in Abu Dhabi last week for the first time in nine months. The negotiations produced few visible results as the parties stuck to their sharply divergent demands. Trump appears to lean toward Moscow Putin welcomed a U.S. proposal to discuss broader European security as part of a possible settlement, an offer that hews to a longtime Russian demand for the West to take Moscow's security concerns into account. Kyiv and its allies oppose the idea, fearing it could allow Russia to divert attention from a Ukrainian settlement and try to pursue its demands. Trump's recent moves have appeared to favor the Kremlin. He has waived tough, new sanctions against Moscow and shocked Ukraine and the Europeans by striking a diesel deal that allowed Russia to resume fuel exports, reversing years of U.S. pressure. He urged Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian refineries, blaming them for spiking diesel prices in the U.S. even though they largely were driven by the Iran war. Ukraine also has reported a throttling of Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, a move that was widely seen as an attempt by the U.S. to force Kyiv into making concessions in negotiations. Both sides have escalated their long-range aerial attacks on each other, trying to seize the initiative as fighting largely stalls along the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line. In a major embarrassment to Moscow ahead of the Shenzhen meeting, Ukrainian drones and missiles seriously damaged the Kerch Bridge, Putin's pet project and potent symbol of Moscow's control over Crimea. Russia, meanwhile, continues to pummel Ukraine's power grid and bridges in Kyiv. Putin acknowledged the damage from Ukrainian strikes but argued that Russia has meted out much more punishment and will retaliate further after the bridge attack. He has rejected Kyiv's push for a ceasefire, saying Moscow wants a comprehensive peace deal, not a temporary truce that would allow Ukraine to rest and rearm. The agenda included trade and arms control Trump, Xi and Putin wrapped up their meeting with a statement expressing their commitment to advance U.N. reforms, to increase the production and supply of oil products to ensure a stable flow of energy, and to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation. - Published
The moment a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros took its first steps at a zoo has been captured on video.
The calf was born at Chester Zoo in Cheshire this week.
The video shows 19-year-old mother Asha with her newborn calf at their enclosure after Asha had been pregnant for 15 months.
Keepers said both rhinos were in good health and the birth was an important step in the conservation of the threatened species.
Tom Garland from the rhino team at Chester Zoo said the calf was the fourth born to Asha and father Beni, who died earlier this year following a short and sudden illness.
"It's always exciting to welcome a new calf and Asha has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters," he said.
"Every birth is important for the future of this species and it's wonderful to see another healthy arrival."
The species was driven to near-extinction in the early 1900s by habitat loss and trophy hunting and remains vulnerable to extinction with around 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos living in the wetlands, forests and grasslands of India and Nepal.
The calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding programme that helps to maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos in human care.
Conservation scientist John O'Hanlan said supporting Asha's 15-month pregnancy had been "really exciting".
"She's one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population," he said.
Mark Brayshaw, Head of Mammals at Chester Zoo, said in addition to safeguarding the genetics of the species, Asha and her calf could also help millions of zoo visitors understand the value of conservation.
"Greater one-horned rhinos are much better protected in the wild than they once were, but many of them are concentrated within one national park in India, which makes them vulnerable to illness and environmental changes," he said.
"They still need people to love and protect them."

2d9b0084bc64.text: Myanmar became the first state the International Court of Justice has held responsible for committing genocide in a landmark ruling Thursday. Why it matters: The decision could have far-reaching implications for other genocide cases, including South Africa's case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. State of play: The court ruled 9–6 that Myanmar's violent 2017 military crackdown was intended to destroy the country's persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority. The onslaught killed thousands and forced more than 740,000 Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In 2021, Myanmar's military coup also sparked a civil war that killed over 100,000 people and displaced 5.2 million, according to the Council on Foreign Relation's Global Conflict Tracker. Myanmar has repeatedly denied allegations of mass rape, murder and arson. Yes, but: The legally binding ruling does not guarantee that the roughly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh will be able to safely return home. The court ordered Myanmar to investigate and punish those responsible, provide reparations to the Rohingya and allow refugees to return. Still, the ICJ has no direct way to enforce its ruling. What they're saying: "This judgment must now translate into real action," UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk said in a statement . "The Court has made clear Myanmar's responsibilities. It sends a strong message to all States around the world that those responsible for genocide will be held to account." Myanmar's opposition National Unity Government welcomed the ruling, saying it would "carefully consider the Court's findings and any orders issued" and remained committed to holding perpetrators accountable and preventing further atrocities. Flashback: In 2022, the Biden administration formally declared that Myanmar's military committed genocide against the country's Rohingya minority and crimes against humanity. The ICJ in 2020 ordered Myanmar to protect Rohingya from genocide while the case was pending. Go deeper: UN court rejects Myanmar's objections to Rohingya genocide case

753b68d6bcf7.text: By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/republican-rep-nick-begich-wins-reelection-for-alaska-house-seat Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Republican Rep. Nick Begich wins reelection for Alaska House seat Politics Nov 19, 2026 11:16 AM EST JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich has won reelection to Alaska's lone U.S. House seat, hanging on during a year that saw Democrats regain control in both houses of Congress. His win Wednesday through the state's ranked vote tabulation process was a rare bright spot for Republicans, whose ranks in the House were decimated in the midterms. It came a day after Democrat Mary Peltola flipped one of Alaska's U.S. Senate seats by defeating two-term Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. READ MORE: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate seat, beating Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan Begich was endorsed by President Donald Trump in seeking a second term and pitched himself as an effective leader who was in lockstep with the president's efforts to expand oil and gas drilling and other resource development in the state. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News In a statement after his win, Begich said he takes the job of U.S. representative seriously and thanked the other candidates. "This process requires engagement, and the perspectives brought forward during the campaign added value for Alaskans as they made important decisions about their vote in this race," he said. READ MORE: Democrats flipped 9 U.S. Senate seats — the most in almost 70 years His main challenger was independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired teacher who was endorsed by the state Democratic Party. He sought to focus on affordability issues, limiting the influence of big money in elections and pushing back against the billionaire class in the U.S. Hill said he called Begich to congratulate him. "I wished him well as he continues representing Alaska in Congress, because all Alaskans have a stake in his success," Hill said in a statement. The race was one of the last House races to be called nationally. Once the ranked choice tabulations were complete, Begich finished with nearly 51.4% of the vote, while Hill had nearly 48.7%. The contest also included Democrat Eric Hafner, who is incarcerated in a federal prison in New York after being convicted in 2022 of threatening to kill judges, police officers and others. Hill's campaign had expressed concerns over Hafner's candidacy, particularly in the final weeks of the race, distributing stickers and yard signs labeling him a "fake 'Democrat.'" Hafner, who received nearly 8% of the vote after the Nov. 3 general election, submitted a candidate biography that appeared in state election materials that made no reference to his incarceration. Hill's campaign and state Democrats had cried foul after voters were sent text messages from an undisclosed source supporting Hafner. Hill's campaign manager, Kevin Groh, and the Democratic Party's executive director, Jenny-Marie Stryker, said they never learned who sponsored the texts. Stryker said the party spent "thousands of dollars to send texts clarifying that the real Alaska Democratic Party endorsed Bill Hill." Hafner's mother, Carol "Kitty" Hafner, responded this week to an email from The Associated Press that was sent to her son. She said it would seem "next to impossible" for voters not to know he was in prison, given the coverage of his candidacy for Alaska's House seat in 2024. She also said the "media has gone well overboard identifying his incarceration status." "Absolutely no one encouraged" Hafner to run, his mother wrote, adding that his campaigns have been "entirely independent of any influencers." "Tell President Trump to Pardon Eric Hafner!" she wrote. Both she and her son lack ties to the state. Carol Hafner ran in Alaska's Senate primary in August, finishing sixth with 0.6% of the vote. They have run for office in Alaska and other states before. The major candidates in the U.S. Senate race were Peltola and Sullivan. But the race also included a second Sullivan — Dan J. Sullivan. Peltola faced allegations that members of her team helped recruit the second Sullivan, but she denied involvement in any such effort. "I personally know that I am innocent, so I don't spend a lot of time hand-wringing" about it, she said in an interview Wednesday after her win. The U.S. Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation, but Alaska's U.S. attorney has not said what potential crimes authorities were looking into. 7b31a78db84a.text: By — Mike Corder, Associated Press Mike Corder, Associated Press By — Molly Quell, Associated Press Molly Quell, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/uns-highest-court-finds-myanmar-responsible-for-genocide-in-historic-ruling Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter UN's highest court finds Myanmar responsible for genocide in historic ruling World Nov 19, 2026 11:01 AM EST THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — In a landmark judgment, the United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation and ordered the Southeast Asian nation to allow people who fled the violence to return home. The decision marks the first time the court has ruled that a state committed genocide and comes as the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine. READ MORE: Rohingya refugees demand safe return to Myanmar on 8th anniversary of exodus to Bangladesh But it remains to be seen how much of the ruling can be implemented. The court's rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no way to enforce them beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News International Court of Justice President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar "has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention." The 15-judge panel of the World Court, which included Navi Pillay, the respected international jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize last month, rejected Myanmar's defense that the 2017 campaign was a legitimate operation against insurgents. Iwasawa said that "the court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers." Rohingya say the ruling validates the suffering of their community The atmosphere following the hearing was electric, with lawyers and members of the Rohingya, some of whom had traveled thousands of miles (kilometers) to attend the reading, hugging and crying. "I'm beyond ecstatic today, hearing the judgment, being read out in detail. A lot of those moments and instances that the judges really went into detail, it really validates the kind of experience that Rohingya have," said Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the court's ornate, wood-paneled Great Hall of Justice for the nearly three-hour reading of the ruling. In Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, refugee Mohammad Rofik welcomed the recognition of the plight of the Rohingya. WATCH: Why more Rohingya refugees are making desperate journeys by sea "Today, the world could recognize and give the victory to the Rohingya community, not only the Rohingya community. It is the victory of the whole community of ... Myanmar," he said. There was no immediate reaction from the Myanmar delegation in The Hague or from the government in Myanmar. The court also ordered Myanmar to commit to reparations including allowing Rohingya "safe, voluntary and dignified return to their place of residence." It ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish people found to have committed genocidal acts and to pay compensation to Rohingya. The amount will be decided in later court proceedings. An umbrella organization of Myanmar opposition groups said in a statement that "the struggle for justice will continue, and this judgment must now be enforced," calling on the international community to ensure it is fully implemented. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the ruling "a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand." Shortly after the ruling was read, U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said his government was expelling Myanmar's defense attache from the U.K. and "calling urgently for a U.N. Security Council session to discuss the judgment." Brutal counterinsurgency campaign triggered the killings and expulsions In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called a clearance campaign in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes. The court said that evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 10,000 Rohingya. Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred, the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya "in whole or in part." About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across Cox's Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions. The case could impact genocide allegations elsewhere In a 2007 judgment, the court said that Serbia "violated the obligation to prevent genocide" in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town. Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide. South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack. "The International Court of Justice's landmark ruling is long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured from Myanmar's military. More U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, new prescription data suggest.
Monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.
Although the data in the new study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.
The new study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.
“Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” says Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.
Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.
There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The new study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press E. Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/no-breakthroughs-from-trump-xi-and-putins-3-way-talks-on-nuclear-risks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter No breakthroughs from Trump, Xi and Putin's 3-way talks on nuclear risks World Nov 19, 2026 10:45 AM EST SHENZHEN, China (AP) — For President Donald Trump, the meeting with the leaders of two other nuclear powers -- China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin -- was supposed to be a diplomatic triumph: It would serve as proof that Trump could negotiate with two of America's toughest rivals. WATCH: Trump lands in China for trade talks and high-stakes summit with Xi and Putin Before the trio met Thursday in a villa in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, the U.S. president sought to flatter both Xi and Putin as his friends. They were to discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran and how to reduce the dangers posed by nuclear arsenals. But after roughly 70 minutes behind closed doors, they agreed to a far narrower agenda. They would like to reform the United Nations, refine more fossil fuels and curb the reach of the International Criminal Court. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting in the end looked like a fleeting photo op. Trump quickly left the villa and boarded Air Force One without saying a word to reporters about his time with Xi and Putin. The agreements were modest, but the rhetoric that came at the start of the trilateral was not. "We are really making history," Trump said. "The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used." Xi earlier said the meeting would focus on "promoting world peace." Putin, for his part, said the countries "hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace." WATCH: Former national security staffer on how presidents prepare for talks with world leaders After the meeting, Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, while Putin described the trilateral talks as open and candid, calling the format "useful and substantive." "It is a serious collaborative work," he said in response to a question about whether the image of the meeting itself mattered more than the substance. The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February, and Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China. But China has less motivation to accept limits given that its arsenal of more than 600 warheads is far smaller than the more than 5,000 warheads believed to be in each of the U.S. and Russian stockpiles. Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, said the meeting could at best start a process that would eventually lead to a sustained set of talks for reducing nuclear arsenals. "We need more than diplomatic theater and photo opportunities between Xi, Putin and Trump," Kimball said. "And one meeting will not likely produce dramatic breakthroughs." The leaders also talked about Iran and trade President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation China Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. Photo by Andres Martinez Casares/ Pool via Reuters The U.S. president earlier had a separate one-on-one with Xi, their third substantial meeting this year. Trump said they had a shared interest in having oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil shipments from the Middle East that was repeatedly shut because of attacks in the Iran war. Trump suggested he would push Xi to buy more agricultural products from America. Xi said that relations between the U.S. and China have been "generally stable and improved" during Trump's presidency. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported that Xi discussed Taiwan with Trump and said the two countries needed to improve communication on economic and trade issues. Trump also added to his calendar a separate sit-down with Putin, marking the first time the leaders have met for talks since their discussions in Alaska last year that failed to broker a deal on Russia's war in Ukraine. "Wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start," Trump said, calling Putin "my friend." Trump has frequently boasted of his rapport with Putin, as relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to have cratered recently. Trump rejected new Russia sanctions, while Kyiv was undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war. After their trilateral meeting, the three leaders took aim at the International Criminal Court for overstepping its jurisdiction, saying government officials should enjoy immunity from its prosecutions. Putin is wanted by the court, and Trump's administration has imposed sanctions on ICC officials and the institution itself as part of a campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel. Trump boasts about his relationships, but the ties between Xi and Putin are stronger President Trump walks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as they participate in a trilateral meeting at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. Photo by Doug Mills/Pool via Reuters The U.S. president's ambitions going into the meeting recalled an era of great power politics when wealthier countries felt entitled to decide the fate of seemingly lesser nations. Trump was negotiating with China and Russia without the involvement of Ukraine — or allies like Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Japan and South Korea that also have stakes in the outcome of any talks.

ea57d62f4256.text: By — John Seewer, Associated Press John Seewer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fiona-the-hippo-swallowed-a-hat-the-cincinnati-zoo-hopes-a-little-shake-will-help-get-it-out Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fiona the hippo swallowed a hat. The Cincinnati Zoo hopes a little shake will help get it out Nation Nov 19, 2026 10:16 AM EST Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's famed hippo, underwent a colonoscopy this week, and now veterinarians are trying a new way to help her pass a knit cap that she swallowed after it slipped into her enclosure. The zoo's animal care team borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, hoping the shaking will help move things along through her digestive tract, the zoo said Wednesday. WATCH: What a 194-year-old tortoise could teach humans about living longer Video released by the zoo Wednesday shows Fiona snorting and moving about her indoor enclosure. Veterinarians sedated her Tuesday for a second time to evaluate her condition, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health. An ultrasound showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she is still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy, using a 9-foot scope, he said. Specialists have told the zoo that surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos, he said. Fiona, who became a global sensation as a tiny newborn after her premature birth in 2017, has inspired books, a line of beer and a bobblehead. During her first year, the zoo recorded her progress while fans worldwide followed her growth online. READ MORE: Thailand's adorable baby hippo Moo Deng has the kind of face that launches a thousand memes She initially couldn't stand on her own and weighed just 29 pounds at birth, 25 pounds less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species. The beloved hippo swallowed the hat just over a week ago. A visitor tossed it into the air, and a ceiling fan caught and catapulted it through a small opening above the area's viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley. Zoo staff are now monitoring her around the clock, trying to keep her hydrated and giving Fiona her favorite foods to help her pass the knit cap, the zoo said. "Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked," Curley said Wednesday. "And they were happy to see her respond." 80546b09b5f3.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-senate-meets-for-legislative-business-as-trump-returns-from-putin-xi-talks-in-china Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Senate meets for legislative business as Trump returns from Putin-Xi talks in China Politics Nov 19, 2026 10:00 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine says he will force a vote on the Senate floor in the coming weeks to require President Donald Trump's administration to calculate the human rights consequences of its policies in Russia. Watch the Senate floor live in the video player above. Kaine is introducing the resolution on Thursday under an arcane provision of a foreign policy law that allows any senator to trigger a vote requiring a report on a country's human rights practices. His measure would request more information about the effects of a diesel deal with Russia that was struck by the Republican president in October and that waived sanctions against Moscow and allowed for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The measure would also require the State Department to report on the consequences of other U.S. policies as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the Pentagon delayed the delivery of Patriot air defense interceptors and that U.S. intelligence that warns of incoming Russian attacks against his country had been interrupted. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Trump said in announcing the deal on Oct. 9 that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote on social media. He did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority." If passed, the resolution would ask the State Department to calculate how Trump's policies have affected Russia's ability to wage war in Ukraine and if they have caused or worsened human rights abuses. It also asks for an update on the current status of negotiations to end the war, which Russia launched in February 2022. Kaine says he hopes the resolution, which he calls a "test of good faith," can pass with bipartisan votes. "If they were to give us a nonstarter human rights report that whitewashes Russia's record, that will tell us a lot and that will tell the American public a lot," the Virginia senator said in an interview with The Associated Press on Wednesday. The resolution — coming as Trump had just wrapped up a meeting in China with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping — is part of Senate Democrats' strategy since the beginning of Trump's second term to force votes on reversing parts of his agenda. Kaine has led efforts to force multiple war powers votes, including several on the war in Iran. Kaine also triggered a vote last year on a resolution to require more transparency from the Trump administration about the human rights effects of deportations to El Salvador. The Senate, controlled by Republicans, voted along party lines to block it. The strategy has proven effective for Democrats as they have taken floor time from majority Republicans and forced them to go on record on the Iran war and other issues ahead of this year's midterm elections, in which Democrats ultimately won control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke of Republican governance in Washington. Kaine said he will continue to find ways to trigger votes even when Democrats take the Senate majority next year. Unlike most bills, the privileged resolutions he has introduced under the Foreign Assistance Act, the War Powers Act and other foreign policy laws prompt a quick vote within weeks and bypass committees. Getting past a presidential veto will be hard, Kaine concedes, but, "I want to make everybody here own what's going on" and be accountable for their votes. "We have to put bills on the president's desk," Kaine said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
