9340b1ea7fd2.text: The Senate passed a sweeping, bipartisan bill Thursday night that's designed to cut permitting timelines for energy and infrastructure projects. Why it matters: The eyes of the entire energy industry are on this bill. If it becomes law, it could transform how America builds energy infrastructure, with major implications for everything from electricity costs to data centers. Getting rid of bureaucratic hurdles and creating a more predictable process for energy projects is a top priority for the fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But critics argue the plan, which has White House support, would unacceptably weaken environmental protections and the rights of Native American tribes. Driving the news: The vote was 62-33. The bill would still have to pass the House before the end of the year, and any differences would have to be worked out by both chambers before President Trump could sign it into law. Catch up quick: It would make significant changes to federal permitting, including: New limits on the duration of lawsuits, and the scope and length of reviews under the Clean Water Act and National Environmental Policy Act. Language that would make it more difficult to revoke permits once they're issued, a priority for renewables groups and Democrats upset with Trump administration barriers. State of play: There are also provisions to ensure that data centers pay for needed grid upgrades, and expand federal authority over the siting and approval of certain interstate transmission projects. Friction point: Many environmental advocates argue that the bill would dangerously erode safeguards in the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. Multiple tribal groups still oppose it despite changes aimed at easing concerns about consultation on historic preservation. Energy and business groups, ranging from renewables developers to manufacturers to the oil and gas industry, are lobbying for the measure. The AFL-CIO and many individual unions back it, too. What's next: The measure now heads to the House. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told Bloomberg last week that he expects to have the votes to pass the plan. Some Democrats have called for hitting the brakes, with some arguing they can write a better package when they control Congress next year. Yet multiple backers within the wider Democratic coalition argue there isn't political space for an altered bill that President Trump would sign.

e354279c70d7.text: On his way back from China Thursday aboard Air Force One, President Trump called in to a meeting his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were holding in Berlin with a group of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. "Putin wants to end the war, he wants the deal done, he is getting tired of this," Trump said, according to people in the room. Why it matters: Instead of turning his historic trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin into a modern-day Yalta Conference, as some European and Ukrainian officials feared , Trump tried to use it to propel his push for peace in Europe. Driving the news: Trump met Putin Thursday on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen. Their meeting wasn't originally on the schedule, but Trump wanted to discuss diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine directly with the Russian president, a U.S. official said. "Who is he? He's my friend," Trump said when he entered the meeting room where Putin was waiting. Later in the day, Witkoff and Kushner told European leaders in Berlin that Trump pressed Putin to move on the peace talks, telling the Russian leader that now is the time to get a deal, according to a European official. Trump also asked Xi for his help in ending the war during their bilateral meeting. "He sent a very strong message to both of them [Putin and Xi] on the desire for peace, and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said at a press conference on Thursday. Behind the scenes: As Trump wrapped up his meetings in China and headed back to Washington, his envoys started their talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Zelensky and other European leaders. Kushner and Witkoff tried to reassure the group that Trump doesn't intend to cut a deal with Putin over their heads. "President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He's not looking to impose anything unilaterally," Kushner said. Shortly after, when Trump called in to brief the European leaders, he urged them to engage directly with Putin. "Friedrich, you can make a call to Putin and this will make a deal," Trump said, referring to the German host. Trump added, "Xi respects Zelensky. Putin is ready to do the deal. Zelensky can do a great deal." What they're saying: A European official said the talks in Berlin were substantive, unlike the summit in Shenzhen, which was mostly symbolic. "We think we have good coordination between the U.S. and Europe," the European official said. State of play: One of the key U.S. objectives at the moment is to get Europe directly involved in peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. At the same time, U.S. officials also want Europe to engage in talks with Russia on a new European-Russian security agreement . Putin said publicly for the first time Thursday that he is open to allowing the Europeans to participate in peace talks with Ukraine. "We understand that it is pointless to discuss security issues, including those in Europe, without them," he said at a press conference after meeting with Trump. Putin added that Russia needs to understand what the Europeans are prepared to bring to the negotiations. Putin also signaled willingness to present an updated proposal for a security agreement with Europe. "Life changes, so it makes no sense to return to geopolitical realities of the 1990s," he said. What to watch: After the leaders' meeting in Berlin, Kushner and Witkoff huddled for another few hours with Zelensky and national security advisers from Germany, the UK, France, Italy and Poland, as well as senior officials from the EU and NATO. The group coordinated ahead of the next round of talks with the Russians, possibly next week. The European official said the group was skeptical Russia will actually allow Europe to participate in peace talks. The bottom line: U.S. officials said their goal is to get the Europeans and Russians to start talking to each other. "We also will go back and relay to the Russians that we see strength and unity and commitment [in Europe], but we also see a real desire for peace," Kushner said. "And I think that we're doing a lot of work to organize on how to give it the best shot to get there."

The US Army is set to detonate five tonnes of degraded explosive material in Middletown, Iowa, and have urged locals to vacate the area or stay indoors for their safety.
The detonations will result in an air plume that could send toxic dust, containing lead particles, over eastern Iowa and into neighbouring Illinois, with the potential for contaminants to settle on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, the army said.
The two controlled explosions will be powerful enough that they could damage buildings and shatter windows nearby.
On Thursday, environmental groups sued in an effort to stop the detonations, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives or give adequate notice.
The detonation was originally scheduled for noon local time (1800 BST) on Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown - a community of about 360 people about four hours west of Chicago, Illinois.
The plant produces medium- and large-calibre munitions for the US Department of Defense.
On Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle delayed the detonation to Monday, saying that "public safety is the Army's top priority".
The planned detonation will be "the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material", he said on X.
The army said that the detonation is part of "a planned and controlled safety operation" to dispose of degraded lead azide. It added that the detonation has been permitted by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under conservation and recovery laws.
Residents have been asked to leave their homes for about six hours - between 08:00 and 14:00 local time - while the operation takes place and the dust settles. The army said that "all humans" should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas.
Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise, feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations and will see a plume of dust, the advisory said.
According to Iowa Public Radio, external, the IAAAP found earlier this year that the lead azide - a highly volatile compound used as a detonator - stored in underground concrete tanks is degrading, becoming too unstable to safely move.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place is the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, said that the substance has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers.
It sits in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, but a routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati told the Associated Press.
The army said the lead azide barrels will be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with barriers full of sand. The soil above will be saturated with water in an effort to reduce the lead in the air.
On Thursday, two environmental groups sued to block the detonation, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council.
"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal."

71d1ef0f8b9a.text:
White House fires cyber director in wake of outages, sources say
Sean Cairncross is to be replaced by Pentagon's CIO; doubts grow about CISA nominee.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross has been fired, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the matter, creating another leadership opening in the Trump administration’s cybersecurity team.
Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will take Cairncross' place, according to a defense official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to communicate the personnel change. Axios first reported his departure.
A source close to the White House told Nextgov/FCW that President Trump fired Cairncross because he lacked the credentials to perform the job. Davies is taking the job in an acting capacity, this source added.
The Office of the National Cyber Director advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates policy across federal agencies, overseeing implementation of the national cyber strategy. It also works with industry to protect systems that government and businesses rely on.
The Senate confirmed Cairncross in August 2025. During Trump’s first administration, he led the Millennium Challenge Corporation and served as a senior adviser to the White House chief of staff.
His work this year has included efforts to address AI security and strengthen cooperation with private cybersecurity companies. In February, Cairncross said his office was developing an AI security framework with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.
After the administration released its national cyber strategy in March, he called for companies to share technical expertise and threat information to help the government respond to adversaries.
The departure comes as lawmakers scrutinize a series of technology failures affecting air travel, banking, Microsoft services and classified communications at the National Security Agency. Senior administration officials told Congress Wednesday that the disruptions were tied to maintenance and security updates rather than cyberattacks.
Trump is also trying to install a permanent director at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps defend civilian federal networks and critical infrastructure.
His nominee, Palantir security executive Michael LoSapio, denied during a confirmation hearing Thursday that the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021, and declined to identify the winner of the 2020 presidential popular vote. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., plan to place holds on his nomination.

In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.
While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.
These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.
"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (Â£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.
"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.
"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.
The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?
"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.

As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.
"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.
While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.
Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.
"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.
"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."
Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.
At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.
The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed".
One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah.
His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border.
Residents in Utah have organised a fierce opposition campaign., external The pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Leary scale down the project by 75%, external, from 40,000 to 13,000 acres.
Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project.
The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality.
The project is billed as "off-grid", external, relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta government exempted the project from an environmental impact assessment, external, arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction.
The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident, Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June , externalthat he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere".
In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years.
Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools.
Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks.
"It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place.
Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace.
He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months.
Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents.
"If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in an August town hall reported on by the Canadian Press, external, held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; Â£6.8bn) AI data centre in the province.
Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings.
This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns.
There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.
On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered in Canada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre, external that will be used by technology giant Anthropic.
But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom.
"AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy.
"I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said.

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.
The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.
He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.
"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In

77883200bfe8.text: By — Laura Ungar, Associated Press Laura Ungar, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/do-you-need-a-measles-booster-shot-now-that-the-u-s-has-lost-its-elimination-status Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Do you need a measles booster shot now that the U.S. has lost its elimination status? Health Nov 19, 2026 7:10 PM EST Now that measles is officially back in the U.S., some Americans are asking: Do adults need a booster shot? Generally, experts say, the answer is no. "Most people are protected without getting a booster shot" because they've either been vaccinated or had measles as kids, said Dr. Richard Martinello at Yale School of Medicine. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The U.S., Mexico and Bolivia lost their measles-free status this week after stubborn outbreaks erased decades of progress. Last year, Canada lost its measles-elimination designation. READ MORE: Can the U.S. regain its measles elimination status? Here's what to know Doctors say getting two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is the best way to protect against one of the most contagious viruses in the world. The vaccine usually protects people for life, as does having had the disease. Americans born before 1957 are considered to have "presumptive evidence" of immunity because almost everyone back then got measles during childhood. For some people, boosters may be a good idea But doctors say certain people should consider getting boosters. One group is healthcare workers born before 1957 without proof of immunity. They're more likely than the general public to come in contact with people who have measles, so they may get it or even spread it to vulnerable patients. Adults vaccinated between 1963 and 1967 also might want to think about boosters. During those years, some children received an inactivated vaccine that uses a killed version of the virus, which was less effective than the current vaccine containing live, weakened virus. Doctors said people who know they got the inactivated vaccine or aren't sure should get at least one dose of the live MMR vaccine. One dose is 93% effective at preventing measles, while two doses are 97% protective. Until 1989, only a single dose was standard. Now the recommendation is for adults to have at least one documented dose of MMR. Two doses are recommended for certain people in high-risk groups who don't have other evidence of immunity. "People who have had no shots should go get vaccinated, if they weren't born before 1957," said Dr. Joshua Sharfstein at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. "If they have had only one shot, they may want to consider whether they're in a risk group for a second shot." That risk group, he said, includes people in school, healthcare workers, international travelers or people living with family members who have compromised immune systems. In places with active measles outbreaks, health officials sometimes recommend that everyone have two shots, Sharfstein said. For people who have only had one shot, especially in an area where measles is circulating, "it's always a good idea to talk with your physician about whether another shot is needed," Martinello said. Tracking down your vaccination status But what if you don't know how many shots you received or even if you've been vaccinated? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests asking your parents or doctor, checking with your high school or college health services or reaching out to previous employers that required immunizations. You can also try contacting your state's health department; some states have registries that include adult vaccines. If you're still unsure about your vaccination status, you can talk with your doctor about an MMR immunity blood test that can show whether you have antibodies against measles. But Martinello said this isn't an ideal measure of how safe you are from the virus. Though the test is accurate, he said, scientists don't know how to link the result perfectly with the level of protection someone might have. Regardless, doctors said getting a booster just to be safe won't harm you unless you're in a group that is not supposed to get the vaccine at all, such as pregnant women. Now that measles is circulating in the U.S., doctors said it's crucial to take measures to protect yourself. "This is a moment to not just check for yourself, but also encourage others to make sure that they are adequately vaccinated," Sharfstein said. "Too many people took measles for granted … or just didn't think about measles. But now it's something to think about." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. U.S. exports of natural gas are surging, and legislation moving through Congress could boost them even higher.
A bill that would overhaul federal permitting for a range of projects across energy, technology and other sectors is expected to unleash a wave of pipeline construction, experts say. Much of that gas could end up overseas.
Exports of liquefied natural gas, or LNG, are already the fastest-growing source of demand for U.S. gas production, which hit a record high this summer. By 2040, those exports are expected to roughly double.
If the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act becomes law, that projected increase could grow by an additional 8 percent to 15 percent, according to modeling by the Rhodium Group.
While some of the bill’s proponents say it would help reduce climate pollution by speeding construction of renewable energy and electricity transmission, many environmental groups are warning those gains would be outweighed by accelerating fossil fuel development.
Ben King, a director with Rhodium’s energy and climate practice, said the biggest winner among fossil fuels would be LNG. The group’s modeling projected a buildout of new gas pipelines, most of which would be oriented to exports, he said.
While LNG growth has faced few constraints, one of them has been a lack of new pipelines, said Mariam Al-Shamma, a director with the Bipartisan Policy Center’s energy program.
“It’s gotten really difficult to build interstate gas pipelines in the United States, and that’s obviously something you need if you want to be exporting LNG and don’t want to have an impact on gas supply domestically,” Al-Shamma said.
The permitting bill would make it harder for states and tribes to modify or reject certain permits needed for pipelines and would also restrict legal challenges by environmental groups or other opponents. These types of challenges have slowed or blocked numerous pipeline projects in the Northeast and Appalachian region.
Beyond pipelines, the bipartisan bill could free more gas for export by reducing demand for it in the United States. While domestic gas use is expected to grow in coming years, driven in part by demand from data centers and others, the bill could help wind and solar energy gain a larger share of that increased electric demand, Rhodium’s modeling found.
Yet rather than remaining underground, the modeling said, that natural gas would likely get exported.
It’s unclear what that would mean for the global climate. If LNG exports displace coal, they could, under certain conditions, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, Rhodium said. (Some studies suggest LNG is even worse for the climate than coal, because of methane leaks.) If they spur new demand or replace renewable energy, they would drive pollution higher. In cases where exports replace gas from Russia or the Middle East, they wouldn’t change emissions much at all.
“The simple fact of the matter is it’s a whole jumble of all those things,” King said.
Modeling aside, some climate advocates are warning that provisions in the bill would effectively lock in a massive wave of LNG exports that has already been approved.
The U.S. Department of Energy had authorized the export of nearly 56 billion cubic feet of gas per day as of September. For a sense of scale, that figure is equal to roughly 40 percent of current U.S. gas production. Only about two-thirds of what has been authorized is either operating or under construction.
The Trump administration has focused on expanding LNG exports. It has devoted billions of dollars in federal subsidies to help build terminals or sell gas overseas and wielded exports as leverage in trade negotiations to secure new deals with foreign governments.

In 2024, the Biden administration paused approving new gas exports, saying it was reviewing its criteria for determining whether they were in the public interest. Provisions in the new bill would make it much harder for a future administration to do the same.
“That kind of project uncertainty is exactly what the legislation is attempting to eliminate,” Al-Shamma said.
An analysis by Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy group, argued current law allows a future administration to modify existing LNG permits if, for example, it determined exports were inflating domestic energy prices. The new bill could erect significant hurdles to this approach, the group argued, by restricting such modifications to a narrower set of circumstances.
What’s more, the bill would impose a new standard for judicial review that would allow companies to sue the government if agencies modified or revoked permits. In those cases, the agency would need to show “by clear and convincing evidence” that its action was warranted. If it failed, the government could face substantial penalties tied to the costs of construction or operations.
If an agency denied or “unreasonably delayed” a permit, and an applicant could establish it was being treated unfairly, the penalties could reach 100 percent of “reasonably expected” costs.
LNG terminals often cost tens of billions of dollars to construct, a sum that experts say could serve as a formidable deterrent to an agency that was considering modifying a permit. Once built, the terminals are meant to operate for decades.
“The project certainty provisions in this bill are quite certainly the worst provisions I’ve seen in 20 years of following congressional legislation on the environment,” said Jeremy Symons, president of the Center for Energy & Environmental Analysis, a think tank. “They are a blank check to industry.”

726934e57ef1.text: By — Meg Kinnard, Associated Press Meg Kinnard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fcc-votes-to-allow-state-prisons-to-jam-signals-from-contraband-cellphones Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FCC votes to allow state prisons to jam signals from contraband cellphones Nation Nov 19, 2026 7:02 PM EST COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — The Federal Communications Commission on Thursday acted to allow state prisons across the United States to jam the signals of cellphones smuggled to inmates as the federal government cracks down on devices that authorities say are the No. 1 security threat in the nation's correctional facilities. The vote was unanimous among the commissioners meeting in Washington. State prison officials for years have sought the right to jam, arguing that blocking the signals of contraband phones would halt inmates' ability to use the devices to run drug rings, coordinate prison riots and even order acts of violence such as attacks on guards. READ MORE: Justice Department finds problems with violence, gangs and poor conditions in 3 Mississippi prisons Under the new rule, prisons are not required to use the jamming technology, they must conduct multiple tests to make sure cell signals outside prisons are not affected and they have to notify officials if the jamming devices are moved. Commissioner Anna Gomez, who ultimately voted for the measure on what she called a "critical" issue, expressed concern for "potential unintended consequences" that could come if jamming zones were improperly calibrated in ways that accidentally disrupted home security systems or blocked emergency response calls. "I want to make sure that we don't harm public safety in the name of helping public safety," she said. Gomez is the lone Democrat on the panel. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who spoke in favor of the measure, visited this week with officials in South Carolina, whose prison directors have led efforts to obtain permission to jam. "This itself is not going to be a silver bullet, but I think it's time that we stop denying this tool to state and local officials," Carr said before the vote. Cellphones have been smuggled inside hollowed-out footballs, whisked in by corrupt employees and sometimes even dropped by drone. The signal-jamming technology was already allowed in federal facilities but needed FCC permission, due to a nearly century-old communications law, to be available for state prisons. U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling, who headed South Carolina's Corrections Department for more than a decade, led an effort from many of his counterparts across the country to gain use of the technology. South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson, elected this month as the state's next governor, organized fellow prosecutors to press Congress to change the law but they were unsuccessful. FCC chair says it's 'ready to take action' While in South Carolina, Carr stood alongside Stirling, Wilson and other South Carolina officials before a display of hundreds of confiscated cellphones and massive drones used to ferry the contraband over prison fencing. He said many people might not perceive the danger. "People really don't understand the threat that these pose," Carr said, noting that 25,000 cellphones were confiscated in the nation's state and local prisons each year. "We're going to put a new tool in the hands of law enforcement, and it's going to make a dramatic difference." Carr cited the case of Robert Johnson, a South Carolina corrections officer who was nearly killed at his home in 2010 in a hit that officials said was orchestrated by a prisoner using a contraband cellphone. After nearly three dozen surgeries and now in "pain 24/7," Johnson said Wednesday that he refers to the phones as "weapons of mass destruction" because of the potential dangers for which they can be used. He has testified in previous FCC hearings over jamming requests and often spoken out on the issue. "No one should have to go through what I went through," Johnson said. "But I also believe that the Lord chose my wife and I to go through this because someone had to carry the banner, and he chose us to do it." South Carolina tested the tech in 2008 South Carolina has been the testing ground for state prison cellphone jamming. In 2008, the FCC allowed the state to conduct a one-time test of a jamming system at a maximum-security prison. A briefcase-sized device emitted a frequency that immediately shut down cellphones around an auditorium; outside, service was uninterrupted. Another test took place at a different state prison in 2019, a first-time collaboration between federal officials and state prison officials. A year earlier, seven South Carolina inmates had died in the worst U.S. prison riot in 25 years, in what officials said was a gang fight arranged in part using illegal cellphones. The FCC has shown willingness to work on eradicating prison cellphones, holding a 2016 field hearing in South Carolina and hosting meetings with members of Congress, prison officials and representatives of the wireless industry. Groups that advocate for inmates' rights have opposed the move, arguing that the high rates inmates must pay to use official prison phones have pushed them toward using contraband cellphones just to stay in touch with family. The telecommunications industry has long argued against it, too, saying that jamming technology risks interfering with legitimate communications. Carr said in South Carolina that he felt the industry was softening on jamming, in part due to recognition of the problem's size as well as agencies' experiments with targeted technologies. "We aren't considering jamming outside this unique context," Carr said. "Maybe people aren't cheering it on from industry, but the opposition has receded substantially." ATTALLA, Ala.—April Phillips is worried about her brother Bubba.
The 46-year-old has cerebral palsy and epilepsy and sometimes suffers from difficulty breathing. So when her two-year-old grandson’s preschool messaged to tell her the facility was closing due to smoke from a nearby fire, she fretted not only about the child, but also her brother.
The blaze, she would soon find out, was less than a mile from her home, at a wood processing facility owned by a company called Omaha Track. Just outside, thick, dark smoke rose above the towering pines of Attalla, a town of less than 6,000 people.
Phillips’ worry kicked into overdrive. No public officials had directly informed her family about the plume of smoke billowing through her community. She checked social media. Local officials were saying that an evacuation of residents within a mile had been ordered. Phillips was confused.
“They ain’t told none of us nothing,” Phillips said. “And here we are sitting here and breathing it.”
Jim Slick, director of the Etowah County Emergency Management Agency, said the fire started in a yard where used railroad ties were being stored before being ground into chips of biomass.
Omaha Track and similar companies take wood products, often treated with chemicals, and process and sell them to be burned as industrial fuel. While the industry has billed its products as a renewable energy source because trees and other organic matter can be regrown, environmentalists have critiqued the carbon-intensive practice as “burning trees to save the planet.”
According to its website, Omaha Track’s Attalla facility receives and processes more than 200,000 tons of railroad ties each year. The company could not immediately be reached for comment.
Lynn Battle, chief spokesperson for the Alabama Department of Environmental Management, said in an e-mail Thursday evening that while the overall size of the blaze had been reduced, the fire is ongoing. Several fire departments are applying water to some areas of the site that can be safely reached, she wrote, but there is no significant runoff from the site.
An evacuation order was lifted Thursday afternoon, local officials said.
Slick, the EMA director, said Thursday he believes there to be “very minimal danger to the surrounding areas, if any danger at all.”
“As it is right now, they are burning, but the surrounding areas, the neighborhoods around the yard, so to speak, are safe,” he said.
Tabitha Brown, a certified nursing assistant who lives near the fire, said she was having difficulty breathing after only a few minutes outside Thursday morning and doesn’t believe the fire poses no health risks.
Brown said she suffers from asthma and that those with existing respiratory illnesses often find even limited exposure to air pollution irritating.
“And we haven’t heard anything about what we’re supposed to do,” Brown said.
Fires of all types lead to air pollution that can cause and exacerbate health issues, according to health experts. Exposure to air pollution from a fire where a chemical like creosote or diesel fuel is burned could lead to additional risks.
Creosote is the name given to a wide variety of products commonly used to protect railroad ties and utility poles from pests and rot.
It can be derived from coal tar, the most widely used source, or wood, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Creosote from coal tar contains a number of potentially harmful chemicals and known carcinogens. Many different creosote products in use may contain various chemical formulations.
The CDC says that “long-term exposure of workers to creosote has been shown to increase cancer in several tissues, including the respiratory tract, skin, lung, pancreas, kidney, scrotum, prostate, rectum, bladder, and central nervous system.”
According to a 1984 technical report prepared by the EPA, burning creosote released potentially hazardous chemicals into the air, including benzo(a)pyrene and dibenzo(a,h)anthracene, pyrene and fluoranthene. The authors found the emissions were roughly 40 percent as potent as coke oven emissions.
Residents living near biomass fuel facilities across the country have repeatedly reported health issues, even from normal facility operations.
Still, Slick said he’s not overly concerned about impacts to residential areas near the fire.
“We looked it up in all of the different manuals and books that we have to look up hazards and things like that, and there’s no—other than if you’re right there involved in the smoke and stuff right on the site, now there would be some inhalation hazards, but the firefighters are using their SCBAs, the self-contained breathing apparatuses, so they’re protected,” Slick said.

Donate Now
Scot Quaranda, communications director for environmental nonprofit Dogwood Alliance, said it’s simply not believable that a fire of this scale doesn’t put residents’ health at risk.
“I don’t know what ‘manuals and books’ they’re reading, but that’s not a little-to-no impact fire,” Quaranda said of local officials in Etowah County. “There’s no way this won’t have health impacts.”
Quaranda said Thursday’s fire is the latest example of an industry that has serious negative consequences for the communities where their industrial plants are located.

f7b693592314.text: It was the summit seen around the world. The first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia resulted in a joint statement that included promises to release more oil and hold formal talks about nuclear weapons. Nick Schifrin reports from Shenzhen. Amna Nawaz: It was the photo seen around the world, the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia. President Trump was largely stone-faced as he walked with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The leaders released a joint statement that included promises to release more oil and, for the first time, hold formal talks about nuclear weapons. Nick Schifrin was in Shenzhen, China, and starts us off again tonight -- Nick. Nick Schifrin: Amna, tonight, President Trump is saying the meeting went great and built fantastic relationships. Vladimir Putin said it's the beginning of a new era of global diplomacy. Now, the countries still have deep divisions, and that joint statement is light on specifics. But U.S. officials tonight are especially highlighting that arms control language after a remarkable, memorable meeting that the entire world was watching. Today, a leader who's already lived a lifetime of made-for-TV moments stood for one of his most indelible images, the world's three preeminent nuclear powers in their first ever formal meeting focused on what Xi Jinping called upholding world peace. President Donald Trump: No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement. Nick Schifrin: In 1945, the winners of World War II divided up Europe and embraced spheres of influence. Today, Russian President Vladimir Putin embraced the historical echo. Vladimir Putin (through interpreter): Our three states are the victors of World War II, and we hold joint responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. Nick Schifrin: But Yalta, a summit of victorious allies, lasted eight days. This meeting lasted just over 80 minutes, a scripted summit with a joint declaration that included a promise to pump more oil, an admonishment of the International Criminal Court, which the U.S. is trying to destroy while the court tries to arrest Putin for war crimes in Ukraine, and plans for a future dialogue to reduce nuclear risks and proliferation after years of China resisting American requests for arms control. President Donald Trump: The United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used. And I think, as long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem. Nick Schifrin: Much of the focus today was for a president who prioritizes personal connections, the body language between old friends, not rival powers. At one point, Xi held President Trump's arm. When Xi's hand slips, President Trump reaches out to reconnect. President Donald Trump: Who is he? He's my friend. Hi. Nick Schifrin: And, earlier, President Trump joked and embraced Putin at a separate bilateral after the Kremlin said Putin left this meeting in a -- quote -- "excellent mood." President Donald Trump: We've had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. Nick Schifrin: It is that affinity for authoritarians that concerns U.S. allies, as Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk put it today. Donald Tusk (through interpreter): Mr. Putin is not our friend, nor will he ever be. Nick Schifrin: President Trump argues only his connections with these strongmen can produce progress. But even an American president cannot defy some international relations gravity. Man: Blackwell. Nick Schifrin: The U.S. and China are at loggerheads over export controls, the U.S. and now Taiwanese chip giant TSMC blocking China's access to high-end chips. Beijing is restricting the release of heavy earth magnets vital to sophisticated manufacturing. And state media reported today that Xi Jinping warned President Trump to -- quote -- "keep doing the right thing on Taiwan," a reference to the president's ongoing delay of a Taiwanese weapons sale. There's also no agreement to extend the U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in just two months, even though President Trump today asked Xi to boost agricultural purchases. President Donald Trump: And I will be asking you to do some more for our farmers, because you have -- China has an insatiable appetite. I can tell you that. And we can fill that appetite. Nick Schifrin: For years, Xi and Putin have been trying to build an axis of authoritarianism, a direct counterweight to American values, as Putin did not hide during an hour-long press conference. Vladimir Putin (through interpreter): What is democracy? Is it a liberal attempt to monopolize power, and, in reality, it's a liberal dictatorship? Nick Schifrin: That sentiment traditionally divides these countries, but these leaders are in their 70s and 80s, focused on their legacies, and convinced they can define the course of history together. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Nick Schifrin.
