US President Donald Trump has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose.
"I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday.
Rose, who died in 2024 at the age of 83, pleaded guilty in 1990 to two counts of filing false tax returns. He was also given a lifetime ban from Major League Baseball (MLB) after an investigation revealed he bet on games.
The baseball star was posthumously reinstated to MLB, in which he played for 24 seasons, last year and made eligible for the Baseball Hall of Fame.
Trump also said on Thursday that Rose's "record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken".
In fact, Rose accumulated a record 4,256 hits - which MLB defines as a batter striking the baseball into fair territory and reaching base without doing so via an error or a fielder's choice - during his career, which is more than any other player. He played a total of 3,562 games.
According to Trump, Rose "was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame. Politics, I guess".
The US Constitution gives a sitting president the broad power to grant a pardon, which represents legal forgiveness and ends any further punishment.
Because Rose's pardon was issued after his death, it is largely symbolic and does not change Rose's Hall of Fame status. The Department of Justice (DoJ) typically does not process posthumous pardon applications, though presidents have still issued them.
The BBC has contacted the Hall of Fame and the DoJ for comment.
The US president had previously floated the idea of pardoning Rose in March last year before the MLB reinstated him.
"Major League Baseball didn't have the courage or decency to put the late, great, Pete Rose, also known as 'Charlie Hustle,' into the Baseball Hall of fame," he wrote on Truth Social at the time.
"Now he is dead, will never experience the thrill of being selected, even though he was a FAR BETTER PLAYER than most of those who made it, and can only be named posthumously. WHAT A SHAME," Trump added.
MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred issued a decision in May 2025 that created a pathway for Rose to be eligible to be inducted into the baseball Hall of Fame - a ruling that also applied to 16 other people - as early as 2028.
In August 1989, Rose agreed to the permanent ban from the sport after MLB investigators found that he bet on his team, the Cincinnati Reds, multiple times while he was playing on and managing the team from 1985 to 1987.
In July 1990, after Rose admitted to failing to report $354,968 (Â£271,107) in income over a four-year period, he was sentenced to five months in prison. He also was fined $50,000 and ordered to perform community service at the time.

077cc76e2531.text: For perspective on the Trump, Xi and Putin summit in China, Amna Nawaz spoke with Dennis Wilder and Fred Fleitz. Wilder was senior director for East Asia and special assistant to President George W. Bush and was the editor of the president’s daily brief during the Obama administration. Fleitz was the National Security Council chief of staff during the first Trump administration. Amna Nawaz: For a perspective now on that three-way meeting in China and what it accomplished, we get two views. Dennis Wilder was senior director for East Asia and special assistant to President George W. Bush. He was the editor of the President's Daily Brief during the Obama administration, is now a visiting professor at Texas A&M. And Fred Fleitz had a decades-long career in the intelligence community, State Department, and on Capitol Hill. He was the National Security Council chief of staff during the first Trump administration. He's now president of the Washington Global Strategy Group. That's an international consulting firm. Gentlemen, welcome to you both. And, Fred Fleitz, I will begin with you, because coverage of the summit has been fairly blunt so far. The Associated Press reported -- quote -- "What was billed as a historic trilateral meeting, in the end, looked like a fleeting photo-op." Specific to U.S.-China relations, in your view, what was actually accomplished during this summit? Fred Fleitz: I think it was a successful summit for many reasons. I think President Trump achieved his main objective, and that is simply reminding the world that he is still around and will have a robust foreign policy for the next two years of his presidency, despite the midterm, like many presidents have lost in midterms and had very aggressive foreign policies. I also think that the president's trying to set the stage for some major agreements. Peacemaking takes time. Peacemaking also requires dialogue. It may feel good, like Joe Biden did, to demonize President Putin as a war criminal and as a killer, but, if you do that, you can't have dialogue. Trump's taking a different approach. He's trying to move forward with an agreement to end the war in Ukraine. I will admit it's going slowly, but there was no effort like this before Trump is president. He's going to keep at it. Amna Nawaz: Dennis, what's your response to that, specific to some of these topics that were brought up, the war in Ukraine, and even arms control, which the president claims there was progress made on? Dennis Wilder: I have no problem with the president building relationships. I believe in leader diplomacy. Certainly, George Bush, and his father were great believers in leadership diplomacy. Here's the problem. Fred says that things are moving slowly. I think they're moving at a snail's pace on many of these issues. Did he, for example, ask Xi Jinping to stop giving Russia arms and assistance for its war effort? Did he ask Xi Jinping to stop supporting the Iranians with capabilities that help them with satellite military photographs? Did he bring up the dissidents in Hong Kong, Jimmy Lai, who has been in jail ever since 2020? Did he bring up the case of an American citizen who was invited to China, an academic, a Ph.D. student who went to Kunming and is now incarcerated as a spy? Did he bring up cyber and cyberattacks by the Chinese that are massive against our own systems? There's just a long slate of issues that I don't hear the president talking about with Xi Jinping. I think we have given Xi Jinping a lot of face. I don't know what we're getting back. Amna Nawaz: Fred, I will give you a chance to respond there and maybe even answer some of Dennis' questions. If none of those issues came up, were U.S. interests advanced at this summit? Fred Fleitz: Of course they were. And, frankly, smart diplomats raise issues like this in private. They don't try to embarrass other nations with it, which is what we have seen other incompetent diplomats do. I think two things I'm hoping progress are made on. First of all, I'm glad the president is pushing China very hard on nuclear disarmament. It has about 400 to 600 nuclear warheads, although China -- Russia and the U.S. have over 5,000. It only takes a couple dozen to destroy the world. We have to have nuclear disarmament. If China wants to portray itself as a world peacemaker, it has to start talking about reducing its nuclear arms and allowing inspections, which it's never done. Second, I admit there's been no progress I can see on the war in Ukraine. But I think what President Trump and his negotiators are saying to Putin is that Trump is Putin's only way out of this war. Putin can't win it. And if there's a Democratic president in 2029, which I hope does not happen, U.S.-Russia relations will get much worse, because I think the next president, if it's a Democrat, will take very radical steps that will really destabilize the situation, maybe immediately admitting Ukraine into NATO and sending NATO troops into Ukraine. I think they tell Putin at every opportunity, you need to make a deal with Trump. This is your only chance to end the war. Amna Nawaz: Dennis, take each of those points that Fred raised there. Is China or could China be more amenable to nuclear arms control after this summit? And could there be some kind of progress on the war in Ukraine? We saw the President Trump called into the meeting of European allies' meeting in Berlin and said that Putin wants a deal. What's your take? Dennis Wilder: Well, first of all, on nuclear disarmament or arms control, I laud the president for bringing up this issue. It's an important issue. The Chinese are massively expanding their nuclear capabilities. They're talking about weapons in space. The Russians are talking about weapons in space. Before we get into weaponization of space, we need to start arms control discussions. So I'm perfectly with the president on this. The problem is, every expert I know says the Chinese aren't going to enter these talks until

003d5d2199be.text: House Republicans chose fighter Jim Jordan over the more experienced Steve Scalise to lead them after taking a midterms beatdown. Now they're facing a similar choice over who should lead them on House Oversight. Why it matters: Whoever gets the top Republican spot on the Oversight Committee will be the first line of defense on some of the most deeply personal issues for President Trump and his inner circle. A pair of Texas House Republicans, freshman Rep. Brandon Gill, 32, and three-term Rep. Pat Fallon, 58, want the job that could make them a national star, or leave them taking the heat if Democrats land damaging revelations. Driving the news: Democrats are preparing a barrage of investigations , putting Trump's family, finances and closest advisers in their crosshairs. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who is running to chair House Oversight next year, sent a dozen letters Wednesday targeting figures including Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner and Vice President Vance. Democratic allies want a plan "to compel disclosure and testimony," according to a Tuesday letter — led by Public Citizen and Indivisible — that was signed by 103 groups and obtained by Axios. The White House is pushing back on Hill Democrats, with its top lawyer warning that some Democratic investigative tactics could cross into criminality. Zoom in: Gill has made a name for himself with fiery committee confrontations and viral moments. He's also proven to be a prolific fundraiser. "Gill is the next Jim Jordan," a source close to Jordan told Axios. "He practices, he's smart." Fallon has served on Oversight since arriving in Congress in 2021. He previously chaired Oversight's subcommittee on economic growth, energy policy and regulatory affairs. "I've built great relationships and a clear resume of rigorous, result-oriented oversight that reflects what the committee has achieved on behalf of the American people," Fallon told the Texas Tribune in September. Between the lines: Gill's lack of seniority doesn't appear to be a major obstacle among Republicans eager to elevate one of their top fighters. "It will be a tight race with he and Fallon. Brandon is quite capable and will do a great job if elected. Not worried about his experience," a member of the House Republican Steering Committee told Axios. The Steering Committee recommends who should lead committees, subject to a vote of the full House GOP conference. The intrigue : Fallon backed Steve Scalise in the GOP party leader race, and lobbied against Jordan's preferred makeup of the Steering Committee. Gill publicly supported Jordan, calling him the "original congressional brawler." State of play: Gill has close ties to Jordan and the public backing of House GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.). Multiple people Axios spoke with believe Gill has effectively locked up the support needed to win. But others cautioned that the race will be competitive, with one House Republican telling Axios that "anyone that says there's a favorite at this point is bad at whipping." "This is a purely messaging game for the next two years. And if I'm looking at who the better messenger is, I mean it's a clear choice," a senior GOP leadership aide said of Gill. What they're saying: "He's smart. He's good looking. He's the future of the party. We need to push him out front every minute instead of these old guys that we keep dusting off," Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.), who sits on the Oversight Committee, told Axios of Gill. "Paying their dues has gotten us killed at the ballot box every dadgum time," Burchett added of elevating more senior colleagues. Yes, but: "He's kind of skipping a few steps here, and he doesn't necessarily have the credentials to do it," one House Republican told Axios of Gill's bid in October. Axios previously reported that some members of the Freedom Caucus want Gill out, with colleagues accusing him of burning bridges and treating fellow Republicans as stepping stones to greater power and influence. The bottom line: Asked about the criticism from Gill's colleagues, Emmer flatly told Axios in an interview last month that Gill "needs to be out front. I don't care where it is." "Brandon is the future of our party, and his communication skills are phenomenal," Emmer added.

71ae0620b8fe.text: House Democrats are largely steering clear of threats to shut the government down in December if Republicans put forward legislation that maintains funding for the war in Iran. Why it matters: Much of the party's left flank — including some members of Congress — think it's a fight they need to pick after their midterm landslide. "The American people were loud and clear on November 3rd: they want an immediate end to Donald Trump's reckless war in Iran," Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said in a joint statement on Wednesday. The pair said they will "oppose any funding package that does not explicitly prohibit funds from being used for offensive operations in Iran" because it would "defy the demands of Americans who want this war to end—now." State of play: The Democrats' majority doesn't officially begin until Jan. 3, while federal funding is set to run out on Dec. 11. Republican leaders are struggling to pass party-line procedural votes and will probably bring up their funding patch under a fast-track process that requires bills to pass with a two-thirds majority. In other words: The GOP will almost certainly need a large number of Democratic votes to pass any funding bill, especially if some of their own members defect. What they're saying: "Whatever they have to do to get it through they should do it, but I hope there's not a shutdown," said Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), the outgoing chair of the center-left New Democrat Coalition. "I don't think we should shut down the government, we take that way too casually as it is, so I'd be leaning into not doing it," said Rep. Scott Peters (D-Calif.). Said Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio): "Everyone should do whatever they can to avoid a shutdown. The impact it has on the economy, but workers in particular, it's just not fair." Between the lines: Even some progressives acknowledged their imminent House majority takes a lot of the pressure off the December fiscal deadline. "If I can defund [the war] in December, I'd vote to defund it. But if I can't, then I'll vote to defund it in January," said Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.). "We still have a month left of these guys." Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "One would argue that we can move a CR, maybe keep it at base [funding levels] ... but then we negotiate the kind of budget we know we expect." Yes, but: "I think we should do everything in our power to keep it in there, and we should also figure out how to claw back some of this ICE funding," Ramirez added. Said Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.): "The American people have waited too long, they want to see us try now. ... When we fight we win, and we certainly don't win unless we try. I think we should try." Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of left-wing group OurRevolution, said in a statement: "Voters gave Democrats more power because they wanted a change in direction." "This is a chance to show them, before January, that their votes changed what Congress is willing to do," he said. The bottom line: Ansari told Axios in an interview on Thursday that she is "personally drawing a hard line on any funding for the war" but agrees "with the sentiment that, especially during the holidays, we are concerned about our federal workers." "Nobody wants a government shutdown. There's no question of that. I don't want there to be a government shutdown," she said. "I just think we should be able to both: Not have a government shutdown and ... deliver on what I think was the resounding message from voters, which is that the war in Iran needs to end."

3d644bfb9727.text: In our news wrap Thursday, a Russian drone damaged the Dutch embassy and a cathedral in Ukraine, President Trump says he posthumously pardoned Pete Rose, record-breaking rains inundated parts of Florida's Atlantic coast and the Cincinnati Zoo says its famous hippo, Fiona, died after she swallowed a visitor's hat. Amna Nawaz: In the day's other headlines: Russia stepped up drone attacks on Ukraine as part of its response to Kyiv's recent strikes on a strategic bridge. In Kyiv, a Russian drone damage at the Dutch Embassy and a cathedral. A Ukrainian official says at least one person was killed. This comes as Russian state media says rail traffic on Kerch Bridge was temporarily halted after a third Ukrainian strike in four days. The bridge links Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula and is vital to Moscow's war effort. In the meantime, Ukraine's allies gathered in Berlin today to discuss the country's future and the meeting in China between President Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for Ukrainian involvement in any future talks. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian President (through interpreter): We will talk separately with the American representatives about when the next meeting will take place and what its agenda will be. And it should now be a four-way meeting, Ukraine, Europe, and America, and Russia. We are really counting on this. Amna Nawaz: Also, at the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters that -- quote -- "A Yalta format will not bring peace to Ukraine." That's a reference to the 1945 meeting of the American, British, and Soviet leaders to plan the post-World War II order. Visa, Mastercard, and J.P. Morgan Chase are the latest institutions to report tech issues today, this time involving the leak of customer data by hackers. Chase says third-party vendors accessed its marketing data, including customer names and contacts. But the company says the incident is not related to a service disruption from earlier this week. Visa says no card numbers were taken in its hack, and Mastercard says there was no impact to its payment network. In the meantime, the European Commission confirmed today that it was the target of what it called an AI-generated cyberattack back in October. Thomas Reginer, Spokesperson: So, while AI can, of course, help to detect vulnerabilities and prevent cyberattacks, it can of course be misused. Amna Nawaz: An E.C. spokesperson says it remains difficult to judge how serious the breach was, and they have not determined who was behind the attack. An investigation is ongoing. Well, there's been bipartisan reaction today to Elon Musk saying he doesn't identify with President Trump's Make America Great Again movement. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit, Musk said -- quote -- "I'm not sure what MAGA means. If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that." In response, President Trump told NBC News that when people veer from MAGA -- quote -- "They don't do very well." And Democrats in Congress say they still plan to investigate Musk when they take control next year. The billionaire CEO spent more than $400 million to support Republican candidates in the midterm elections, which he now says was -- quote -- "pretty foolish." President Trump says he has posthumously pardoned baseball legend Pete Rose, the all-time hits leader who was long banned from the game for sports gambling. Rose was convicted of federal tax crimes back in 1990 and spent five months in a federal prison. Today's pardon comes two years after his death and more than a year after he was reinstated by Major League Baseball's commissioner. That means it is possible for Rose to one day be inducted to the baseball Hall of Fame. The earliest that could happen would be 2028. Record-breaking rains have inundated parts of Florida's Atlantic Coast, and the downpours are showing no signs of easing. The National Weather Service says heavy rain will continue through tomorrow, with many regions under flood alerts. Florida's governor has declared a state of emergency for the affected areas, and schools were closed today in some counties. Residents say they have never seen anything like it. Jade Jaime: This is the highest that I have seen the lakes rise. This is the highest that I have seen, like, surrounding the trees, and it kind of -- we have two canals right here. It looks like they're very close to becoming friends, so, again, just kind of concerning. Amna Nawaz: Earlier this week, torrential rains caused the roof of this synagogue to collapse in the city of Hollywood, Florida. So far, no injuries or deaths have been reported as a result of the rain or flooding. On Wall Street, today, stocks struggled again amid ongoing AI concerns. The Dow Jones industrial average tumbled more than 1,100 points. The Nasdaq dropped more than 2 percent. The S&P 500 fell for a sixth straight day, its longest losing streak since 2024. And the Cincinnati Zoo says its famous hippo, Fiona, died today, more than a week after she swallowed a visitor's hat. Veterinarians were giving the beloved Nile hippopotamus round-the-clock medical attention since the knit cap was accidentally flung into her enclosure. The zoo says it made multiple attempts to get Fiona through what ended up being a medical emergency, but, in the end, their efforts were not successful. Fiona's premature birth in 2017 and her fight for survival turned her into a global sensation. The zoo's Web site describes her as a -- quote -- "beloved symbol of hope and a source of inspiration for millions."

9b7dabd94959.text: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic completed the largest initial public offering of all time. Even as CEO Dario Amodei celebrated the huge launch, he reiterated his commitment to developing artificial intelligence responsibly. William Brangham discussed more with Jessica Lessin, the editor-in-chief of the technology website The Information. Amna Nawaz: Today marked a blockbuster stock market debut for the artificial intelligence giant Anthropic. The company completed the largest initial public offering of all time, raising more than $80 billion. William Brangham has more. William Brangham: Anthropic initially priced its IPO at $83 a share. But when stock trading began this morning, it soared to over $111. That's a 30 percent jump. The price dipped later and ended up closing at $97 a share. Even so, that puts Anthropic's market value above $1.2 trillion. By comparison, just two years ago, the company was worth $18 billion. Even as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei celebrated the huge launch, he reiterated his commitment to developing artificial intelligence responsibly. Dario Amodei: And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. William Brangham: Given that this was the first of the so-called frontier AI labs to go public, it marks a huge initial test for the AI boom. For more on this, we are joined by Jessica Lessin. She's the founder and editor in chief of the technology Web site The Information. Jessica, thank you so much for being here. There are so many issues involved with Anthropic's' emergence. Let's talk first about the financial ones. Why is such a young company going public right now? Why do they need this money? What are they using it for? Jessica Lessin: Great question, William. And they're using it for compute. Unlike other technologies and the Internet, consumer Internet boom, AI requires billions, tens of billions, hundreds of billions of dollars of compute and infrastructure. And while Anthropic's revenues are soaring, so are their compute bills, and that's really driving this financing. William Brangham: So, like a lot of AI companies, Anthropic has these huge costs, the data centers that we have all been reading about. They have struggled to make a profit on those revenues. They owe hundreds of billions of dollars in contracts down the line. So how do they square this? How do they argue that they will get to profitability? Jessica Lessin: Investors are very focused on that top-line growth rate. And it's been extraordinary for Anthropic. I mean, I think seeing their ARR, their annual recurring revenue, soar double, triple, beyond is really giving investors a lot of confidence that eventually the profits will follow. They have also been very efficient in how they have used compute, even while spending huge amounts of it, and so -- especially compared to other AI companies out there, OpenAI among them. I think investors are hopeful that those efficiencies will carry through and keep those bills lower than they are elsewhere in the industry. William Brangham: Another looming question here is, given that this is the first of the big AI labs to go public, is today's valuation a sign of AI's permanence and solidity, or are we still in this fear that many have that we are in a bubble? Jessica Lessin: I think we should be cautious in extrapolating too far in terms of impact in the industry. They are a singularly unique company in many dimensions, both having the most advanced models and a very efficient business. But I also think you can be other AI companies and be encouraged by this. You can see that investors are interested, that they're valuing growth, that they're putting aside some of the existential longer-term questions. So it keeps the party going, I think, but it's also uniquely a situation that Anthropic is in versus the others. William Brangham: Let's talk for a second about those other existential questions. As we heard Amodei saying, he says, again, I understand the threat of AI running amok, and that my company will do everything it can to make sure that doesn't happen. But then he's also now in the marketplace, and he is going to have to answer to shareholders. Is there a contradiction in there? Jessica Lessin: There's certainly a tension. Now, Anthropic has a unique governance structure where it has sort of separate trustees who can appoint the board who to provide maybe some insulation from the whims of shareholders, but it really is a core tension that makers of AI are dealing with. And by their own admission, they don't even know what the technology is yet capable of. And so I think we have to be very vigilant in holding them to those claims of being responsible and following it and really understanding what -- the decisions inside these companies that are being made around these issues. So, to me, it's still a very, very open question. William Brangham: I mean, the moment that a lot of AI analysts worry about is what's called RSI, recursive self-improvement, where the AI itself starts making and building better versions of itself. And many believe that, if that moment occurs, that's when humans really lose the ability to control these systems. Doesn't a trillion-dollar valuation speed us much faster to that moment? Jessica Lessin: Potentially, but in AI, in particular, the narrative has gotten so ahead of the reality on many points. Perhaps it's behind in some as well, but I like to distinguish between the narrative that, again, has encouraged investors and talent to flow into these companies versus the reality. We're seeing advancements in cyber or some enterprise use cases that are very different from perhaps what we're seeing in health or other disciplines. So I think the large labs have an incentive to suggest that their technology is going to be this sort of panacea intelligence improving on all dimensions. We

e2b8f21b595e.text: A historic judgment from the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. The ruling comes years after Myanmar’s Muslim minority was forced to flee. Stephanie Sy discusses what the genocide verdict means for international law and the future of the Rohingya people with Adil Ahmad Haque, author of "Law and Morality at War.” Amna Nawaz: An historic judgment from the International Court of Justice today, ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority. Stephanie Sy details how the ruling comes years after Myanmar's Muslim minority was forced to flee. And a warning, this report contains images that some viewers may find disturbing. Stephanie Sy: Today, a sliver of justice for the Rohingya Muslims of Myanmar. Judge Yuji Iwasawa: The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group. Stephanie Sy: The landmark 9-6 decision is the first of its kind. Before today, the International Court of Justice, a United Nations body, had never held a state responsible for genocide. Judge Yuji Iwasawa: The only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely, the Rohingya population in Northern Rakhine State. Stephanie Sy: Today's ruling comes seven years after the case was first brought by Gambia. Dawda Jallow: The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived. They testified. Almost a decade ago, Myanmar's military executed what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State in response to a Rohingya insurgency that killed more than a dozen officers. Can they expect restitution? Is there a safe way for them to go home? Adil Haque, Rutgers University: Thanks very much for having me. So, certainly, that is what the court has ordered, restitution and compensation. That process will take several years to determine the form and amount of restitution and compensation. And then we have to see if Myanmar will comply. Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (Â£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.
The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune is racing to spend the final days of unified Republican power in Washington on confirming lifetime judicial picks, finishing bipartisan deals on permitting and college sports, and avoiding another shutdown.
But the debt ceiling will become Democratsâ problem.
The South Dakota Republican told Semafor on Thursday afternoon that his party likely lacks the votes to raise the debt ceiling along party lines in either the House or Senate. Any party-line reconciliation bill is a long shot at this point in the year, but if they do one it will focus on defense funding â not avoiding a default.
The debt ceiling âprobably ends up getting puntedâ into next year, Thune said â and with extra steps by the Treasury Department, he forecasted a deadline in the second half of 2027. That means President Donald Trump will have to make a deal on it with a Democratic House and Senate for the first time since he took office.
âObviously thereâs a theory out there that if we did a [reconciliation] bill, that we could use that to do the debt ceiling like we did last summer, but weâve got vote issues both here and in the House,â Thune said. âWhen the Dems have the gavels, theyâll probably have to enter into negotiations with the White House about how theyâre going to address it.â
Given all that uncertainty, Thune is spending his remaining days as majority leader plotting out how to rack up a few more Republican victories before he leads the opposition. That starts with preserving the Senateâs carefully negotiated work.
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., said in a statement on Thursday that the House wants to âpass strong antitrust protectionsâ and alter the Senateâs bipartisan sports bill while keeping together the fragile coalitions in both chambers. Thune said it would be a âbig mistakeâ to change that bill.
âPeople will filibusterâ an amended college sports bill in the Senate, Thune said. If the bill sees major changes he described himself as âworried it doesnât get done. I donât know how we can process it over here with all the other stuff we have to do, and itâs just a function of the calendar.â
To some degree, that bill is out of Thuneâs control now that itâs passed the Senate. Funding the government past Dec. 11 is more in his power, and it will need at least seven Democratic votes in the Senate. Yet Democrats are currently busy with a leadership challenge to their leader, Chuck Schumer, from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.
Thune said heâs âtrying not to weigh inâ on the race but itâs nonetheless affecting his job. Van Hollenâs bid has chilled negotiations to fund the government as the Marylander pushes the caucus to insist on including language that would prohibit funding for the Iran war.
âThat is not happening at all because of the leadership race. I think theyâre waiting till they have that resolved. Weâve basically been told: âWeâre not talking until after thatâs over with,ââ Thune said. âThey donât want to do anything that rocks the boat, jeopardizes, tips the field at all in that leadership race based on something they might do on funding the government.â
That race will conclude on Dec. 1, which will likely supercharge government funding talks. All that in mind, Thune is making sure heâs following through on what he can control: judicial confirmations at a simple majority threshold.
Heâs teed up four judges for the Senate to confirm before the Thanksgiving recess and said he will soon move to set up votes on three more which just cleared the committee. Those could receive votes as soon as this weekend if Thune decides to keep the Senate in session.
Ultimately, Thune foresees confirming 23 additional judges throughout the lame duck, though some need to get through the Judiciary Committee first.
âWeâre trying to make the most use of the time we have left on the clock and get as much done as we can. So a lot of thatâs confirming the judges that are left, the executive branch nominees. Weâll do a stack of those,â Thune said. And, âweâve got to fund the government.â
Backup plans
Thune said he views a Pentagon-funding reconciliation bill as an âoptionâ if bipartisan talks with Democrats fall through, even though a targeted defense-only spending bill right now lacks the requisite 50 votes from Senate Republicans.
Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., agreed that Republicans arenât precluding a budget reconciliation bill if talks with Democrats falter. But he said moving forward with a party-line defense spending bill could prompt a shutdown.
âItâs no idle threat. If we do that, then they shut down the government,â Johnson said. âWe donât want to shut down the government because we always get blamed, even though itâs the other sideâs fault twice this year. We get blamed. So weâre a little gun-shy about that.â
Room for Disagreement
Trump and Thune are largely on the same page after the election on lame-duck priorities. But Trump is still pushing Thune to pass a bill making Daylight Savings Time permanent and has called Thune âI donât know how many times on it.â
Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton âwill filibuster it,â Thune said. âSunrise in Pierre would be like 9:25 in the morning. Itâs a Northern Plains type issue, and thatâs a lot of Republican senators. Itâs Montana, Idaho, Nebraska, Iowa, South and North Dakota.â
Burgessâs view
Thuneâs last month and a half as leader is no cakewalk. Heâll probably need Trumpâs help to get the House to finesse the sports bill and clinch deals on funding the government.
But it pales in comparison to the months before the midterms, when he was telling Trump the GOPâs voter ID bill couldnât pass and that there werenât the votes to gut the filibuster.
Thune would much prefer being the majority leader, of course, but his life may be easier in the minority â which involves a lot of fighting with Democrats and less internecine combat.

242034fa8f3c.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/americans-will-pay-more-for-thanksgiving-dinners-this-year-says-farm-bureau-survey Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Americans will pay more for Thanksgiving dinners this year, says Farm Bureau survey Economy Nov 19, 2026 6:30 PM EST Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday. The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for 10 will rise 6% from last year to $58.63. The group tracks grocery prices using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico. READ MORE: U.S. inflation report highlights strain of rising food, energy and housing costs The Farm Bureau, which has been tracking Thanksgiving costs for 40 years, said it's the first time since 2022 that Americans will see the price of the meal increase. The price hit a record of $64.05 in 2022. High diesel prices have made it more expensive for farmers to process and transport Thanksgiving staples like milk, dinner rolls, potatoes and cranberries, the Farm Bureau said. Diesel prices have surged since the start of the Iran war and hit a record average of $6.53 per gallon in the U.S. in September, according to AAA. On Wednesday diesel averaged $5.96 per gallon, up 58% from a year ago, AAA said. Turkey prices have also risen sharply over the past year. The Farm Bureau said the 16-pound turkey in its survey cost an average of $23.68 this year, up from $21.50 last year. Bird flu has been decimating U.S. turkey flocks since an outbreak began in 2022. But cases have been waning, and turkey production increased substantially this year, said Mark Jordan, the executive director of Leap Market Analytics. At the same time, turkey demand has been rising, as more Americans seek out lean protein and U.S. turkey exports rise. That strong demand has limited U.S. turkey inventories and raised prices. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects the wholesale price of a whole frozen turkey hen will average a record $1.76 per pound this year, up 29% from last year. "Over the last few years there's been a lot of doom and gloom for the turkey industry," Jordan said. "This is one of those years that turkey producers are feeling a little bit better about their lot in life." Jordan said diesel costs likely didn't impact turkey prices this year, since so much of the decision-making and timing related to the turkeys that will be consumed this Thanksgiving happened before diesel prices spiraled. But diesel costs could have a notable impact on turkey prices next year, he said. A few of the items on the Thanksgiving menu are cheaper than last year, the Farm Bureau said. A 1-pound vegetable tray featuring carrots and celery is 5 cents cheaper, while a 16-ounce bag of frozen peas is 4 cents cheaper. Frozen pie crusts are also slightly cheaper, although a can of pumpkin pie filling is more expensive. And in some cases, stores will price turkey and other Thanksgiving staples lower in order to draw shoppers. Aldi said its feast for 10, which mirrors the Farm Bureau's menu, costs $39 this year. Walmart, which adds items like corn muffin mix and marshmallows but doesn't include carrots and celery, said its feast for 10 is $35. Persistently high grocery prices have been frustrating Americans since the pandemic and played a role in Republicans' recent losses in the midterm elections. Prices for food eaten at home jumped 22% between October 2021 and October 2026, according to U.S. government data. That's almost double the usual pace of food price inflation. This year, the USDA predicts prices for food eaten at home to rise 2.3%. That would be lower than the recent annual average of 2.6%. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Victoria Broderick is a tech support worker from rural Tennessee who unseated eight-term Republican Rep. Scott Desjarlais. She did so despite raising less than $100,000 and receiving zero investment from the national party. Liz Landers spoke with Broderick about her win. Amna Nawaz: When Democrats take control of the House in January, one of their new members will hail from a district no one expected them to win. Representative-Elect Victoria Broderick is a tech support worker from rural Tennessee who unseated eight-term Republican Congressman Scott DesJarlais. She did so despite raising less than $100,000 and with zero investment from the national party. Correspondent Liz Landers has more. Liz Landers: Broderick first ran for this seat two years ago, losing by 40 points. This year, the margin was just a few hundred votes. The incumbent conceded the rematch earlier this week. And, tonight, Congresswoman-Elect Broderick joins us from Capitol Hill. Congresswoman, welcome to "News Hour." Victoria Broderick: Thank you for having me. I'm so excited to be here. Liz Landers: Tennessee Republicans redrew the state's congressional maps in an attempt to sweep all nine of those House districts. Your district was not expected to be competitive. You didn't have much money. You didn't have name I.D. that other Democrats had. How did you win? Victoria Broderick: I won because I continued running since May of 2024. I never stopped running for Congress. And when it was redistricted, I just essentially said, well, the district stayed the same and actually became more competitive. So the work's going to start speaking for itself real soon. And we saw that happen. We saw it happen in the primary, where I was outspent 12.5 to one. And then we saw it again happen in the general election. And what I have learned running in Tennessee is, it takes time to build relationships. And time is the only thing you can't get more of. So I used my 2.5 years wisely. Liz Landers: You have won by fewer than 400 votes in a district that President Trump carried by 24 points. 2028 is unlikely to feature another huge blue wave. Are you going to govern like you're going to be in for a just one term? Victoria Broderick: I mean, the -- that's the goal of running for office is, it's a two-year term. So if I'm not doing my job, then, yes, get me out. But past that, I plan to pass very good legislation so that we can protect our rural hospitals and protect housing, because those are things that we can do day one that are already bipartisan legislation. So these are things that we can put forward, as well as every politician should be running like the time is up, because we have to get the work done. Liz Landers: You mentioned rural hospitals as an issue that you think will bring both conservatives and Democrats that you represent together. You have said that you would work with President Trump if he is willing to play ball. What are areas where you see alignment with him? Victoria Broderick: I mean, this is the situation. He has to sign it and go across the desk. So it's really down to him. Realistically, Congress needs to take its power back. And that's what we have not seen the last couple of years. And now we have a Congress that represents more of the district, represents what people are like and what they're experiencing. So I would push back and say that it's Tennessee's not a conservative state. It's not even a red state. It's a nonvoting, voter-suppressed state. And what that means is that they're not being properly represented, which means that a 16-year incumbent who neglected the district gave up his seat because I worked -- outworked him. Liz Landers: The average member of Congress is far wealthier than the average American, but you are a working mom. What is stretching your budget right now, and how can Congress help Americans balance their own? Victoria Broderick: Groceries. I mean, I drive across state lines because I take advantage of Alabama's state grocery taxes. They're cheaper. So I save on average between $50 and $100 on groceries. And I have two young children who think that chocolate milk comes from chocolate cows. So I want to make sure that every single person understands that coming to Congress and making it more affordable, we're not talking about the economy when it comes to like Wall Street. We're talking about groceries, eggs. Rich people don't have to think about that. They don't have to think about their grocery prices when they go in the store. I do. And like most of the people in my district, I want to make sure it's easier for every single person. Liz Landers: You also campaigned on Medicare for all. Senator Bernie Sanders wants to phase it in over four years starting with an eligibility age of 55 or older. Incoming Leader Jeffries, probably Speaker Jeffries, has endorsed lowering the age. Is that enough for you? Victoria Broderick: It's not enough for me, but it's a complicated system that we have to work towards. And now we have a Congress that represents that and can possibly can push that forward. So I think that that's a good starting point, but I want to see better. I also am not opposed to making capitalism work for everyone and forcing companies to give better health care and better benefits to their employees, because, if capitalism is the goal, then they need to make it more competitive. Liz Landers: Speaking of Hakeem Jeffries, do you think that he is the best person to lead Democrats in the new Congress as speaker? Victoria Broderick: As far as my opinion on the Speaker Jeffries, he has agreed to a bold progressive agenda. So, realistically, we're all on a notice. We all have worked that needs to get done. And my job is to hold whoever becomes speaker accountable and make sure that they're doing their job. So, I mean, whoever comes out, it doesn't matter. We're all her

It began as an impromptu kitchen experiment.
Saurabh Munjal, Nikhil Doda and Saurabh Bhutna - three cousins in India's north-western Punjab state - were messing about at home post dinner one evening, when Doda casually brewed up a tangy cumin-flavoured fizzy soda using regular pantry ingredients.
They enjoyed its earthy, piquant taste so much that they decided to explore options to sell it commercially.
Cumin-laced sodas had always been sold at street-side stalls in India, but it was a broken market of local companies. Not many had built a carbonated beverage brand around the flavour.
The trio persuaded their families to invest some capital and launched Lahori Zeera in 2017. Zeera is the Hindi name for cumin.
Almost a decade on, the drink has become a bit of a sensation in India, challenging the entrenched monopoly of global cola giants, especially in the all-important mass-market ten-rupee ($0.11; Â£0.078) beverage category - it will close this year with revenues of $115-120m.
Its popularity reflects a growing consumer preference for distinctly Indian flavours and drinks perceived to be more healthy, say analysts.
Lahori Zeera is one of several cumin-flavoured soda brands that have mushroomed across the country over the past decade.
There's Jeeru from Mumbai-based Xotik Frujus, Campa Jeera from billionaire Mukesh Ambani-owned Campa Cola and at least half-a-dozen other variants from regional players including Fizz Jeera Masala from House of Bindu.
Bindu launched their cumin soda nearly 25 years ago, but sales were flat until some years ago, according to Megha Shankar, a director with the company.
"Now it is the fastest growing category among carbonated beverages," Shankar told the BBC. "Its contribution to our revenues has doubled from 20% to 40% in the last five years."
Soaring demand for the product has pushed House of Bindu to widen its footprint across the country, after being largely based in southern India for over two decades.
Parle Agro, external, one of India's oldest consumer brands, also rolled out its own cumin soda brand Dhishoom nationally last year after exclusively selling it in rural markets since 2012.
Online orders for these fizzy drinks, meanwhile, were up 900% this summer according to a report from one of India's online delivery companies.
The cumin frenzy is reshaping India's non-alcoholic beverages market, which was valued at $32 billion in 2024 and projected to double by 2033.
According to a report from Kotak Mutual Fund earlier this year, Lahori Zeera, Campa and other smaller challengers - now dubbed as India's "ethnic beverages market" - collectively doubled their share of India's carbonated soft-drinks market to around 15% by September last year, while the combined market share of Coca-Cola and PepsiCo fell from roughly 93% to 85%.
"This is a "Jio moment" for beverages. Just as telecom incumbents bled market share when data prices crashed, beverage incumbents are bleeding volume," the Kotak report said, drawing an analogy to the disruption caused by the entry of Reliance-owned Jio Telecom in India's telecoms market in 2016.
"In global markets,â¯establishedâ¯duopolies rarely lose more than 1-2% share annually; anâ¯8% swingâ¯in less than a year is a structural disruption."
Saurabh Munjal, CEO of Archian Foods which manufactures Lahori Zeera, told the BBC that the company has "always been in a situation where we are sold out each year. We've doubled our capacity to 1.2 million bottles per day last year and are still unable to meet demand".
For decades, the colas have had a dominant presence in India, appealing to the aspirational part of the population as lifestyle products that were cool to consume.
With millions of dollars in marketing budgets splashed out on billboards, Bollywood stars and cricket championships, they sold a very western idea of hydration to India, says Munjal.
But home-grown brands are now mounting a serious challenge with a combination of smart distribution, attractive pricing and a turn towards nostalgic Indian flavours such as cumin, raw mango, kokum fruit and tamarind.
Munjal says that for long, there has been a tendency among consumer brands in India to either westernise Indian products or "Indianise" western products. But with Lahori Zeera, which uses the tagline "apna desi thanda", meaning India's own cold drink, his desire is to change that.
Shankar says her brand has also recently launched a zero-sugar version of their cumin soda to capture the growing market for healthier non-cola drinks.
This success notwithstanding, sustaining this winning trajectory will not be easy for these ethnic beverage brands, say analysts. The very factors that propelled their rise could also limit growth.
"The million-dollar question is how big can the cumin-flavoured drink market become. And I suspect it won't become as big as the colas," Rajiv Agarwal, a professor at Mumbai-based SP Jain Institute of Management, who advises family businesses on strategies to succeed against multi-national corporations, told the BBC.
The 10-rupee price point, which accounts for the bulk of sales volumes in India's cumin-flavoured carbonated drinks market, is another double-edged sword.
While it has driven up sales, the soaring cost of plastic, packaging, sugar and other raw material amid the global energy shock could start to hit margins, which are already very thin.
Raising prices, meanwhile, could affect volumes, forcing brands to further reduce bottle sizes, something the cola companies had resorted to a few years ago.
Then there is always the threat of bigger, deep-pocketed players coming in to disrupt the category.
"Competition is extremely aggressive," says Agarwal. And the established global players are better organised in terms of systems, processes, distribution channels and bottling arrangements.

768953f1f23b.text: At the National Book Awards, Abdelrahman ElGendy won the nonfiction prize for his book "Huna," a memoir of his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt. But ElGendy wasn't there to accept the award. His visa to travel from Europe was denied by the U.S. government. Amna Nawaz spoke with ElGendy for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Amna Nawaz: At last night's National Book Awards, novelist Hannah Lillith Assadi won the Fiction Prize for her novel "Paradiso 17" about a Palestinian man's post-1948 exile journey. Brenda Hillman won the poetry award for "Still House in the Desert" on returning to her childhood home after her mother's death. And Abdelrahman ElGendy won the Nonfiction Prize for his book "Huna," a memoir of his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt. But ElGendy wasn't there to accept the award after his visa to travel from Europe was denied by the U.S. government. As part of our arts and culture series, Canvas, Abdelrahman ElGendy joins me now. Welcome to the "News Hour." Congratulations on your award, and thank you for joining us. Abdelrahman ElGendy: Thank you so much for having me. Hi. Amna Nawaz: So I want to get to the visa denial in just a moment. But, first on this award, you saw on Tuesday night finalist after finalist take the stage to deliver remarks dedicate their remarks to you. We saw your editor take the stage to accept the award on your behalf. What was it like for you to watch all of that unfold from across an ocean? Abdelrahman ElGendy: Yes, there is a particular cruelty to being, I guess, forced to outrun the fruits of one's labor all the time and to watch one's work bloom from afar. I have written recently about this, the idea that my book -- my book keeps making into room that I can never be. And I don't know what to do with that sometimes. But, to me, what I keep reminding myself of is that, when I was in prison, I fantasized about a day when these would be my problems, a life beyond prison where my dreams could be crushed in this way even. That was the dream back then. So it was very bittersweet, but it was still sweet. And I think particularly, as you mentioned, because of the solidarity, I -- awards are often spaces that are built on the idea of scarcity and competition. And I think the fact that my fellow finalists managed to turn it into the space of such abundance and love and to find that tenderness to extend toward me, to me, that was so meaningful. It was worth it. Yes, it made it feel like as if I were there in a way. So, that was very meaningful for me. Amna Nawaz: You mentioned having to move around a lot. We should point out for folks you lived in the U.S. for years. You left in April of 2025. You wrote about this. You said you were worried that you could be targeted for your pro-Palestinian advocacy and your criticism of the U.S. government, specifically relations with Egypt, and you resettled in Europe. So, when you applied for the visitor visa to attend this ceremony, did you think that it might be denied? Abdelrahman ElGendy: Of course I thought it. I mean, they never disclosed the reasons. Of course, U.S. consular officers, they have broad discretion to deny visa applications. So I can only speculate about why they denied it. But, of course, I was gutted but unsurprised, because anyone familiar with this current administration can make an educated guess. It's widely known and reported and documented that visa applicants are being scrutinized for public publicly criticizing the U.S. government and expressing support for Palestine. And you have the sort of catch-tall term that is used, like protecting national security. So many of us are familiar with how this administration defines national security and whom it considers to be a threat to it. So, yes, while I cannot know for certain because they don't provide it in writing, I think there are very reasonable grounds to suspect that my political views may have played a role in the rejection of that visa. Amna Nawaz: I don't want the story in your book to be lost amid all these other headlines, because the book, "Huna," we should say, means "here" in Arabic, it tells the story of your years from the age of 17 on as a political prisoner in Egypt, a book, as you pointed out, you smuggled out a few pages at a time. Why did you want to write that story? What is it that you hope people take away from that book? Abdelrahman ElGendy: Yes, I mean, as you said, huna means here in Arabic, and it was inspired by a popular Arab protest song, "Sawfa Nabqa Huna" which means "We Will Remain Here." And I first heard it up close on my third night in detention. We were in excruciating physical conditions, 68 people crammed into this tiny room, piled on top of one another. Some of us were shot and wounded. Then, out of nowhere, the guards finally allowed our families to bring in homemade food. So for the first time since the arrest, we got a taste of home. And something magical happened. We started singing. And one of the songs was "Sawfa Nabqa Huna," which goes: "We will remain here until the pain subsides. We will remain here. The melody will sweeten." And as we sang together, I kind of felt these chills running down my arms. But I started thinking, fascinated, I didn't want to remain here, right? Like none of us could wait to escape that room fast enough. So, what was this here, this huna, that we were touched by, that we were somehow choosing to inhabit together? So, my whole book is actually a six-year pursuit of this huna, which grows more complicated and illuminated with each passing day behind bars, but it traces how the sense of nonphysical hereness and witness repeatedly saves me from being wholly conquered by prison. And so I write -- so I want people to take that away from the book, but also all the people that I write for and toward that I left behind in prison, that I call a ghostified population, people who are so used to being erased by people who leave them behind, to me, it's really im

77f09ccc3dd2.text: In New York, house music pioneer Crystal Waters is bringing together major figures like Deborah Cox and Billy Porter with a live orchestra. It's all to celebrate the genre’s 30-year legacy. Geoff Bennett spoke with Waters about “I Am House Orchestrated” and how the music has grown into both a cultural revolution and a space for self-expression. It’s for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Amna Nawaz: Tonight, at the Palladium in New York, house music pioneer Crystal Waters brings together major figures like Deborah Cox and Billy Porter with a live orchestra, all to celebrate the genre's legacy 30 years on. Geoff Bennett recently spoke with waters about the production called "I Am House Orchestrated" and how the music has grown into both a cultural revolution and space for self-expression. It's also part of our Canvas coverage. Geoff Bennett: Crystal Waters, welcome to the "News Hour." Crystal Waters: Thank you. Thank you for having me. Geoff Bennett: There's an entire generation who knows the music of a Beyonce or a Drake, but what they don't know is that that sound has a direct line to house music. When you hear their music, what strikes your ear? Crystal Waters: Well, first of all, Beyonce and Drake, I would have to thank them for doing a house album, because I think house music kind of got forgotten here in America. But once they did that, people remembered all of our songs, all -- of where it -- they don't remember where it came from, but they remember our songs, and it gave at least me an opportunity to sell people because, house music is blown up. It's like a $53 billion business, and people think it started in Europe. So, for me, my mission is to make sure everybody knows that it started in Chicago. It started with the Black, brown, and queer community, and that's where it's -- that's where it started, and that's who should be celebrated with that. And it's grown. I'm really happy to see that it's grown. But people need to know where it started. Geoff Bennett: Yes, because before it became this global phenomenon, it was really a refuge for marginalized communities. Who were some of those early pioneers? Crystal Waters: Frankie Knuckles is known as the Godfather of House, because what happened was, when disco died, I don't know if you remember the story about them burning all the disco C.D.s, house went back underground. I mean, the music went back underground. And Frankie Knuckles always said that house is Disco's revenge. So, it was Frankie Knuckles, David Morales. It's Louie Vega. There's Tony Humphries, a lot of folks in Chicago and New York. And I think New York and Chicago kind of mixed, because the deejays would fly back and forth, so the sound kind of carried from Chicago to New York. Geoff Bennett: And one of your biggest hits was about homelessness. (MUSIC) Geoff Bennett: Why did you choose to tell such a serious story through dance music? Crystal Waters: Yes, well, I was here at Howard University. And I had this song. I had met The Basement Boys. They sent me the track to write to. And when I wrote, I had the la da di, la da da. (MUSIC) Crystal Waters: And I couldn't find any words that would fit those syllables. So I thought about this woman. She was homeless. She was -- but she had a full face of makeup, fully dressed in black. And I had this bad attitude. I was like, you need to go get a job. But then the local paper did a story, and they talked about how she lost everything within a matter of days, her job, her home, everything. And it changed my whole perspective on homelessness. And the thing that stuck with me was that she said the reason why she did that with the full face of makeup is because she felt, if she was going to ask you for money, she should look and be respectable. And it just stuck with me. So when I said that she was singing that song, that's who I thought of. That's why it starts off, "She wakes up early every morning just to do her hair because she cares." Geoff Bennett: All these years, I never knew that was written about a real woman. Crystal Waters: Yes, it's a real person, that song. Geoff Bennett: And by the time your song "100% Pure Love" became a hit, house music was certainly on its way to being huge. Did you realize then that you were part of something so transformational in music? Crystal Waters: I had no idea I was a part of something. When I started with house music, people would tell me, that's not real music, Crystal. When are you going to go do some real music? And we got beat up pretty big that it was going to be a fad in the past. So to be here 35 years later and to see how big it's grown, all the genres, and how it's still loved, and to know that I was a part of it from the beginning, it's really an honor. Geoff Bennett: How did you find your way to it? Crystal Waters: To house music? I found -- I used to hang out with deejays in the club more than I should have been. (LAUGHTER) Crystal Waters: But I really got introduced from The Basement Boys, because when I started singing, I was doing music more like Sade. I wanted to be the next Sade. And then they handed me some of these tracks with these beats, and I was like, the beat was different. But when I sat and wrote to them, it was very natural, very natural. Then, when I got to New York, I just kind of fit in with the crowd, and I was like, this is my home. I love this. So I -- after that, I never looked back. Geoff Bennett: What have you come to understand about the emotional resonance, the emotional power of house music that you might not have understood at the outset? Crystal Waters: I think I understand now that it feels like community. It's hard -- they say house is a feeling, and it's hard to kind of put into words, but it is community. It feels like a connection. It feels like you can be yourself and not try to be anybody else. That's what the house music was all about. You could come be yourself. You could wear red wig. You could put on roller skates, whatever you wanted

California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.
Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs â and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.
The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.
The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.
Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.
In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)
Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.
It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

3cc8a3bc44d4.text: By — Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press Elaine Kurtenbach, Associated Press By — Kanis Leung, Associated Press Kanis Leung, Associated Press By — Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Aamer Madhani, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/3-takeaways-from-trump-xi-and-putins-historic-summit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 3 takeaways from Trump, Xi and Putin's historic summit World Nov 19, 2026 5:58 PM EST SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin on Thursday was the first-ever sit-down for the leaders of the three countries. They started with talk of a shared responsibility for keeping peace as the victors of World War II and as global powers. But post-meeting readouts by the three nations reflected more symbolism than substance. READ MORE: No breakthroughs from Trump, Xi and Putin's 3-way talks on nuclear risks The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran. It said they agreed on the need for reforms to the United Nations, on increasing oil supplies and on reducing nuclear risks. The statement did not spell out the type and extent of the U.N. reforms the leaders agreed to. The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, opposing what they called "jurisdiction abuse" by the International Criminal Court, the reports said. Here are key takeaways from the talks, which lasted over an hour. China's Xi presided over the summit of 21st century powers Xi added to China's already burgeoning diplomatic stature merely by hosting the event. He said the talks with Trump and Putin were positive and fruitful, and that the three nations had aligned views on safeguarding world peace, according to China's Xinhua official news agency. They agreed major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously and believe differences should be resolved through negotiation and cooperation, Xinhua reported. "As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace," Xi was quoted as saying. "The seeds planted at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit." China's insistence that it has the right to recover the democratically governed island of Taiwan, possibly by force, was not addressed in the leaders' broadly worded agreement. China considers that a domestic issue. China likes to position itself as a different kind of superpower from the U.S. and Russia — one that doesn't get involved in wars and advocates for smaller states, said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. Beijing's priority was steering the meeting away from specifics, she said. "Beijing wanted to be seen as the adult in the room." Trump claims a place in history Trump heralded the leaders' gathering as "really making history" and he suggested to Xi and Putin that together they were shaking things up by ditching the "old school" way adversaries engage. The White House set low expectations for the talks. But Trump framed them Thursday as only the beginning — a chance to get the conversation rolling on solving some of the world's thorniest issues. "A lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start," Trump told Putin during a one-on-one meeting prior to their three-way meeting with Xi. The carefully crafted event was a welcome break for Trump after a couple of rotten weeks for his presidency in which his Republican Party was trounced in the midterm elections, widespread tech outages spooked Americans, and Iran escalated attacks on U.S. allies. Trump said Iran was on the agenda as was Russia's war against Ukraine. China and Russia carry enormous sway with Tehran and also have been accused by the U.S. of supporting the Islamic Republic. He reiterated Thursday that he and Xi agree Iran needs to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for world energy supplies that has become a chokepoint since the start of the war. They also agree that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon, Trump said. But there were no signs that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict. Following the talks, Trump dialed into a meeting in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort. Trump told the Berlin gathering that he spoke to Xi and Putin about finding a peaceful end to the Ukraine war, Witkoff said. Putin shares spotlight with Trump and Xi For Putin, the three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit — and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier — offered a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to signal that he heads a superpower on par with the United States and China. Trump and Putin found common ground in their opposition to the ICC. The Russian leader is wanted by the ICC under an arrest warrant for his alleged war crimes in Ukraine. The U.S. opposes the ICC's arrest warrant against former Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. READ MORE: For Putin, sharing a spotlight with Trump and Xi boosts his profile on the global stage Putin last attended an APEC summit in 2017. His presence as an honored guest and Russia's status as a top global power — at least at the gathering in Shenzhen — mark a diplomatic breakthrough. Just before the summit, Russia sent a pair of nuclear-capable Tu-95 bombers on a visit to Vietnam in a reminder of its nuclear might. And as Putin arrived in China, Russian TV zeroed in on an officer in his retinue who was carrying a briefcase with the codes for Moscow's nuclear forces. Putin addressed Xi as "dear friend" during their talks on Wednesday, and smiled contentedly on Thursday as he shook hands with Trump, who called him "my friend
