From premature baby to social media star - Famed hippo Fiona dies
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.
Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species. She reached 1,000 lbs in 2018.
Over the years, Fiona became a favourite among visitors and a star on social media. This video captures moments from her life, from her early days as a calf to celebrating her fifth birthday and receiving treatment just a few days ago.

The Scene
Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston knows shareholders hate his deal. âItâs been a rough go,â he told Semafor in a Thursday interview. He has a message for them: Bear with us.
Lumentum was looking to buy a chip company for months. âWe felt like we needed semiconductor properties, so we were actually in the market,â Hurlston said. âMarvell got word we were on a shopping spree and they said, âHey, you know, rather than do that, why not combine with us?ââ
Lumentum and Marvell agreed to a $115 billion all-stock deal earlier this month that tacks Hurlstonâs optical tech business â a key part of the data center buildout that allows high-powered GPUs to actually get their data onto usersâ screens â to Marvellâs chips businesses. On paper, the deal made all the sense in the world, Hurlston said.
âIf you accept the premise that we needed to have a semiconductor asset, Marvell is the best semiconductor [maker] in this area,â Hurlston said.
Investors howled. Shares in both Marvell and Lumentum are down roughly 40% since the deal was announced on worries over how much runway the AI trade has left. Some Lumentum shareholders also say the company sold too soon.
âThe deal hasnât worked as we expected, right?â Hurlston said. âThe view from investors is, you took some of your upside off the table, and youâve now hitched your wagon to a company whose upside is a little bit less known.â
Market Jitters
Hurlston says he expects shares to rebound once the companies can share more information with analysts, portfolio managers, and other shareholders through regulatory filings and other meetings. And while thereâs still a chance the deal falls apart â there is a material adverse change clause baked into the deal terms â âweâre going to have to see this thing through, unless shareholders vote no, or if we donât get regulatory approval,â Hurlston said. âThe set of circumstances under which we can exercise a MAC are very limited.â
There is a bit of portfolio-manager-on-portfolio-manager violence going on, Hurlston noted. Despite overlap in the two companyâs shareholder bases â 80%, by Hurlstonâs math â portfolio managers may hold Marvell but not Lumentum, or vice versa, triggering some forced selling.
âThe name of the game in hyperscaling, from a supplier, is continuity of supply and time to market,â Hurlston said. âWhat this system-sell enables is for us to deliver to our customers massive time to market,â he continued, because Marvell and Lumentum products can be shipped out to data centers as one finished product.
The companies will also face regulatory review in both the US and in China, which is likely to draw more scrutiny following the Nvidia chip scandal. Nvidia is both a shareholder and major customer of Lumentumâs.
Hurlston noted that both he and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have gotten deals through Chinaâs State Authority on Market Regulation, or SAMR, before, and that they already have a good sense of what to expect. âThey really want their supply to be there, and weâre a critical supplierâ of transistors into the Chinese market.
Semafor has also reported that Marvellâs Murphy could be tapped to take the CEO position at Nvidia following Jensen Huangâs resignation. Hurlston said he didnât know whether Murphy was considering the role or whether he would take it, but said, âI think he can do the job.â
âThe board is not going to want somebody who has any sort of besmirchment, and I think you want to have somebody whoâs been a sitting CEO,â he said. âThereâs no argument that this guyâs done a terrific job [at Marvell].â

24c29e7a6ce7.text: By — Scott Bauer, Associated Press Scott Bauer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/prosecutor-declines-to-charge-wisconsin-officer-who-fatally-shot-black-man-in-madison Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Prosecutor declines to charge Wisconsin officer who fatally shot Black man in Madison Nation Nov 19, 2026 5:48 PM EST MADISON, Wis. (AP) — The Wisconsin police officer who shot and killed a 38-year-old Black man in Madison in July will not face criminal charges, a prosecutor announced Thursday, sparking calls for justice from the victim's family members and community advocates. The shooting of Corey Ruiz sparked racial justice protests, and city leaders were bracing for more protests in the wake of the decision not to charge the officer, who is white. The victim's brother, Adam Ruiz, told reporters the prosecutor has "mistreated" his family. "We're destroyed," he said. "We won't accept this." Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, an officer with more than a decade of experience in law enforcement, fired the shots that killed Ruiz on July 22. Baitinger-Peterson was one of four officers who responded to calls about someone checking out parked cars and an alleged burglary attempt, police said. They surrounded Ruiz, who was on a bicycle. "I conclude it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody," Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne said in a statement announcing his decision. READ MORE: Police officer's fatal shooting of man with knife roils Madison, Wisconsin The Wisconsin Department of Justice said immediately after the shooting that two officers attempted to use a Taser on Ruiz but weren't successful. Ruiz "brandished a knife and injured" Baitinger-Peterson, the department said. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who represents the Ruiz family and was surrounded by them at a news conference Thursday, said there was nothing in the videos that the district attorney showed them to justify the shooting. "In the video you see they tackle him, they tase him, they kick him and then the police officer executes him," Crump said. "The video is the objective unbiased witness here." Madison Police Chief John Patterson said he has trust in the city's police officers, but he realizes the decision not to bring charges "will bring various emotions." He urged protesters, however, to remain peaceful. Patterson said the police will now conduct an internal review of the shooting, and all of the officers involved will remain on administrative leave. Prosecutor shows the Ruiz family video of the shooting Ozanne said he reached his decision after reviewing evidence that included police reports, diagrams, surveillance videos, police squad car videos and citizen videos. Madison police officers do not wear body cameras. Crump said it is one of the worst cases of excessive force that he has worked on. "When you are shooting a man who is on the ground, three (times). It hits him in his chest and the kill shot hits him in his head," he said. Crump said the medical examiner told the Ruiz family he would have survived had the third shot not been fired and hit him in the head. When asked if the family would be filing a lawsuit, Crump said his team will "explore every possible avenue." Ozanne said his decision was a correct interpretation of the law. "A person does not have to like and/or agree with the law, however I am sworn to apply the law to the facts at hand," the prosecutor said. "The law applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not." The Wisconsin Department of Justice released its investigative files concerning the shooting Thursday, including photo and video evidence. One police dash-camera video captures the moment three officers tried to wrestle Ruiz into submission. They repeatedly yell, "He's got a knife! He's got a knife!" The weapon is visible in his right hand, the blade pointed downward, as a fourth officer arrives and deploys a Taser. Ruiz stumbles and falls onto his right side before Baitinger-Peterson fires three shots at close range. Days of protests followed the shooting Baitinger-Peterson has not replied to an email sent Thursday seeking comment. Baitinger-Peterson told investigators during an interview days after the shooting that he got on his knees and grabbed Ruiz's right arm before realizing Ruiz was holding a knife, according to records released Thursday. He said he was struggling to control the arm and feared that Ruiz would stab the officers. He said he fired a third time because he didn't think the first two shots had struck Ruiz because Ruiz's facial expression and body did not change. Jim Palmer, executive director of the police union Wisconsin Professional Police Association, said in a statement the decision that the officer's use of deadly force was legally justified "is supported by the evidence and consistent with the legal standards governing the use of force by law enforcement officers." It was the third time since 2012 that Madison police had shot and killed someone in the same neighborhood. The killing sparked days of protests and forced the city to reckon with calls for police reform to address racial justice issues. Baitinger-Peterson and the other three officers who interacted with Ruiz that day have been on paid administrative leave since the shooting. While bystanders captured the confrontation on video, there is no body camera footage because Madison police officers don't wear them. All Madison police officers could be equipped with body cameras by the end of 2027 thanks to a $350,000 donation from a local nonprofit that city officials announced in September. The donation will help cover operational expenses, while other costs are being funded through grants and other means. Associated Press journalists Claud

A judge in Florida has declared Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, to be mentally competent to stand trial for possessing indecent images of children.
The hearing came after an evaluation by a court-appointed psychiatrist conducted on Prince Harry's 82-year-old father-in-law.
Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was ordered to stay in jail pending trial earlier this month after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home that specialises in dementia. His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.
Markle appeared in court in Tampa in a wheelchair, and his lawyers did not dispute the court-appointed psychiatrist's finding that he is mentally competent to understand the nature and consequences of the charge against him.
His next court hearing is scheduled for early December, but any trial is expected to take place in California, where the federal charge was filed.
Inside the storage units in Los Angeles the FBI says agents found about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades.
Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".
He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.
On Monday, police in the Philippines asked prosecutors to charge Markle with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
Last month, police there obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018, and he did not attend her wedding in London that same year.
The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

9dcbd1f5eced.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-issues-14-day-extension-of-order-blocking-trumps-triumphal-arch-construction Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge issues 14-day extension of order blocking Trump's triumphal arch construction Politics Nov 19, 2026 5:39 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Wednesday temporarily extended an order blocking the Trump administration from breaking ground on a towering memorial arch in the nation's capital. READ MORE: Trump's triumphal arch is blocked for now, but a new website highlights the plans The temporary restraining order was due to expire on Thursday, but U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended it by 14 days. That would keep President Donald Trump's construction project on hold until Dec. 3 or until Chutkan rules on a pending request for a more permanent preliminary injunction. The decision followed a Nov. 5 order Chutkan issued shortly after a hearing of the National Capital Planning Commission ended with the Trump-heavy commission giving the arch its final approval in an 8-4 vote, despite dozens of witnesses who opposed the construction. Please check your inbox to confirm. The administration said the work could begin as soon as the approval and the Interior Department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service. In issuing the latest delay, Chutkan granted a request by plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch construction. The case has grown more complicated as separate groups have filed lawsuits asking that the project not be allowed to go forward. Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with the Public Citizen Litigation Group that is representing the plaintiffs in the original lawsuit, said they were "gratified to see that the judge recognized that the circumstances that required emergency relief two weeks ago haven't changed. We're hopeful the additional two-week pause will give the court the opportunity to assess our arguments in favor of a longer-term preliminary injunction that will block construction of the arch while the lawsuit proceeds." "An activist district court has again blocked the construction of the long-awaited Military Triumphal Arch. The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle in an emailed statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The District of Columbia and Virginia filed suit Oct. 31. Chutkan consolidated that suit with the original, filed by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. Members of the Kennedy family filed a separate lawsuit Nov. 10, citing the impact the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would have on family members buried at Arlington National Cemetery. The Arlington County Board filed a lawsuit Oct. 8 in federal court in the Eastern District of Virginia challenging the speed with which the project was being undertaken and the harm it would cause to the county, which is immediately adjacent to the proposed site. Chutkan said the 14-day extension of the order is warranted because nothing has significantly changed in the litigation in the two weeks since she issued it. She decided to maintain the status quo pending her ruling on the injunction request. The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats take control of Congress. Many of those plans are being challenged in the courts. The federal government Thursday filed a notice of appeal to a 14-day temporary restraining order issued Nov. 14 in the golf course case. The original plaintiffs in the District of Columbia case — three veterans and a retired architectural historian — had asked Chutkan to prohibit the administration and the National Park Service "from taking any steps to construct, or to direct or facilitate construction of, any structure in Memorial Circle, absent congressional authorization, during the pendency of this litigation." Critics, including the plaintiffs, argue the administration must seek congressional approval for the arch and say that, once built, it will disrupt the sightlines connecting historic landmarks in the nation's capital. The administration has argued that Congress decades ago cleared the way for a monument at Memorial Circle. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 4393151b5d6a.text: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said Thursday Congress is going to reclaim powers long ceded to the executive branch at the Axios Future of Defense summit. Why it matters: As the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Meeks is putting the Trump administration on notice that it's foreign policy decisions are going to be challenged through legislation and oversight hearings. What they're saying: "Whether it's a Democratic president or Republican president, we've ceded too much and we've got to stand up and take it back," Meeks told Axios' Colin Demarest. "We do, at times, have to make some difficult decisions, and not just punt them away to the executive branch, because when you do that, it's hard to get them back." Meeks also suggested that incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) may be willing to take the Trump administration to court if needed to enforce congressional oversight. "If it takes some litigation to do that, we will do that," Meeks said. "Speaker Johnson wouldn't do it. I think Speaker Jeffries will do it." Catch up quick: Meeks will likely become Foreign Affairs committee chair in January, riding the blue wave that gave Democrats the ability to control Congress' legislative agenda. Zoom in: Meeks didn't rule out calling Secretary of State Marco Rubio to testify before the committee. "The jurisdiction of the House Foreign Affairs Committee is the State Department," Meeks said. Later, he added more broadly, "[y]ou can run, but you can't hide... We're going to use the power that the committee and the Constitution gives us to make sure that we're calling in members of that administration, so they have to answer to the American people, why what has taken place has taken place." Zoom out: Meeks has already sent document-preservation letters to seven agencies, including the State Department, USAID and the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, warning them to avoid destroying records that could be relevant to oversight efforts. He threatened the possibility of criminal referrals if someone is found to have done otherwise. What we're watching: Meeks said Democrats plan to address affordability concerns and introduce another War Powers Resolution aimed at the Iran war. He also floated litigation and using Congress' power of the purse, including withholding funds, as ways to force the Trump administration to comply. "The people have spoken loudly and clearly that they are against the war in Iran," Meeks said. "They see how foreign policy directly now connects to domestic policy." He added that Democrats need to investigate what's happening in the Middle East, and explain to Americans what's at stake in the war. "That is the job, a part of the job, of the Foreign Affairs Committee, and that's exactly what we're going to do on day one." Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

6dc5fe639985.text: The White House named Kirsten A. Davies to be its new national cyber director Thursday as President Trump overhauls his AI team, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Davies, who currently serves as the Pentagon's chief information officer , has more experience in the field than the outgoing director , Sean Cairncross . Cairncross' departure was described as amicable by two sources. But two White House officials said President Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, sought the change and pushed out Cairncross because, one said, he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." The search for Cairncross's replacement was begun two weeks ago, a third source said. Zoom out: The Office of the National Cyber Director coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. The position requires Senate confirmation. Davies previously was cleared by the Senate as the Defense Department's chief information officer. "Kirsten has the credentials to excel in this position and has already been Senate-confirmed," an administration official said. At the Pentagon, Davies has been the top adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "on all matters relating to information management, information technology, cybersecurity, and information assurance," according to her bio. Before serving in the Trump administration, Davies worked for Unilever and "led global cyber resilience for one of the world's largest consumer goods enterprises," her bio says. Davies' career also has included technology and cyber roles at Estée Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard and Siemens. She founded the Institute for Cyber, a nonprofit organization dedicated to citizen safety and security in the digital universe. State of play: The administration's AI team has taken shape on the fly , but Cairncross was involved in key decisions. He held technical meetings with Anthropic leaders over the summer after Commerce Department export controls effectively scrubbed the company's models from the internet. Cairncross brought experience in Republican politics and national security, having worked with the intelligence community and dealt with cyber threats at the Republican National Committee. During Trump's first term, Cairncross represented the White House chief of staff on National Security Council committees before leading the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. Cairncross' head of policy and senior adviser Thomas Lind left in June and joined OpenAI in October, further depleting the Trump administration of technical expertise. The big picture: The latest turnover in cyber personnel comes as the country grapples with critical infrastructure outages and increasingly powerful AI poised to empower cyber defenders and hackers alike. Democrats have criticized the administration's response to outages and warned that U.S. cyber defenses are falling behind AI-fueled threats. What we're watching: Trump is also filling other key cyber positions. His pick for the top job at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps defend federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure, Palantir executive Michael LoSapio, faced a combative confirmation hearing Thursday. What they're saying: In a written statement, Cairncross said, "it has been the honor of a lifetime to serve President Donald J. Trump. I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence." This story has been updated with details on Davies' appointment and background.

1aa026162e64.text:
The Army wants its units to use more data, but many aren’t built to do so
AI might help move intelligence more quickly up and down the echelons, Army and industry speakers said.
Recent Army field exercises keep revealing a missing key to the data-driven future envisioned by service leaders: the ability to move information quickly and effectively between echelons. Some put it this way: “The Army doesn’t have a data issue, it has a data-management issue.”
A major takeaway from Project Flytrap, a Poland-based exercise, is that the way combat units, communications units, and headquarters share information and make decisions can’t keep up, according to a junior signal officer who helped manage data for the exercise earlier this year.
“The battlefield is so massively complex, and there's such a vast amount of things you have to account for,” Capt. Gabriel Glazer, a graduate student at Carnegie Mellon University who most recently served in the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, said Thursday at an Armed Forces Communications and Electronics Association event near Washington, D.C. “It is, frankly, almost impossible for any unit, the way it is structured now, to account for them, and it's almost impossible for any leader to make the best decision at a speed at which it's going to be relevant for their success or failure in whatever operation they're in.”
It’s a gap artificial intelligence could potentially fill, Glazer said, to shorten the time it takes to get intelligence from individual units on the ground up to division and corps headquarters, then disperse it throughout the entire formation.
“Getting the data down to the lower level is absolutely critical, because we obviously can't do that, especially in every situation, especially if we're going to be in a denied or degraded environment,” he said.
While the Army has been testing its next-generation command-and-control platform by linking up ever-larger formations, Glazer argued there needs to be a lower-level fix to help junior officers make decisions, while also sending their data up to higher echelons.
“I think that a platoon leader on the ground is going to want the information coming from a division or a corps, but they are going to need a system that enables them to react and make the best decision to the drone swarm that is going to be approaching them, if they are in that type of environment,” he said.
Even the most advanced networks are still only transmitting data and making decisions at human speed, said James Craven, Anduril’s NGC2 program manager.
“Imagine that we have indications and warning of an anti-radiation missile, or an aircraft capable of launching anti-radiation missiles at the division HQ, as it is now,” Craven said.
That information has to get from the intelligence shop to the operations shop, who will set the division’s electromagnetic posture, then to the signals battalion to physically change the configuration of the radios to protect them from interference.
“There's a seam and gap there, but it occurs at people speed,” he said. “It's not going to be fast.”
There are opportunities for AI to ease some of that friction, said Melissa Daminski of L3 Harris.
“AI is going to be native, and so there is that dual-sided AI aspect of cellular communications, where we will need to be sensing the spectrum and maneuvering within a 5G, 6G signal as our adversaries are doing the same,” she said. “And similarly, we'll need AI and other smarts to say, okay, it's time to get off of this channel and move to another one.”
For now, Glazer said, the Army Data Operations Center is troubleshooting individual data-flow issues as they pop up.
“As those barriers are broken down, we're going to see lower-level, tactical-level units finding solutions to problems that propagate throughout the entire course, and I'm really excited for that,” he said.

1f15dc93cd9d.text: By — Maria Sherman, Associated Press Maria Sherman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/ella-langley-sweeps-the-2026-cma-awards-and-wins-entertainer-of-the-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ella Langley sweeps the 2026 CMA Awards and wins entertainer of the year Arts Nov 19, 2026 4:56 PM EST It didn't take a crystal ball to see: The 2026 Country Music Association Awards were always going to be all about Ella Langley. The Alabama-born-and-raised singer was named entertainer of the year during Wednesday's event — beating the host of the evening and last year's winner Lainey Wilson, as well as Cody Johnson, Luke Combs and Chris Stapleton, for the top prize. READ MORE: Raye leads 2027 Grammy nominations as women dominate top categories "At this point, I'm sick of me," she started her acceptance speech with a joke, after having spent so much of the show on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life." Wilson emerged with a bedazzled broom because, "I told you, you was going to sweep, girl!" she said as she embraced Langley. It really was Langley's night from the jump. The 60th annual CMA Awards, broadcast live from Nashville's Bridgestone Arena, started and ended with her. Langley accepted the first award of the night, single of the year, for her history-making "Choosin' Texas." Competition was fierce: Taylor Swift's song for the "Toy Story 5" film, "I Knew It, I Knew You," was also nominated in the category, as were Langley's own "Be Her," Wilson's "Somewhere Over Laredo" and Johnson's "The Fall." And then Langley was back on stage almost immediately afterward — to perform her joyous "Loving Life Again" with a string quartet and to pick up another award, when "Choosin' Texas" was named song of the year. "This song is the gift that keeps on giving," she said in her speech. She also won female vocalist as well as album of the year, the latter for her thrilling, old-soul country "Dandelion." "My lip is already quivering," she said. "I'm at a loss for words." The return of Taylor Swift and a tribute to Dolly Parton Swift was in the building. The pop powerhouse lit up the CMA Awards by performing "I Knew It, I Knew You" with a bit of her 2006 country hit "Our Song" mixed in for good measure. She began her set in the back halls of the arena before hitting the stage — joined by Keith Urban on banjo, no less — as if no time had passed. But it's been 13 years since Swift last performed at the CMA Awards, a decade after her last appearance there and 17 years after being named the youngest entertainer of the year in the show's history. Consider it a treat in a night full of them. The show began with a powerful tribute to the larger-than-life Dolly Parton. The American icon died in August at age 80, and her legacy will be felt for many decades to come. Host Wilson got the celebration started, duetting Parton's "I Will Always Love You" with the legendary singer-songwriter Vince Gill. Then she was joined by singer Brad Paisley in a funny opening monologue where the pair sang modern parodies of famous country songs: Loretta Lynn's "Coal Miner's Daughter" became "Data Miner's Daughter," and Willie Nelson's "Always On My Mind" was transformed into "Always On My Phone." No shortage of awards and performances here A standout set arrived early: Kacey Musgraves and Miranda Lambert duetted "Horses & Divorces" — a song from Musgraves' latest album, "Middle of Nowhere," that doubles as a delicious resolution from the pair of former frenemies — with its norteño accordion and shout-along lyrics. The stage was set to look like an '80s beauty parlor, recalling one of Parton's most famous acting roles: the 1989 film "Steel Magnolias." Tim McGraw brought it back to the '90s, singing "Don't Take the Girl." Megan Moroney slowed things down with her big-hearted ballad "Beautiful Things." Tucker Wetmore was joined by a brass band for a bit of his single "Who Told You That" before launching into some of Hank Williams Jr.'s 1984 hit "All My Rowdy Friends Are Coming Over Tonight." Combs tackled his song "Miss You Here." Lambert and Langley brought some country-disco with "Snakeskin Boots." Mumford & Sons teamed up with Stapleton for "Here." Later, Stapleton would hop back on stage to join Stephen Wilson Jr. — and to be awarded male vocalist of the year, for a ninth time in his career. Lainey Wilson performed a brand new one, the full-throated "Just A Woman." It was a bit of a theme: The modern traditionalist Zach Top also debuted a new track, the bluegrass-y "Moonshine." Before he left the stage, Dierks Bentley joined in for a tribute to the late John Anderson. They sang his 1983 single "Swingin'." Best new artist went to Stephen Wilson Jr.; vocal group went for a second year in a row to the Red Clay Strays, who also performed their song "Revival." Brooks & Dunn took home vocal duo for the 17th time. "I love to hear myself talk, and I've actually run out of things to say," Kix Brooks said in his acceptance speech. "Thanks for making us famous." "Follow the yellow brick road," added Ronnie Dunn. Later in the night, they received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award. Halestorm, Marcus King, Brothers Osborne, Hardy and Luke Bryan paid tribute to the legendary country music duo, covering some of their biggest hits: "Boot Scootin' Boogie," "Rock My World (Little Country Girl)," "Hard Workin' Man," "Hillbilly Deluxe" and "Play Something Country." Prizes are nominated and voted on by members of the Country Music Association, which includes music executives, artists, publicists, songwriters and other industry professionals. 8de1e9be8c1a.text:
Data centers have become a key focus of the acrimonious debate over the bill Senate leaders hope to pass this week to overhaul the federal permitting process.
Progress on the measure ground to a halt Thursday in part over a fight to add a provision that would ban data centers on federal lands. President Donald Trump’s administration has expressed interest in using public lands for that purpose.
Authors of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, maintain that the bill would not change the law on the siting of data centers. On the contrary, it includes provisions that would mark Congress’ first demands on artificial intelligence facility developers, requiring them to pay costs that until now have been foisted on electricity ratepayers. Supporters say it would mean a $35 billion infusion into the electric grid, intended to ease consumer costs.
But opponents of the sprawling 495-page legislation argue that its overall effect would be to speed data center development, even though few data centers require federal permits. That’s because all data centers need copious amounts of energy, and the bill would make it easier to build pipelines, mines, transmission lines and power plants. The largest driver of demand for this new energy infrastructure in the United States is the artificial intelligence build-out, and public anger over data centers helped propel Democrats to victory in the midterm elections.
“This bill doesn’t just roll out the red carpet for data center developers, it puts them on a greased-up slide into towns across America,” said Sen. Edward Markey (D-Mass.) on the Senate floor.
With new research out this week showing that U.S. data centers are churning out greenhouse gas emissions far beyond previous estimates, Markey and other BAAJA foes warn that the legislation would accelerate climate pollution, spur a surge in natural gas prices that could erase any electricity cost savings and lock in decisions the Trump administration is eager to make to site data centers on Western public lands.
Trump and Republicans solidly support BAAJA, with Sen. Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), former chief executive of the gas pipeline giant Williams Cos., even citing its potential to spur data center development as a selling point.
But Democrats are bitterly divided. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-Nev.), who negotiated the permitting deal with Republicans, argue that far from driving new emissions, the bill will supercharge a clean energy transition by removing the barriers that have held back solar, wind and battery storage. On Wednesday night, after some Democratic support for BAAJA eroded, leaving them only six votes from losing the 60 needed for passage in the Senate, the pair posted a video on X to “do a little myth-busting,” in Whitehouse’s words.
“I don’t know that there are two Senators who care more about protecting the environment than we do,” Whitehouse said. The bill doesn’t lower standards, but sets deadlines and “lets the clean energy that is going to protect the environment get built,” he said.
The battle this week in the Senate, set to move soon to the House, is being waged between Democrats like Whitehouse and Heinrich, who have faith that cheaper clean energy will win out, and opponents like Markey who fear that fossil fuels will flood the zone that BAAJA opens up.
The natural gas industry is winning already, they argue, because of its success in promoting itself as the always-on, easily deployable and abundant solution to feed the data center industry’s voracious energy appetite.
Ratepayer Protection, But Looming Gas Trouble
The first peer-reviewed research measuring big data center carbon emissions in the United States showed that the problem is two to three times larger than previous estimates would suggest. So-called “hyperscale” facilities, the 400 largest and most powerful data centers in the United States, are together responsible for emitting 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually, according to the study published Monday in Nature Sustainability by researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative. That’s similar to the CO2 emissions of Bolivia and larger than those of more than 120 countries.
The Harvard researchers found that roughly 54 percent of the electricity powering the hyperscale data centers was generated by fossil fuels—38 percent by natural gas and 15 percent by coal.
Clean energy industry advocates who support BAAJA say the legislation would change that mix, expanding electricity transmission and getting renewable energy projects that have been stuck in the interconnection queue hooked up to the grid.
“One of the measures we wanted to insist upon as we designed this bill was major emissions reductions, and it produces gigaton-scale carbon emissions reduction,” Whitehouse said in the Wednesday video posted on X.
Analysts at Rhodium Group estimated that BAAJA’s removal of barriers to the grid interconnection process would indeed produce such large net economy-wide greenhouse gas reductions, even though the bill also reduces the cost and accelerates the pace of building natural gas pipelines.
Another key selling point of the bill has been that it would save consumers money by enacting an enhanced version of the Ratepayer Protection Pledge that Trump promoted at the White House earlier this year and that the House passed 417-3 in September.
Usually, utilities spread the cost of grid upgrades among all customers, but under BAAJA, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission would write new rules to ensure all data centers—new and old—are charged both for upgrades they require as well as for their use of the existing grid. The consulting firm Grid Strategies estimates the data center industry would pay an additional $35 billion in electric transmission costs (for a total $55 billion) over the next 10 years.

Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near MoÅodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," he said.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa DÄba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland and in July a cruise missile also landed in Poland.

- Published
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.
This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.
A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.
Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.
His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.
Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.
Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.
When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".
He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."
Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.
"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"
The use of pentobarbital has been under renewed scrutiny since Pike, a 50-year-old convicted murder, survived two attempts at execution via the lethal injection in September. She was taken to hospital in a critical condition and has since returned to prison.
Her botched execution captivated and shocked the world.
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states, which can choose their own methods.

974fdeb4375a.text:
- Published
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least eight dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".
The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.
Seven medical personnel were injured during the night's assault, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Of the eight fatalities confirmed so far, six were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.
The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.
The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit â¬70bn (Â£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.
The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.
On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country.
It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.
Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.
Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.
France's foreign minister Jean-NoÃ«l Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.
He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

e98163caed77.text:
The News
Large-scale trials of three vaccines against the deadly Bundibugyo Ebola strain in the epicenter of DR Congoâs outbreak could yield a breakthrough early next year if security challenges can be overcome, the head of a global vaccine body told Semafor.
The Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no proven vaccine, has killed more than 5,500 people since Mayâs declaration of an outbreak â now the second-largest ever recorded. Most of the cases, amounting to more than 11,000, have been concentrated in the conflict-hit east of the country.
The Tumaini trial â a study to test vaccine candidates â will see jabs tested on at least 1,000 people to check their safety and efficacy. A trial of Ervebo, a vaccine developed by Merck that has been approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, began on Oct. 23. The two other vaccines, which were designed to target the Bundibugyo strain and will join the trial in the next few days, are a jab developed by Oxford University scientists and another by Moderna that harnesses technology used to create vaccines for COVID-19.
âIn a best case, we could look towards early next year for a result,â said Richard Hatchett, CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations. He added that even if data suggested a vaccination was effective and safe, Congolese and global health regulators would still take time to conduct a review before issuing a formal decision about authorizing it for emergency use. âThere is the potential, if the regulators approve, for expanded access to the vaccine while that review is going on,â he said.
Emanuele Capobianco, director of global health security at GAVI, a global vaccine alliance, in a separate interview, said if trials were successful, vaccines could potentially be deployed in the first half of 2027.
The Ervebo trial kicked off in Ituri, the worst-affected province, but the CEPI chief said the testing area could be widened to include other provinces, including the eastern region of North Kivu.
Conflict and misinformation
The Congolese army has for decades fought various rebel groups including M23, which DR Congoâs government has accused neighboring Rwanda of supporting â claims denied by Kigali. The conflict has hampered efforts to bring the outbreak under control, with thousands of people forced to flee their homes. Health workers and surveillance teams have also come under attack in communities that distrust outsiders.
Both Hatchett and Capobianco warned that insecurity in the east of the country was a major obstacle to trialing vaccines.
âThereâs lots of conflict, thereâs lots of misinformation,â said Hatchett. âThe biggest variable is how quickly can we enrol the necessary number of subjects, and that is a dynamic process,â he said.
Similarly, Capobianco â who called eastern DR Congo a âcomplex environment in which to operateâ â said the involvement of healthcare workers, religious leaders, and community authorities would be crucial in moving forward with trials.
The View from Geneva
âWhile the response has slowed transmission in the initial epicentres, 400 to 500 new cases continue to be reported each week,â the World Health Organization said in an update this week. It said delays in paying frontline health workers and responders also created tension and slowed the response to the outbreak.
Notable
- The director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention warned that the outbreak is still not under control, six months after being declared.
- US pharmaceutical company Gilead signed royalty-free licensing agreements with three generic manufacturers for potential future access to an antiviral being trialled as a treatment for people exposed to the Bundibugyo strain.

9a36ec57e02a.text:
The News
South Africaâs African National Congress is negotiating with smaller populist parties for control of three cities that anchor the countryâs economy.
The proposed deal, following local elections this month, could leave the Democratic Alliance in opposition in all three, even though it finished first in each. The two parties govern together nationally, but now the prospect of a fight across Gauteng province â which is home to Johannesburg, the financial hub of Africaâs biggest economy â is adding to investor anxiety about how long that partnership can last.
On Thursday, Helen Zille, a former DA leader and Western Cape premier who ran as the partyâs mayoral candidate, conceded defeat in her bid to become mayor.
Zilleâs concession came as a frantic bargaining window entered its final week. South Africans voted on Nov. 4, and councils have until Nov. 27 to hold their first meetings, following the publication of elected councillors in the Government Gazette. Nationwide, 140 of 213 councils emerged without a party holding a majority, roughly twice as many as in 2021.
Herman Mashaba, whose ActionSA party finished third in Johannesburg, told Semafor the proposed deal would return him to the mayorâs office, which he held from 2016 to 2019. He said ActionSA would also share power with the ANC, Economic Freedom Fighters and uMkhonto weSizwe Party in two other Gauteng cities, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni.
For the ANC, the deal would mean returning to power in Gautengâs cities with the help of its own radical-left populist breakaways. The EFF was founded by Julius Malema after his expulsion from the ANC in 2012, while uMkhonto weSizwe was founded by former president Jacob Zuma, whose campaign helped cost the ANC its national majority in 2024. Mashaba, who left the DA, completes a coalition of defectors. Voters who deserted the ANC in the metros would find it back in government, supported by parties that campaigned against it.
âAll parties, large and small.â
The ANCâs national leadership gave its negotiators a broad mandate last week to talk to âall political parties, large and small.â Within a day, Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula was in talks with the EFF. A source familiar with the leadershipâs discussions said the ANC remained open to a deal with the DA, despite calls from the ANC Youth League to end the national partnership.
For investors who had hoped the ANC and market-friendly DA would extend their national partnership to Gauteng, the proposed deal would be a setback. It would give the EFF and uMkhonto weSizwe influence over two major cities, adding uncertainty for businesses planning around municipal rates and infrastructure spending. The bigger concern is whether the dispute will undermine confidence in the Government of National Unity.
Samâs view
The GNU was a marriage of necessity. After the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time in May 2024, it assembled a 10-party coalition with 287 of parliamentâs 400 seats. The DA brought its votes and standing with investors while the ANC kept the presidency and most of the cabinet. The parties have since clashed over the 2025 budget, VAT, land expropriation, national health insurance and schools policy, but neither has walked out. A collapse would reopen the question of who governs Africaâs most industrialized economy and threaten reforms investors are counting on to revive growth.
Ronak Gopaldas, a director at Signal Risk, told Semafor the national coalitionâs stability âis itself being used as a bargaining chip in the municipal negotiations.â His firm expects the coalition to hold, partly because of the market backlash a breakup could trigger. He sees practical reasons for the ANC and DA to keep governing together, even as recurring disputes limit what they can deliver.
President Cyril Ramaphosaâs position, potentially, compounds the risk. His term as ANC leader ends next year, although he remains president until 2029. A source familiar with the partyâs discussions said its national executive took collective responsibility for the election defeat, shielding Ramaphosa from being singled out. But the argument over the coalition he built will carry into the succession contest, when every compromise with the DA could become ammunition against him within his own party.
If the ANC helps put Mashaba in the mayorâs office, the DA could spend the run-up to 2029 fighting the ANC across South Africaâs economic heartland while governing alongside it nationally. Both parties may have enough reason to stay in the cabinet. Agreeing on what to do there could get harder with every fight outside it.
Room for Disagreement
Hill-Lewis said this week the DA was not yet considering pulling out of the GNU. But its ministers could find themselves defending a national government while their councillors fight ANC-backed administrations across Gauteng. That contradiction could make it harder for DA ministers to compromise with the ANC on budgets and economic reforms.

7186af778cec.text:
The News
South Africa is âconsidering its optionsâ over a decade-old concession to US chicken producers after Washington decided to take away the benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act preferential trade program, a government spokesman told Semafor.
Kamill Allieâs comments come as relations between the two countries deteriorate following the US decision this month to strip the country of duty-free access to its markets, and opens an early test of the extent to which Pretoria is prepared to unwind compromises made with Washington.
A decade ago, the country agreed to allow a quota of American poultry to enter Africaâs biggest economy without anti-dumping duties as part of a deal to retain its benefits under AGOA. This act, which gave eligible sub-Saharan African countries duty-free access to the US market, has been the cornerstone of US-Africa trade since 2000. But South African poultry producers said the concession had run its course, with Izaak Breitenbach, head of industry lobby group South African Poultry Association telling Semafor that it should disappear now that the country is no longer benefiting from AGOA.
A South African customs notice published on Nov. 6, days after Washington announced the countryâs AGOA exclusion, did link the annual US chicken quota to the preferential trade agreement.But the concessionâs suspension requires written confirmation from Trade Minister Parks Tau.
âNothing in returnâ
Breitenbach said the industry has repeatedly asked Tau to withdraw the rebate, including after Washington imposed additional tariffs on South African exports. Pretoria, nevertheless, preserved the concession. âWe got nothing in return,â Breitenbach said, while acknowledging that the industry was not party to the government negotiations with Washington.
The chicken deal dates back to South Africaâs last big fight to remain in AGOA, agreeing in 2015 to allow 65,000 tonnes of US poultry to escape anti-dumping duties each year in a politically contentious compromise that helped preserve the countryâs place in the program. The quota has since risen to about 74,000 tonnes.
Its fate lands amid a broader deterioration in relations between South Africa and the US, which has imposed visa restrictions on South African officials over Pretoriaâs race and land policies, falsely accused it of persecuting white South Africans, and ejected it from AGOA in a decision Ambassador L. Brent Bozell III called âpredictable and preventableâ.
Notable
- The leaders of the US and South Africa have not spoken in the 18 months since an Oval Office meeting that Cyril Ramaphosa now calls an âambush,â a silence that has coincided with the steepest decline in relations between the two countries since apartheid ended.

Separate energy and climate discussions on opposite sides of the world showcased the changing face of the debate, with concern over prices outpacing worry over global warming. As the COP31 climate summit in TÃ¼rkiye neared its close, negotiators haggled over a narrow draft deal that activists said was limited even by the standards of recent meetings; the representative for co-host Australia acknowledged that officials were âfinding the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow.â
In the US, meanwhile, the Senate passed a landmark bill aimed at accelerating building major energy projects. The plan, which now faces a tough test in the House of Representatives, garnered momentum from this monthâs midterms, in which cost-of-living concerns topped votersâ priorities.

London and Brussels are poised to sign a deal aimed at resetting relations still blighted by the UKâs vote to exit the EU a decade ago. The limited agreement would allow increased food and drinks trade, a re-linking of their carbon markets, and closer migration cooperation. But the details mask a potentially grander ambition: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he hopes Britain will rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, and the country is seeing a revived debate on the benefits and costs of membership.
Brussels would probably be welcoming, but equally is unwilling to make major concessions. âWe didnât want them to leave,â one European diplomat told Politico. âThey broke up with us. Now we are over them.â

US President Donald Trump is âopenâ to extending Ukraine a NATO-like security guarantee, his envoy said, adding momentum for Kyivâs push for deeper integration into the West as part of any peace deal with Russia. The remarks came after Franceâs president urged the alliance to âreopen the questionâ of Ukraineâs membership; Kyiv is also pushing forward with efforts to join the EU, though that is likely to be a protracted process.
Russiaâs president, for his part, signed a âdeclaration of peaceâ with his American and Chinese counterparts after trilateral talks yesterday â though his forces followed that up hours later by bombing bridges in Kyiv and a giant power substation elsewhere in Ukraine.

Myriad efforts to harden US relations with China were underway in Washington, underscoring the gulf between rhetoric and reality a day after the superpowersâ leaders held largely convivial talks.
Nikkei reported that American officials have denied visas to several Chinese humanoid robot makers ahead of a major Las Vegas trade show, the White House is mulling whether to require US companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI as part of efforts to discourage them from relying on it, according to Reuters, and lawmakers are nearing a deal to ban Chinese cars entirely, Bloomberg said. Further restrictions could also be afoot: Washington should pull contracts with any defense firms with investments in Chinaâs aerospace sector, one Congressional committee argued.

Scrutiny of the broader US semiconductor sector intensified amid growing hawkishness in Washington sparked by the controversy surrounding chip giant Nvidiaâs sales to China. Since 2022, the US has fitfully sought to curtail Chinese access to cutting-edge chip technology, but that effort has been catalyzed in recent days by an espionage scandal that led to the ousting of Nvidiaâs CEO.
California officials are now investigating whether the company misled investors about its links to Beijing, while federal lawmakers released files showing the US approved sales of nearly 880,000 chips to China â including to firms seen as fronts for the Chinese military; Caixin reported Chinaâs tech giants were âreelingâ from the prospect of sudden, new semiconductor restrictions.

Asian stocks tumbled and US markets looked set to follow on worsening tech-sector sentiment, although experts said the selloff was likely overdone.
