- Published
Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.
This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.
The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.
In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.
The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.
The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.
Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.
It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.
Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.
The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, "forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside", police said.
The owner's wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made.
On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year.
General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her.
The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September.
The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba's was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region.
He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo's death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg.
Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area.
In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" to find those behind the killings.
Last year, he declared that violence against women was a "national disaster".

9b0b3e496490.text: America's religious "nones" have gained a visible foothold in Congress: Five lawmakers will claim no religious affiliation in January, up from a single member just two years ago. Why it matters: Washington remains far more religious than the nation it represents. But the last two election cycles have put a series of cracks in that political glass ceiling. By the numbers: Religiously unaffiliated voters made up 27% of the 2026 midterm electorate, up from 23% in 2024, according to preliminary Fox News voter polling . Just three of 532 lawmakers surveyed at the start of the 119th Congress claimed no religious affiliation, according to Pew Research Center . Pew counted one additional humanist. All three lawmakers who claimed no affiliation — Reps. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.), Abraham Hamadeh (R-Ariz.) and Emily Randall (D-Wash.) — won reelection in November. State of play: They'll be joined in January by Democratic Reps.-elect Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Fred Wellman of Missouri — who publicly acknowledged their nonreligious identities before winning their Nov. 3 elections. Rabb, a five-term state lawmaker representing a majority-Black Philadelphia district, won the seat of retiring Democratic Rep. Dwight Evans. Wellman, a retired Army officer, ousted seven-term Republican Rep. Ann Wagner in suburban St. Louis, flipping a longtime GOP stronghold. Their wins mark a breakthrough for congressional candidates who openly embraced their nonreligious identities before Election Day, according to Secular Coalition for America. Zoom in: Rabb thanked atheists for supporting his campaign after winning his May Democratic primary. Wellman defeated Wagner roughly 51% to 46%, according to Ballotpedia . His pitch? Affordability, corruption and accountability — not his lack of faith. Zoom out: The nonreligious political bench stretches well beyond Capitol Hill. More than 100 openly nonreligious lawmakers are expected to serve in at least 38 state legislatures, up from 81 in 33 states, according to the Center for Freethought Equality . Humanists, atheists or agnostics will serve in the legislatures of Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Ohio and West Virginia for the first time, the Center for Freethought Equality reports. In Texas, Democrat Jon Rosenthal won a statewide race for the Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry. He identifies as agnostic and "multireligious." Yes, but: Don't mistake "none" for a unified political creed. An October Pew survey found 81% of atheist registered voters and 75% of agnostics supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 48% of those claiming "nothing in particular." Nor did Rabb and Wellman break entirely new ground. Former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema, who left Congress as an independent after being first elected as a Democrat, identified with no religion when first elected to the House in 2012. Nothing in the results proves voters chose either candidate because of his religious identity. "It's not an anti-religious constituency by any stretch," Robert P. Jones, president and founder of the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI), tells Axios. Jones said many religiously unaffiliated Americans grew up in churches, and some walked away over teachings about gay and lesbian people. Their political opposition, he said, focuses more on white Christian nationalism than on religion itself. Between the lines: The Constitution prohibits religious tests for office, but public expressions of faith have long carried political currency in Washington. The Congressional Freethought Caucus , founded in 2018, now counts 37 members — believers and nonbelievers — promoting church-state separation and science-based policies. Rabb and Wellman's victories suggest candidates can acknowledge a lack of faith without making it their campaign's centerpiece.

2a3e04866a9f.text:
The News
The Trump administrationâs push to secure access to DR Congoâs critical minerals is fast becoming entangled in a political fight over President FÃ©lix Tshisekediâs controversial efforts to change the constitution and potentially extend his rule beyond 2028 when his second term is due to end.
Tshisekedi says implementing the US minerals pact, which gives American investors preferential access, requires constitutional changes, linking the deal to judicial reforms while raising the prospect of a third term. His opponents fear that this is a pitch to claim he is the only guarantor of the agreement and they have also pledged to honor it. Analysts said Washington will be wary of being seen to endorse the presidentâs political ambitions.
The US is seeking access to DR Congoâs vast copper and cobalt reserves, essential for electric vehicle batteries and artificial intelligence, as it tries to challenge Chinaâs dominance of global critical mineral supply chains. The two minerals alone generated $31.5 billion in Congolese export earnings in 2024, according to central bank data.
Barred from running again in 2028, Tshisekedi last week signed a law allowing a new constitution to be adopted by referendum. If approved it would reset the count, argued Christian Moleka, a Kinshasa-based political analyst: âWe will no longer be talking about a third term, but about a first term under a new constitution.â
Days after the law was signed, Frank Garcia, the State Departmentâs top Africa official, told a congressional hearing that the administration has âhad diplomatic discussionsâ with Tshisekedi on constitutional changes, but despite being asked Garcia did not specifically mention the prospect of a third term. However, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle were more forthright on the risks.
Sen. Jim Risch, the outgoing Republican chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told Semafor it would be âill advised for President Tshisekedi to take actions that would deepen the political and security crisis in his country.â Rep. Gregory Meeks, the Democrat expected to chair the House foreign affairs committee from January, said eliminating term limits would risk âthreatening opportunities to partner with the United States.â
Joseph Kabila, Tshisekediâs predecessor, who now leads Rwanda-backed rebels in the east, said in October that the US minerals deal was guaranteed by âthe continuity of the state, not by the survival of the regime in power.â Weeks later in Rome, major opposition leaders including MoÃ¯se Katumbi and Martin Fayulu pledged that âlegitimately elected leadersâ would preserve the agreementâs âstrategic commitments.â
Christian-GÃ©raud Neema, a non-resident scholar at the Carnegie Endowmentâs Africa Program, said the pledges target an unspoken bargain: âThere seems to be a quid pro quo coming from Washington that Tshisekedi is our man and as long as he does things regarding our interests, we would not do anything against him.â
A quieter Washington
The State Department pointed Semafor to the agreementâs text. âWe do not engage in hypotheticals,â a spokesperson said, calling peace and security fundamental to the partnership. Rep. Johnny Olszewski, the Democrat who questioned Garcia in the hearing, told Semafor the administration âmust do more to make clear to President Tshisekedi that his actions are not acceptable and will have consequences.â
Garcia was more critical about the national dialogue Tshisekedi announced in August, The three-month process, meant to cover peace, national unity, and rebuilding the state, has been rejected by the main opposition coalition, and armed groups are excluded. âWe havenât seen it tasked out, we havenât seen it organized, we havenât seen an agenda, and these are not indicators that thereâs truth behind that,â he said.
âThereâs no condemnation, but no support either, and that silence can be read as a kind of tacit green light,â analyst Moleka said, referencing the third term. For Kinshasa, he added, Washingtonâs silence âcan be used as a narrative at home to say: Washington is not opposed to this project.â
Joshua Walker, an associate fellow at the Chatham House think tankâs Africa program, said the opposition saw the referendum law as âa kind of provocation,â and he fears what comes next. âMy concern is that thereâs going to be a political escalation and that thereâs going to be a military escalation in the east,â he said. âItâs almost becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy.â
Room for Disagreement
Some analysts argue Congolese politicians on all sides are overestimating Washingtonâs staying power. âPersonally I donât think itâs a good strategy,â Neema said of the Congolese oppositionâs pitch, because he doubts the US has a lasting stake in the country. âDRC importance to the US has always been wildly exaggerated,â he said, adding that if Trump leaves power, âI donât foresee the US having that level of apparent invested interest in the DRC.â
Notable
An âAmerica firstâ policy âis likely to favor close relations with Congolese political leaders over democracy and human rights,â an approach that could end up destabilizing the country, DR Congo experts wrote in Foreign Affairs.

8ab9901e455d.text: Democrats' sweeping electoral wins jump-started prospects for Medicaid expansion in red and purple states that rejected full expansions of the program under the Affordable Care Act. But budget realities could make newly elected Democratic governors pump the brakes. Why it matters: The changing of the guard sets up a test of whether states can expand coverage to more low-income residents right after Republicans in Congress weakened financial incentives for doing so. States that are facing serious budget shortfalls and daunting cost projections already are signaling they may defer until conditions are more favorable. State of play: Incoming Democratic governors in Wisconsin, Georgia, Texas and Kansas who campaigned on Medicaid expansion are now in a position to expand health coverage, and have more Democrats in their legislatures to help. Wisconsin Democrats have arguably the most leverage now that they've captured the state Senate and Assembly in addition to keeping control of the governor's office. Plus, the state already covers adults with incomes up to the federal poverty level. Expansion advocates in Georgia and Texas face a heavier lift, with Republicans still controlling at least one legislative chamber. And in Kansas, the GOP lost its supermajority in the House, a key obstacle in past Medicaid expansion fights, but still controls both chambers. Between the lines: Each state faces unique considerations. But one thing is true for all of the holdouts: The incentives for expanding aren't what they used to be. Though the federal government still would pay for 90% of the expansion cost, last year's GOP reconciliation law made major policy changes and cuts to the program. Expansion states now face stricter limits on provider taxes used to finance Medicaid, as well as on extra payments they make to hospitals and other providers to go beyond standard Medicaid rates. They've also lost an important bonus: A temporary 5% increase in federal assistance for newly expanding states expired at the beginning of this year. What's more, states will have to enforce new work requirements and document whether recipients perform 80 hours per month of work or other qualifying activities, or if they're subject to exemptions. While the Trump administration delayed the requirements for six months, they aren't likely to go away. What they're saying: "You're going to see a lot of [expansion] conversations start, but I don't think they'll be slam dunks. It's complicated and nuanced," said Matt Salo, a health care consultant and former executive director of the National Association of Medicaid Directors. Incoming Wisconsin Gov. David Crowley already is acknowledging that reality and exploring alternatives for expanding coverage in the near term, including establishing a state-run health insurance exchange with a public option, per the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel . In Texas, some lawmakers are considering a "trigger" bill that would start an expansion only if the incoming Democratic majority in Congress succeeds in rolling back some of the restrictions in the federal law, the Texas Tribune reported. Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms intends to pursue a full expansion next year, but also wants to streamline the state's existing limited expansion program, called Pathways to Coverage, as an interim strategy until full expansion is achievable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported. Democratic victories in the Texas and Georgia lieutenant governor's races still could boost Medicaid expansion prospects, since the lieutenant governor presides over the state Senate in both states and influences which legislation is considered, Max Reale, an analyst for Gordon Haskett Research Advisors, wrote in a note. He pegged Wisconsin as the likeliest to expand its program and Kansas the long shot, since control of the governor's office alone failed to advance Medicaid expansion in past legislative sessions. But cementing the four as expansion states would diminish the prospects of further Medicaid cuts under a GOP-controlled Congress and free lawmakers to pressure the six remaining holdout states to adopt expansion post-2028, Reale said. What we're watching: New Democratic governors in purple states that already expanded their Medicaid programs could also pursue changes, said Katie Keith, director of the Center for Health Policy and the Law at Georgetown's O'Neill Institute. She noted that Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand promised to end the state's contracts with three Medicaid managed care companies due to high rates of improper denials of care, and to have Iowa's Medicaid agency or a nonprofit take over processing and paying claims. Incoming officials in Iowa and Ohio could also go to court for relief from the most burdensome parts of the work rules, Keith wrote in Health Affairs .

The News
Chuck Schumer and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are steering clear of each other for now â yet their political futures are increasingly entangled.
As the Senate Democratic leader battles an underdog leadership challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., some of his members are hoping for signals about his reelection plans for 2028. If Schumer seeks another six-year term, progressives are agitating for a primary challenge.
And if Ocasio-Cortez passes on a White House run, many on the left want her in the Senate. Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., said the 37-year-old should challenge Schumer, 75, âif sheâs not running for president.â
Ocasio-Cortez is keeping fellow Democrats guessing about her plans. While allies like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are backing Van Hollen, she also appears to be staying out of Schumerâs leadership race. Ocasio-Cortez told Semafor in a brief interview that his future as majority leader is âfor the other chamber to determine.â
Schumer is similarly mum on 2028, even when talking with Democratic senators. He views winning the majority leader job and a future reelection bid as separate choices, with the former having no bearing on the latter, according to a person familiar with his thinking.
His decision has an undeniable effect on her options, however. Ocasio-Cortez would likely clear the field in an open primary to succeed Schumer, the only septuagenarian among the top four Hill leaders. Schumer also has good reason, despite Van Hollenâs challenge, to take his time deciding after helping his party flip a historic nine Senate seats this year.
Ocasio-Cortez may choose a primary fight for higher office, according to several House Democrats. She made her name eight years ago by dethroning Joe Crowley, a former member of House leadership, and she would be a formidable statewide candidate regardless of Schumerâs decision.
âIâm sure sheâs thinking about it. Iâm not sure sheâs thinking about it in the context of what Chuck does,â said Rep. Joe Morelle, D-N.Y. âSheâs probably just trying to make a decision on what she thinks she can best contribute.â
Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., predicted that âthere will beâ a primary bid, adding that Ocasio-Cortez âhas so many options in front of her.â
Schumerâs plans
Schumer hasnât tipped his hand to even close allies in the caucus about running for another term. He is the heavy favorite to defeat Van Hollen but taking the battle seriously.
Still, sharing his views on 2028 could âobviouslyâ help him more handily defeat the Marylander, one Democratic senator told Semafor.
âI donât think Leader Schumer needs to make some public pronouncement about his future plans, but I think it is helpful for us as a caucus to be thinking about what kind of leadership team and what kind of leader we want in this moment for the next two years â and going forward,â this senator said. âBecause they may not be the same.â
The question of Schumerâs future is complex: He is singularly focused on leading Democrats through the last two years of President Donald Trumpâs term, but itâs also rare for Senate leaders to run again after facing dissent within their own ranks.
Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi took her own version of that step in 2022 by announcing she would leave leadership so incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries could rise, though she served another two-year term. Schumer won the Democratic leader job in one day after former Leader Harry Reid announced his retirement and backed Schumer in 2015.
Most Democrats speculate, without direct knowledge, that Schumer is leaning against another Senate term.
If Ocasio-Cortez ran for president or stayed in the House, Schumer could potentially survive a primary challenge from another opponent. The crowded bench of candidates who might jump into an open primary includes Rep. Pat Ryan, D-N.Y., whom Democrats have long considered a potential statewide candidate.
Ryan doesnât sound eager to challenge Schumer head-on yet. He told Semafor that Schumer âdeserves a tremendous amount of credit for those wins, for putting us in the position weâre in, and then itâs his decision to do whatever he wants to do next.â The 44-year-old added that he didnât want to get ahead of âwhat [Schumer] wants to do.â Whether Schumer should be majority leader was âup to the Senate side,â he said.
âHow to yield powerâ
Senators generally are not influenced by House membersâ opinions on their internal matters or politics. But indicating that heâs not running could affect Schumerâs ability to lead the caucus over the next two years, some Democrats said.
âThatâs the kind of calculation that he has to figure out for himself,â said Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., who supports Schumer. âAnd also, what does that mean for actually holding power, how to yield power â does it help you use influence? So, those are the kind of decisions that he has to make.â
El-Sayed, who defeated a Schumer-backed primary foe in Michigan, did not seem interested in fueling a primary challenge to the leader. In an interview, El-Sayed said he has ânothing against Senator Schumer. Itâs not about him.â
âThe most important priority for us right now is that we have to have a plan to legislate in ways that the American public can understand, identifying their problems, identifying legislation thatâs going to solve their problems, and then executing on that,â El-Sayed added.
Room for Disagreement
If Schumer did indicate to his caucus that he wonât seek reelection, heâd be sharing more than most Democratic senators do. None of the ambitious Democrats he leads have said explicitly yet that they are running for president, for all their visits to early states and ambitious agendas.

Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March.
The changes are estimated to add Â£10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.
In January, the government introduced a Â£15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.
But the autumn budget cut Â£1bn from the programme to pay for defence.
Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets.
How do heat pumps work?
Heat pumps run on electricity instead of gas and are more efficient than traditional boilers. They warm buildings by absorbing and amplifying heat from the air, ground or water.
Air source heat pumps - the most common type - suck in outdoor air and pass it over tubes containing refrigerant fluids. The heat from the outdoor air causes the refrigerants to evaporate into a gas. Compressing the gas increases the temperature, and this heat is passed around the home.
The system consists of a box measuring about 1m x 1m x 0.4m (3ft x 3ft x 1.3ft) which stands outside the property, as well as a heat pump unit and hot water cylinder inside the property.
The indoor unit is about the size of a gas boiler, while the size of the cylinder depends on the property.
Ground source heat pumps are more efficient than air source models.
However, they are typically more expensive and less commonly used, as they require either a deep bore hole or a large horizontal system dug into the ground.
How much do heat pumps cost and what funding is available?
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme provides a grant of Â£7,500 towards the cost of an air source or ground source heat pump for homeowners in England and Wales.
Households typically spend an additional Â£5,000 on top of the grant, which the UK's spending watchdog warned is too high for many.
The grant can be used for existing homes and non-domestic buildings. The property must have an eligible Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) - a measure of how your property is performing - issued in the last 10 years.
Properties no longer need to have existing loft or cavity wall insulation to qualify for the grant, which can save around Â£2,500 in upfront costs.
For low-income households and those in social housing, the government is providing an extra Â£5bn for the Warm Homes Local Grant, external and the Social Housing Fund, external.
Scotland, external and Northern Ireland, external have separate schemes to help make homes more efficient.
UK households can also apply for low and no interest loans of between Â£7,500 and Â£35,000 to install green technologies under the Warm Homes Loan Scheme, external.
Have heat pump subsidies been cut?
The government has promised to keep funding for the Boiler Upgrade Scheme at Â£400m in 2027-28 before increasing it in line with inflation.
However, this represents a significant cut compared to what was previously announced.
Some of the money the energy and environment departments have to spend on loans and investments is also being diverted towards the Â£4.7bn "Your First Home" scheme, which aims to help people purchase a property.
This could mean further cuts to the Warm Homes Scheme, but the government has said it "remains committed to heat-pump deployment".
Heat pump installations currently benefit from a 0% VAT rate, but this is set to rise to 5% in April 2027.
Can heat pumps cut bills?
While the upfront costs remain substantial, heat pumps could become cheaper to run than gas boilers, according to the Climate Change Committee (CCC), external, which advises the UK government on cutting emissions.
Savings depend on energy prices and how efficiently the heat pump works.
Electric heat pumps use around three to four times less energy than gas boilers, but electricity typically costs much more than gas.
At the moment the cost of electricity is mostly driven by gas prices in the UK and around the world, but the government expects this to change as renewable energy expands.
A modest reduction in prices is also expected from the scrapping of VAT on electricity bills.
Households who install solar panels can potentially save more by generating their own energy rather than relying on the grid.
The innovation charity Nesta estimates that the average home with a heat pump and solar panels could cut its annual energy bill by nearly Â£1,000.
Are heat pumps noisy?
Previously, homeowners needed planning permission to install a heat pump within 1m (3ft) of a neighbour's property because of concerns about noise.
The rule was dropped to encourage uptake.
Newer devices are also quieter and must be below 42db, which is similar to the level of noise produced by a fridge.
Rules specifying the size and number of heat pumps which households can install have also been relaxed.
How many heat pumps have been installed in the UK?
More gas boilers continue to be installed in the UK than heat pumps, which are found in fewer than 2% of homes.
Installation rates are also lower than in other major European countries, like France, Germany and Italy.
Sales have increased significantly in recent years though there are concerns progress is slowing.
Double the number of heat pumps were installed in the first half of 2026, external compared to the same period of 2021.
However, this is 22% fewer than were installed in the first half of 2025.
The CCC says sales need to rise to nearly 450,000 a year by 2030 and 1.5 million by 2035 to help meet climate targets.
It says around half of UK homes need to have heat pumps by 2040.
Significantly more trained heat pump installers are needed to achieve this.

a4600d27a831.text: Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego wants more tech investment in her city — but on her terms, as data centers strain resources and frustrate residents. Why it matters: Phoenix has become a bellwether for the AI industry's growing demands on electricity and water in an increasingly hot, resource-constrained world. As the mayor, Gallego is navigating an outsized dilemma facing communities nationwide: How to embrace the AI boom while protecting residents and resources in an increasingly hot world. "I do want us to lead in technology, and I want us to be a tech-forward community," Gallego said at a recent event co-hosted by the University of Chicago's Institute of Politics and Energy Policy Institute, and moderated by Axios. But she added: "I want companies who care about our community and will give back to it, and not just a race to see who can get the deepest incentives and the cheapest" power. "We're open for business, but we're not for sale," she said. Zoom out: Arizona's Democratic sweep could give Gallego more allies in her efforts to strike the balance she wants. Democrats flipped both legislative chambers and Gov. Katie Hobbs won reelection, giving the state full Democratic control for the first time since 1966. Affordability dominated the election, with data center subsidies and community impacts part of that debate, Gallego said. Catch up fast: Phoenix ranks fourth among major U.S. data center markets by operational capacity. Now the debate is expanding from how much development the region can accommodate to what communities should demand in return. State of play: Gallego, the longest-serving current mayor of America's 10 largest cities, has spent recent years trying to balance that. She helped push to eliminate Arizona's generous data center sales tax exemptions. The state enacted a three-year pause on new applications this summer. She opposes a blanket construction moratorium, favoring more local control over where facilities are built, particularly near homes. Phoenix adopted tougher zoning rules last year requiring special permits for new data centers. Gallego says communities should have more bargaining power over data centers, including where they're built and what residents get in return. That could mean more permanent jobs, transparency about electricity and water use, and benefits for neighbors affected by development. By the numbers: Data centers have requested so much electricity in the Phoenix region that, if all the projects materialized, they could account for roughly two-thirds of the area's power demand, Gallego said. Many may never be built, but Gallego warned: "That's not a balanced economy, and that's not economically sustainable." Friction point: Phoenix's efforts to rein in data centers have sparked legal challenges, with developers originally seeking roughly $750 million in compensation over zoning restrictions adopted last year. The city has granted several exemptions while fighting other claims in court. "We have been open and good partners to the industry, and it's deeply disappointing that they don't want to work with us," Gallego told Axios. The other side: Developers argue the restrictions infringe on their property rights and diminish land values, entitling them to compensation under Arizona law, though industry allies have also acknowledged tensions . Reality check: It's unclear whether Gallego can have it both ways: attracting more tech investment while limiting its costs to residents, especially as developers challenge the city's regulatory authority. Gallego is also navigating the tradeoffs between electricity, water and heat in the desert. Newer cooling technologies can reduce water consumption at data centers but often require more electricity, shifting some of the water footprint to power plants. "We're seeing many of these data centers get power from natural gas plants in an area of our state that is very constrained around water," Gallego said. The intrigue: Data centers are adding another source of heat to a region already struggling with dangerously high temperatures. An Arizona State University study published in May found that data centers can raise nearby temperatures by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit. Gallego, who established the nation's first publicly funded municipal heat-response office in 2021, said she's "jealous of Midwestern mayors" who can reuse data centers' waste heat to warm buildings. What we're watching: Gallego worries Arizona might be betting too heavily on an industry whose long-term trajectory remains uncertain. She compared the risk of abandoned data centers to Phoenix's vacant Kmart stores, many of which have been difficult to redevelop. "What will I do in a community if we have these giant windowless boxes" that are no longer operating, she asked. "How will we redevelop or make them not become blight?"

South Korea's education ministry says 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.
Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities said on Friday.
Half a million students sat for the college entry exam, also known as Suneung, which took place this week under the shadow of several recent high-profile cheating scandals.
Prior to the Suneung, authorities announced anti-cheating measures such as emergency alerts sent to every single mobile phone in the country to detect unauthorised devices in exam halls.
On Friday, Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung called for an overhaul of the exam system to tackle AI-assisted cheating.
In South Korea, public examinations "significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources", Lee said, adding that using AI to cheat in such tests "rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust".
Concerns over academic dishonesty had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
Last month, two candidates were caught cheating with AI glasses during university entrance exams.
The education ministry said earlier this month that four students across middle and high schools were caught using AI glasses to cheat this year.
These fears came to a boil over the weekend, when the top scorer of South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam admitted to cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," said the candidate, 34-year-old Han Won-seok, in a video published on Sunday.
His confession, days ahead of the Suneung, prompted authorities to introduce last-minute measures to prevent cheating during the national exam.
The measures included nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea tapped on its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times that he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told news outlet Yonhap that he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.
Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.
Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.
The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.
Many South Koreans see the Suneung as a culmination of years of formal education - and a turning point that determines their university placements, careers, and social statuses.

Big Win Sets Up Democrats To Intensify Probe of Trump’s Obamacare Purge
A week before the midterm elections, a dozen Democratic senators sent harshly critical letters to 10 health insurance company CEOs.
Why, the letters asked, had those insurers cooperated with what they called a “potentially unlawful” Trump administration effort that resulted in the rapid cancellation of coverage for 760,000 Affordable Care Act enrollees in late August?
Then came the Democrats’ stunning electoral sweep that, come January, will put them in control of both the House and Senate. The power shift lends new weight to the insurance investigation, led by Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, who is expected to chair the powerful Finance Committee starting next year, and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who is expected to chair the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.
“Some insurers might view this inquiry as more high-stakes than before given that Democrats will have the power to subpoena documents, hold hearings, and otherwise investigate perceived abuses or missteps,” said Katie Keith, a director of Georgetown University’s Center for Health Policy and the Law.
“Senator Wyden will continue investigating the secret arrangement between corporate interests and the Trump administration that has deprived Americans of their health care,” Wyden spokesperson Taylor Harvey said in an email. “Senate Democrats will use every tool at their disposal to get answers.”
New Oversight Muscle
For months, the administration has promoted the idea that fraud is rampant in government health programs — from the ACA to Medicaid and hospice — and that the Republican Party is the one to thwart it. The White House and some GOP candidates used this talking point to try to counter Democrats’ campaign messages about affordability.
The Trump administration’s anti-fraud efforts are ongoing. The August cancellations are part of a larger initiative by the administration to remove from Obamacare plans people who have other coverage and more strictly scrutinize the information people provide to qualify for premium subsidies. Courts blocked some of the administration’s new rules, including heightened income verification for certain low-income enrollees and a moratorium that would have kept up to 19,000 new agents from helping people sign up during the current annual open enrollment period. Ongoing, however, is scrutiny of an additional 419,000 ACA enrollments in a second phase of the cancellation operation.
Also, new Trump administration requirements compel some people signing up during open enrollment to undergo additional online identity proofing. Insurers were sent guidance in October asking them to look for suspicious patterns among agents and brokers and take action, including cutting commissions, if they found problems. It’s unclear if any insurers have taken those voluntary steps.
The letters from the Democratic senators to insurers provide a look at what the new majority could pursue in its ongoing inquiry into the administration’s ACA actions.
Were proper procedures followed for removing people? How many legitimate enrollees were kicked off the rolls? Did the criteria used to target those enrollments — lack of Social Security number or other key data, not having used medical coverage, a full subsidy without a response to outreach efforts — serve as reliable proxies for determining fraud?
“The tone of these letters underscores just how much of a black box this process was,” said Keith at Georgetown.
Administration officials, however, have defended the cancellation effort.
At an Oct. 14 press conference, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz was asked about the initial round of cancellations in late August.
“That is fraud, we believe,” Oz said. “That is insurance brokers creating, manufacturing accounts without putting Social Security numbers in and has resulted, we have already determined, in 760,000 phantom accounts that we can’t even get in touch with. We call, we write, we send carrier pigeons — like, no one answers.”
After some of their executives were grilled early in the year over rising healthcare costs, the insurers were given until Nov. 6 to respond to 28 questions from the senators about the cancellation effort, which began in June when they were asked to try to reach more than a million enrollees the administration targeted as suspicious. They handed back to CMS the names of policyholders who did not respond to emails, phone calls, or letters within 30 days.
The senators sent letters to Elevance Health, Cigna, Oscar Health, AmeriHealth Caritas, Centene, Florida Blue, Health Care Service Corporation, Imperial Insurance Companies, Molina Healthcare, and UnitedHealthcare.
By Nov. 10, Harvey in Wyden’s office reported “varying levels of responsiveness” from the insurers.
What Happens Next?
Few dispute that there are problems with improper ACA enrollment. This category includes, the administration says, sign-ups with missing or incorrect data; people who fudge their income estimates to get subsidies; “phantom” enrollees, meaning people who either don’t exist or don’t know they have coverage; and those signed up by rogue call centers or agents to garner commissions.
But there are questions about the relative scale of those problems and the steps by regulators to thwart them.
“The question is whether they overreached and set up a situation that led to many people who are eligible losing their coverage,” said Chip Kahn, a visiting fellow at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News, and the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank. “They will be pushed hard by the new Congress to come up with the goods in terms of making it crystal clear what’s been done, who has been dropped.” Kahn is also the former president and CEO of the Federation of American Hospitals, a trade association of for-profit hospitals.

Data centers and increased energy costs brought attention to typically low-profile utility commission races in states across the country during this year’s midterms.
Nine states, all historically Republican, held elections for their utility regulators this year. Democrats won five of the 15 contested seats, flipping four Republican-held seats and retaining one, while Republicans won 10 seats, including one flipped from a Democrat in Louisiana.
Every state has a commission responsible for regulating its utilities, with authority over decisions that affect how electricity is generated, delivered and priced. Most are called Public Service Commissions (PSCs) or Public Utility Commissions (PUCs), and their structures vary. Some have three members, others five or seven. In most states commissioners are appointed officials, while in 10 states they are elected in partisan races.
In this election cycle, the biggest shifts occurred in Georgia and Arizona, where Democrats made historic gains. In Georgia, they won control of the PSC for the first time in 30 years, while in Arizona, they ended Republicans’ 5-0 hold on their commission. Both states have seen a surge in data center development, bringing new scrutiny to electricity costs and how to meet growing energy demand.
In Georgia, Democrats Shelia Edwards won her first PSC election while Peter Hubbard was reelected to his first full term, an early endorsement of the job he did his rookie year as commissioner. Joined by Commissioner Alicia Johnson, who won a seat last year, Democrats now hold a 3-2 majority on a commission that was entirely Republican just two years ago.
In Arizona, Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill won the first Democratic seats on the commission since 2020.
Pratte also became the first Indigenous woman elected to statewide office in Arizona, bringing a unique perspective and set of goals to the utility regulator.
“We’re the sunniest state in the union; we could be generating a lot of our own solar rather than relying on fossil fuels,” Pratte said. “We need to be collaborative, and reach across the aisle to help Arizonans.”
Pratte noted that in addition to fossil fuel reliance, energy costs and transparency among utilities were key issues in the state. She also hopes to make meetings more accessible for the Navajo Nation.
Of the nine states to hold elections this year, Georgia and Arizona have experienced the most data center development. All four of the elected Democrats promised increased scrutiny for data centers, ensuring they pay their fair share of energy costs and preventing unchecked expansion.
“I think data centers definitely played a role in Democrats’ success in Arizona and Georgia,” said Jared Heern, a political scientist at Connecticut College who studies utility commission politics across the country.
In Arizona, concerns about data centers’ water use likely played a particularly large role, according to Heern. Hill, a scientist, campaigned on protecting natural resources, including water, an increasingly prominent issue amid concerns over the Colorado River’s declining supply.
“Incumbents who got booted out in those states can be directly tied to data center development,” Heern said. Utility commissioners have the ability to shape how data centers are powered and who pays for the infrastructure needed to serve them.
Hill and Pratte defeated incumbent Kevin Thompson in the statewide, at-large election for two commission seats.Thompson owns a consulting firm and acknowledged having a data center client.
Outside spending across the two states topped $7 million. In Arizona, Democrats received the most support, largely from a PAC called Arizonans for Affordable Energy. In Georgia, Republicans received the most outside support, much of it from a group called Powering Georgia’s Future, which supports “pro-growth” policies and a stronger industrial base. Spending in Georgia reached a record high for its PSC election.
Activists and energy watchdogs also played a big role in the elections, helping raise awareness of the little-known regulatory bodies. Grassroots groups like Georgians for Affordable Energy ran social media campaigns and distributed flyers, while national groups like the Sierra Club endorsed the Democratic candidates in Georgia and Arizona and educated members on the stakes of utility commission elections.
“The increased awareness of these bodies over the past few years has translated into frustration and anger as the public sees they are not doing their job,” said David Rogers, deputy director of the Beyond Coal Campaign at the Sierra Club. ”I think that’s what really showed up at the polls.”
While Democrats’ biggest victories came in Georgia and Arizona, they also picked up a seat in Nebraska. Former state Sen. Wendy DeBoer won Nebraska’s 2nd District, which includes Omaha, by more than 30 points, breaking Republicans’ single-party hold on the state’s PSC. DeBoer campaigned on modernizing the state’s infrastructure.
But despite Democratic gains in those red states, Republicans held onto control of eight of the nine commissions that held elections. They also flipped a historically Democratic seat in Louisiana.

âCook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing â and indeed, has a duty to âthe Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine [its] âindependence,â Abbe Lowell wrote to the Trump administration earlier this week, citing the involvement of Trump adviser Kevin Hassett and the demand for Cook to produce documents before the White House reveals its evidence.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment on whether officials, who said last month they may âdraw adverse inferencesâ against Cook if she did not attend, would hold the hearing without her.
If they do, it will undoubtedly feature prominently in congressional Democratsâ oversight next year of Trumpâs attempts to bend the central bank to his will, given many have repeatedly condemned his campaign against Cook.
âTrump is convening an illegitimate show trial in his dangerous quest to illegally take over our nationâs central bank,â said the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, panning Trump for âplaying judge in a kangaroo court of his own making.â

Trump administration officials hope that a new press secretary will be named by the âend of year,â as one adviser told Semafor.
President Donald Trump has been without a press secretary since Karoline Leavitt departed months ago, barring a five-day stint from Katie Zacharia. He has a few names in mind for the role, as Semafor previously reported, with conservative commentator Ben Ferguson among those under consideration. 4ea500e050f1.text:
The Trump administration says the string of recent tech outages across the country can be attributed to companies rushing to patch their networks as AI exposes vulnerabilities in old software.
Cybersecurity experts say the government is largely telling the truth about the crashesâ causes, but the situation reveals a bigger problem: Much more digital instability is coming, and it will be worse.
At the same time, President Donald Trumpâs hands-off approach to AI signals to the private sector and Congress that the government may not be there to help as outages multiply, or when AI-enabled attacks inevitably result in even more mayhem.
A tech lobbyist and a Hill source told Semafor that a letter this week from Sens. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Mike Rounds, R-S.D., to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton urging the AI task force he leads to âlaunch a national effort to confront a new generation of AI-enabled cyber threatsâ is a bipartisan sign of things to come from Capitol Hill come January.
Bolstering AI cybersecurity will emerge as a key legislative goal along with broader AI bills on catastrophic risk, the sources said.
âItâs one thing that Hugging Face got attacked,â the lobbyist said. âWait until itâs a mid-sized community bank. Whatâs the event that will get Congress and the White House to do something?â
Meanwhile, the agency charged with protecting US infrastructure from cyber threats, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, may go even longer without a permanent director.
Sens. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said they would place holds on Trumpâs nominee, Palantir Chief Information Security Officer Michael LoSapio, after he denied Thursday during his confirmation hearing that there was an attack on the US Capitol on Jan 6, 2021, and refused to say who won the 2020 presidential election.

2f1c3a5a5bf7.text:
The News
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out and is being replaced by Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies, multiple officials told Semafor Thursday.
The shakeup follows a series of disruptive tech outages that have raised fears about US cybersecurity â and has kicked off a heated dispute about whether Cairncross was fired or left voluntarily.
One White House official and a person familiar with the White House told Semafor that Cairncross was fired on Thursday; the official said that finding a new cyber director was one of the first things Stephen Miller did in his new role as White House chief of staff, and both said Trump had supported Cairncrossâ removal.
But another senior White House official and a person familiar with the matter strongly disputed the idea that Cairncross had been fired, telling Semafor that he resigned â and not because he was asked to.
A second source familiar with the matter, who said Cairncross had been fired, said the past week exposed the need for someone âmore competent, with the expertise needed to execute this position.â
Axios first reported the news of Cairncrossâ departure and Daviesâ new job.
Ashleyâs view
Someone was bound to take the fall for a string of tech outages that have left the country terrified about what services might get disrupted next â even if the most basic (and likely true) explanation is that organizations are rushing to patch software bugs discovered by AI programs and are crashing their systems in the process.
Cairncross told me as much this week after I interviewed him on stage at Semaforâs Silicon Valley & The World, in what would end up being his last public interview as a White House official. Director of National Intelligence Clayton echoed his words two days later, so I donât think being off-message here was his issue.
The alarming and disruptive outages over the last week, at least one of which appears to be ongoing, may have provided Cairncrossâ detractors the perfect opportunity to bump him. But long before Miller took over for Susie Wiles, some in Washington said theyâd seen Cairncross, whose previous experience includes being a lawyer for the Republican National Committee, as unqualified to be a cyber official. Rumors of his potential ouster go back as far as this spring, though he helped shape the administrationâs June executive order on AI and cybersecurity, including its framework for voluntary pre-release testing of frontier models.
He survived the âMythos momentâ â when Anthropicâs latest model made Washington freak out about AIâs cyber capabilities â but he couldnât make it through FAA routers failing, Microsoft Outlook crashing, JP Morgan pausing services, and the NSAâs internal comms network going down. Davies does not have an easy job ahead; she will have to prove the public can trust her to help the country get through the precarious digital moment weâre in.
I asked Cairncross this week if the administration would ever fully release that June executive order, much of which has not been public. âI expect that we will be making it much more clear how this is working in practice,â he said.
He also told the room of CEOs that if they have questions about preparing for this cyber moment, they should reach out: âIf you havenât heard from my office, we are more than willing to engage,â he said. âWeâre happy to be hyper-responsive.â

The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a string of tech outages which hit the National Security Agency (NSA), the US air traffic control system and some banks.
Sean Cairncross had been national cyber director since August 2025.
CBS, the BBC's US news partner, reported he had been fired, external after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross was fired, in a move supported by President Donald Trump.
The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.
Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.
In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.
He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.
The White House has not publicly confirmed the departure or given a reason to why Cairncross left his role.

8b7d36e01128.text:
Navy will likely fly CCAs sooner than F/A-XX, White House nom says
William Toti, who’s been doing the job since May, is up for permanent appointment as Navy undersecretary.
The Navy wants to fly its own collaborative combat aircraft as soon as it can, with existing aircraft—instead of waiting for its next-generation fighter to be delivered, the White House pick for Navy undersecretary told lawmakers Thursday.
“I think we can probably start integrating systems before F/A-XX delivers. Having said that, F/A-XX is a critical capability. We're going to have these aircraft carriers around for the next 50 years, and the notion that the F-35 is the last last airplane that's going to be launched from them is just a non-starter,” William Toti, who has been performing the duties of Navy undersecretary, said during his confirmation hearing before the Senate Armed Services Committee.
In September, the Navy picked Boeing to build the F/A-XX, which is expected to fly in the 2030s. But the Trump administration offered only the barest support for the program in its 2027 budget request.
The ability to control collaborative combat aircraft—often dubbed “robot wingmen”—will likely be built into the F/A-XX “from ground up,” Toti said. “But I think it's a capability we'll be able to use with F-35, specifically, as well.”
In September, the Navy issued a prototype-focused request for information on CCAs, detailing what it was looking for, including integration with aircraft carriers.
A month later, the Air Force, which has been developing CCAs for several years, tested two of them in air combat maneuvers.
“CCA aircraft are an element of the future air fleet, the future combat capability of our aircraft carriers,” Toti said. “The Air Force has been leading this issue. We are following closely behind, but the integration of CCA aircraft in the [carrier] air wing is critically important as we go forward. We need low-cost attritable assets in our air wing, and CCA will provide that.”
Toti is a retired Navy captain and former defense company executive. He was previously the CEO of Sparton Corporation before taking a Pentagon senior advisor role in 2024. Toti began performing the duties of the Navy undersecretary in May.

Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.
The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.
The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.
Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.
The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.
"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add Â£5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.
He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Appearing on BBC Breakfast on Friday, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage described the agreement as a "very, very expensive and costly error" and said Burnham has no "democratic mandate to do any of this".
He added that the Labour party manifesto was clear that the UK would not go back towards the single market and asked: "Where is our democracy?".
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".
"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.
The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.
It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.
Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.
The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.
It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.
He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.
He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.
Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.
"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.
However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.
He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.
Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.
At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.
"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.
Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.
Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.
Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.
Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.
If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Ponds are to be restored and freshwater habitats created for amphibians and reptiles at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire.
The Froglife charity has been awarded nearly Â£890,000 of Lottery cash to carry out the work in Rother Valley, as well as at sites in North and West Yorkshire.
Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands were originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s.
Sheila Grundry, from Froglife, said staff were "delighted" to work in the area because "freshwater will make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife and it's a great way for local people to learn new skills".
The Â£889,761 investment in Froglife's Coalface to Wildspace project will also help local communities connect with nature, according to the charity.
The aim of the project across Yorkshire is to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats and establish new "neighbourhood wildlife corridors" like small ponds and bug hotels.
These "corridors" will act as stepping stones for local wildlife from insects to birds, providing food, shelter and water to improve biodiversity across former industrial sites and help wildlife move between one habitat and another.
Conservationist Andy Goff, project manager in Yorkshire, said the transformation of the sites would be for everyone.
"We want people to engage with the nature that is on their doorstep and wildlife in general," he explained.
"I'm really excited about getting people involved from all over Yorkshire."
The Coalface to Wildspace project is funded by The National Lottery Heritage Fund for the next four years, with Froglife having already run similar projects in the Midlands and Scotland.
Rother Valley MP Jake Richards said the project was important for the area.
"These former industrial sites are an important part of our area's history," he said.
"This project will help transform them into thriving habitats while creating opportunities for local people to get involved."

After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.
It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.
"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.
"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.
So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.
"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."
Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.
Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.
A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.
An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.
A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.
Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.
The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.
"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.
"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gentlyâ¦ As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."
With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.
Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.

The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; Â£57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,
Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.
The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure saw pre-orders and first day sales total more than 24.5 million units, raking in about $2.36bn (Â£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.
In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas.
GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.
The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.
At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.
The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.
GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.
The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.
Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.
Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.
That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.
Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.
The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.
If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.
Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.
GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.
The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play.
Its launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles.
The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China.
