Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines on Wall Street, where stocks tumbled to end the week, as worries about AI rattled the market. (BELL RINGING) Amna Nawaz: By the closing bell, all three major averages were deeply in the red, as investors weigh the health of the AI sector following Nvidia's leadership upheaval and Anthropic's record IPO. Looking at the numbers, the Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 900 points on the day. The Nasdaq dropped more than 5 percent, erasing all its gains for the year. The S&P 500 is now down more than 10 percent from its recent high, meaning it's now in what investors call correction territory. A second federal judge is blocking President Trump's Memorial Arch in Washington, D.C. The judge in Virginia called the project a rush job today, saying it lacks a legal basis. She put construction there on hold indefinitely, pending the outcome of legal challenges to the arch. Earlier this week, a separate judge extended a previous block for two more weeks. President Trump is trying to build a 250-foot Memorial Arch near Arlington National Cemetery, which has led to criticism from veterans groups and local environmentalists. In Iowa, a federal appeals court is blocking the U.S. Army from detonating several tons of bomb-making chemicals amid concerns over environmental and health risks. The controlled explosion has been scheduled for today, and was expected to send lead dust as far as 60 miles around the area. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had agreed to postpone the detonation until Monday. But he warned that a coming drop in temperatures could further destabilize the material. It's unclear whether the court will weigh in again before Monday. In Florida, heavy storms are moving north after drenching parts of the Atlantic coast. Torrential rains turned roads into waterways, with some areas already seeing their wettest November on record. The National Hurricane Center is warning of severe widespread flash flooding for parts of Eastern Florida and says the threat could carry into next week. In the meantime, across the country, in California, heavy flooding left some neighborhoods in Los Angeles underwater, as surging waters affected a large stretch of the California coast. In Poland, authorities say two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in Polish territory overnight. In Southeastern Poland, CCTV footage showed a large explosion and a bright flash. The crash site was around 20 miles from where European troops from 11 countries were taking part in rare military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar Ukraine mission. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incursions an intentional provocation and said Poland, which neighbors both Ukraine and Russia must be involved in future peace talks. Donald Tusk (through interpreter): It seems that we are dealing with an intentional provocation. It is no coincidence that these objects fell near the site where military exercises are taking place. I will always act with great prudence. No one wants the situation to escalate or worsen. Amna Nawaz: Meantime, Russia carried out news strikes on Ukraine overnight and into today as part of its response to Kyiv's recent attacks on a strategic bridge. Authorities in Western Ukraine said a Russian attack on a railway station killed at least two people. And officials in the Southeast say a Russian-guided bomb hit a residential area, injuring at least four people, including a child. The U.K. and the European Union agreed to a series of deals today, as the two sides seek closer ties a decade after Britain voted to leave the bloc, also known as Brexit. The agreement would relax restrictions on agricultural trade, cut carbon taxes on some exports, and allow 100,000 young people to live and work in each other's countries. Today's summit in Brussels did not resolve questions about university fees and the broader post-Brexit relationship. But European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the deal a turning point, while Britain's prime minister described this as a historic moment. Andy Burnham, British Prime Minister: This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe. Britain in 2026 is in a different place, but so is Europe. And people look at the world and they would think people of like mind need to work together. They need to get closer. Amna Nawaz: The U.K. formally exited the E.U. in 2020 after nearly half-a-century of membership. Polling suggests that most British voters are now in favor of closer ties with Europe amid a sluggish economy and growing global tensions. Well, a spacecraft is about to enter orbit around Mercury for only the second time in history. The BepiColombo mission is a joint European and Japanese effort. It launched eight years ago and traveled roughly six billion miles to reach the planet closest to the sun. The probe will split in two to map the planet's surface and interior. Researchers are hoping for clues into how mercury formed and how ice and other materials have survived on its surface, among other questions. NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft was the first to orbit Mercury, collecting data between 2011 and 2015. And Rockstar Games says "Grand Theft Auto VI" set a record with nearly $3.8 billion in global sales in just its first day. Rockstar also says it sold more than 32 million units in presales, another record. The standard edition of the open-world crime series retails for roughly $80 in the U.S. It's the first franchise release in 13 years. 49222ef2805d.text: President Trump has replaced the nation’s top cybersecurity official following a string of seemingly unrelated technology outages over the last couple of weeks. Officials have repeatedly stressed that these outages were not the result of intentional attacks, but given the growth of AI, there’s growing concern that attacks are on the horizon. William Brangham discussed more with Chris Krebs. Amna Nawaz: President Trump has replaced the nation's top cybersecurity official following a string of seemingly unrelated technology outages over the last couple of weeks. Those outages raise serious concerns about the stability of crucial digital systems. William Brangham has more. William Brangham: Amna, these disruptions, which happened across major computer networks, demonstrate how a single failure can affect critical systems used by millions of Americans. In just a matter of days, outages have affected Microsoft, which left millions of users without e-mail access, the FAA, which triggered a nationwide flight stoppage for several hours, major U.S. banks, like J.P. Morgan Chase, which temporarily snarled customer transactions, and the National Security Agency, where its internal communication network was interrupted. Officials have repeatedly stressed that these outages were not the result of intentional attacks, but, given the growth of artificial intelligence and its ability to identify vulnerabilities in our software, there's growing concern that attacks are on the horizon. For more on this, we are joined again by Chris Krebs. He's the founder of The Krebs Group and used to be the nation's top cybersecurity official during the first Trump administration. Chris, great to have you back on the program. Christopher Krebs, Former Director, U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency: Thanks for having me. William Brangham: Before we get to this new cybersecurity official that the president has announced, let's talk about these outages. As I mentioned, officials keep saying these are not attacks, these are patches being done to fix glitches that have been discovered in the system. What do you make of that analysis? Christopher Krebs: I think it's spot on, based on my conversations with folks in some of the affected organizations. Yes, there were patches. There were bugs that were discovered in software that were subsequently fixed. What's happening in the background, though, I think is the real story. Since April of 2026, when Anthropic released Mythos preview, which is an AI frontier model, which means it's the best of the best -- it was trained specifically for cybersecurity research. And basically what you have is an amalgamation of every hacker, every security researcher that's ever existed on the face of the Earth that will work tirelessly on its goal. It doesn't sleep, it doesn't eat, it doesn't need a coffee break. And those models have been used by the good guys, by companies like Microsoft, by companies like IBM and Google. And they are looking at their code that exists today, and they're trying to find as many bugs as fast as they can before the bad guys that are also using AI, not as good as these frontier models, but nonetheless they have AI, and trying to get those patched. And, in part, what's happened over the last several days is these companies that are patching their systems to get -- to hide these bugs to get rid of these bugs, they're doing it in a way that's very fast, but it's also stacking up a number of bugs or patches for those bugs. And any time you patch a system, you introduce a nonzero chance of destabilizing that network. And, unfortunately, that's what happened this week. But, again, they were all outages that were brief, they were blips. If this was a real cyberattack, you would either see those systems never recovering or taking days, if not weeks, to get back up and running. William Brangham: So, if these are just patches, as you said, and, in a sense, benign, that these are attempts to put Band-Aids on little wounds that are being found, it still does demonstrate the fragility, it seems, of so many systems that undergird our entire society. Christopher Krebs: A thousand percent. And it's more than that. It shows how much of our daily lives today is driven by technology, is connected. And that's only going to increase going forward. I don't know what five years down the road looks like, but I will tell you that more things are going to be connected, more things are going to rely on digital technology. What we have to do is keep using AI. The good guys have to keep using AI to find as many of those bugs as possible, patch them, fix them before the bad guys do. Do I know how long that's going to take? No. And anybody that says they know, I don't think they're telling the truth. But this could be a extended period of time. And I'm not talking just a couple months. Could be a year or more until we root out all these bugs, patch them, and make sure the Internet's a safer place. I do think that there's a silver lining to all of this. William Brangham: Don't you fear someday, though, that this AI arms race, that the bad guys, as you call them, have tools that are equivalent to the good guys, and that we do start to see it used not as a detective tool, but as an offensive tool? Christopher Krebs: It is already today being used as an offensive tool. Over the last couple of weeks, a number of organizations have been hit by what's known as an agentic offensive framework, known as ARTEX. There are a couple others, but basically it's software harness that sits on top of models, like some of the open-source models we have here, or DeepSeek and Kimi and GLM that are Chinese open-source models. And like I said, they're being pointed at systems. They're scanning, doing recon on a network on a company. They're looking for vulnerabilities, and they never stop. f0f9407882c1.text: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is fresh off a reelection campaign that gave him another four years in office and Democrats majorities in the state House. Now Shapiro is turning his attention to foreign policy, laying out his prescriptions to solve pressing global crises. Amna Nawaz sat down with the governor to discuss his vision for how the United States should engage on the world stage. Amna Nawaz: Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro is fresh off a reelection campaign that gave him another four years in office, and Democrats majorities in the Statehouse and in Washington. Now Shapiro, among the many potential candidates eying higher office in 2028, is turning his attention to foreign policy, laying out his prescriptions to solve some pressing global crises in a speech at the University of Pennsylvania today. I sat down with the governor at Perry World House to discuss his vision for how the United States should engage on the world stage. Governor Shapiro, welcome to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-PA): Great to be with you. Thank you. Amna Nawaz: So I got to ask you, what's the governor of Pennsylvania doing delivering a speech on foreign policy if he's not running for president? Gov. Josh Shapiro: I must tell you that it matters to governors what is happening across the globe. It matters that we have stability across the globe to get investment in our states. It matters for the citizens that we represent. And I spoke about that today, the importance of strengthening both security and prosperity and the benefit it could have for the people of Pennsylvania. Amna Nawaz: I want to ask you about news this week, because you said in your speech: "The chaos, the cruelty, the corruption of this administration has made the U.S. less secure at home and abroad." We just saw the president lead this sort of historic trilateral meeting. You have got the president of China there, the president of Russia. This administration would argue, you have to meet with these kinds of leaders, that that kind of meeting actually makes America more safe. You could potentially work to end the war in Ukraine. You could strike some kind of nuclear arms deal. Do you agree those meetings are necessary by world leaders? Gov. Josh Shapiro: Well, it's one thing to have dialogue. I'm not arguing with having dialogue. But I thought what the president did was, he showed himself to be profoundly and pathetically weak on the international stage. You mentioned in your question that you have to dialogue to address Ukraine or address other issues. Absolutely. The problem is, the president didn't address it, didn't address AI, didn't push back on the Russians and their aggressions toward Ukraine, didn't do anything to push back on the work that China is doing to undermine our economy. None of that. He just enjoyed the pageantry. And I actually thought that he ended up looking like the junior partner on the international stage. Amna Nawaz: What do you mean by that? Gov. Josh Shapiro: We are being led around by a weak individual, who is bringing chaos to the global stage. I thought, in particular, when the three of them, Putin, Xi, and Trump, were walking together, it was clear that Xi was dominating that scene. Amna Nawaz: At the center of the three of them. Gov. Josh Shapiro: And Trump looked incredibly small. Amna Nawaz: On the war in Iran, you also mentioned in your speech that you think these midterm wins for Democrats give you an opportunity to develop a new foreign policy. You say you want Democrats to use their new majorities to try to end this Iran war. What does that specifically look like? What kind of legislation can they be passing, especially when they don't have a veto-proof majority? Gov. Josh Shapiro: Well, they have a war powers resolution and they got the power of the purse. And they've got to use their leverage to end this war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. I have confidence in the speaker-designate and his majority in the House and the new majority in the Senate to do what is necessary to use their leverage to stop this war, this war that is creating chaos overseas and in the Arab world, and a war that is driving up prices for people here at home. Amna Nawaz: There's another big issue that continues to really divide members of your party, in particular, and that is the U.S. approach and support for the state of Israel. You saw earlier this year a number of Senate Democrats, including many folks who are sort of eying a 2028 run, voting to block some arms sales to Israel. Would you support efforts like that? And would you have voted with them? Gov. Josh Shapiro: Look, I think, in many ways, this issue is being resolved. You saw before that the president and the current prime minister in Israel have indicated that they are planning to end the military aid that's existed for decades to Israel. I support that. I think it is important to end that military aid. I do think it is important for Israel to be able to have the weapons they need to defend themselves from attacks from terrorist organizations, be it Hamas, the Houthis, the Iranians. And why do I think that? Because it's in America's national security interest. Amna Nawaz: You mentioned in your remarks sort of tying together America's economic future and its national security future, the message that needs to be delivered to allies. You specifically mentioned as well even Canada signing a new deal with China. We've seen this with a number of our allies working around or without the U.S. What kind of message can you deliver to allies to convince them that this is a long-term relationship that they can rely on if they're believing that every four years with a new administration policies could shift? Gov. Josh Shapiro: Look, I meet regularly with foreign leaders, ambassadors, foreign ministers, in some cases prime ministers. And I want them to understand that there are other voices in America that believe in alliances, other governors

406ca1ee192d.text: By — Obed Lamy, Associated Press Obed Lamy, Associated Press By — John Seewer, Associated Press John Seewer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/fionas-caretakers-and-fans-mourn-the-beloved-hippo-after-her-death-at-cincinnati-zoo Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Fiona's caretakers and fans mourn the beloved hippo after her death at Cincinnati Zoo Nation Nov 20, 2026 6:39 PM EST CINCINNATI (AP) — A necropsy on Fiona the hippo showed that the hat she swallowed nearly two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine, causing her death this week, the Cincinnati Zoo said Friday. Fiona, whose premature birth and fight for survival captured hearts nearly a decade ago, died Thursday after an attempt to locate the blockage. She was 9 years old. READ MORE: Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, more than a week after ingesting a hat The hat Fiona ate after it was accidentally flung into her enclosure was so far into her digestive system that no supportive care could have saved her, the zoo said in a statement. Since her death, Fiona's fans have covered a hippo statue at the zoo with flowers and notes written in crayon. Others left behind watermelons and pumpkins, some of her favorite treats. "She brought so much love in her lifetime," said one note. Born prematurely almost a decade ago and given slim odds of survival, Fiona became not only a source of hometown pride but also a worldwide symbol of hope and inspiration for many — from teachers to parents to children. During her visit to the zoo Friday morning, Jessica Grieshop, who often brought her daughters to see Fiona, called the hippo an inspiration for "anyone that was going through hard times." Zoo leaders said Fiona will be remembered for many years. "The support that we're feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. "She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles." Fiona makes her debut to the media in Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo in Cincinnati, Ohio, May 2017. File photo by Liz Dufour/USA TODAY Network via Imagn Images via Reuters One of Fiona's keepers, Jenna Wingate, posted a heartbreaking message on Instagram, saying it was like losing a family member. "It has always felt like we grew up together, and I often used to smile thinking about growing old with her and her still being around when I retire," Wingate wrote. "We lost her in the most horrific and tragic way." She ended: "She was our family. I love you Fiona and I am so sorry." Fiona wasn't the first hippo to die at the zoo after ingesting a foreign object. In 1923, a hippo "came to an untimely death due to a small boy who threw a rubber ball into its mouth," according to records at the Field Museum in Chicago, which confirmed Friday that it received that hippo's remains from the Cincinnati Zoo. A taxidermist created a lifelike mold of the original specimen, but it's no longer part of the collection. The zoo's team couldn't reach the hat in Fiona Unlike the watermelons and pumpkins she easily devoured, Fiona's digestive system wasn't meant to break down synthetic fibers, experts said. Hippos have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants and a very large gastrointestinal tract that swallowed material must pass through. Blood work showed her health was failing Thursday, so the zoo's animal care team tried to locate the hat using a scope and an ultrasound, said Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health. Removing the hat surgically was impossible based on its location and the hippo's anatomy, he added. Fiona died during recovery from the procedure, he said. The necropsy found the hat was 25 feet (7.6 meters) beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet (15.2 meters) from the end of her intestines. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said. Jenike called the zoo's staff heroic in their efforts to save her. Zoo worked around the clock to save Fiona At first, Fiona showed no signs of distress after swallowing the hat 11 days before her death. A zoo visitor tossed the hat, which a ceiling fan caught and flung into the hippo habitat. But a few days later, her appetite started to decline, zoo officials said. By Monday, the zoo announced Fiona was undergoing veterinary care. Officials were cautiously optimistic she could pass the hat. The zoo's animal care team gave her fluids through an IV, conducted a colonoscopy, and tried to shake the obstruction loose with a vibration table borrowed from a horse farm. Fiona is mourned by many worldwide Fiona inspired millions in her first months and final days, bringing people together across political divides and other boundaries. Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of one of their children face-to-face with Fiona through the glass wall of her enclosure. Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton posted photos of her behind-the-scenes encounter with Fiona, writing that she would treasure "the smiles she gave me." Fiona wasn't expected to survive her first weeks Fiona was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), far below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time. The zoo's staff went to extraordinary lengths to keep her alive, raising her by hand. She couldn't nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother to feed her. She became a celebrity during her nine years. Hippos typically live 40 to 50 years in zoos. Her story marked an uplifting turn for the Cincinnati Zoo after months of backlash over the 2016 shooting of Harambe. The gorilla became a pop culture phenomenon after he was killed because a child got into his enclosure. Associated Press writer Holly Ramer in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed. Alabama Power announced Friday its electric rates would decrease across the board next year, saving its 1.5 million customers approximately $160 million on their energy bills.
The company attributed the savings to projected increases in revenue from large data center contracts next year.
“In January, our customers will see their rates go down because of the growth we’re seeing across the state,” Alabama Power CEO Jeff Peoples said in a news release. “Alabama is growing and we’re making sure that growth works for all of our customers.”
The company news release said that a home or business using 1,000 kilowatt-hours each month would save more than $50 a year, compared to current rates.
Electricity costs have been a major political issue in Alabama for the past year, after an Inside Climate News investigation last November showed Alabama Power customers paid the highest total electric bills in the country in 2024, driven by its above-average rates and Alabama’s very high electricity usage.
In filings made Friday with the Alabama Public Service Commission, the company announced a projected 2027 income of $1.76 billion, higher than its currently allowed rate of return set by the PSC.
Unlike most regulated utilities in the United States, Alabama Power operates under a formula-based rate mechanism called the Rate Stabilization and Equalization factor, created by the PSC in 1982.
Under that system, rates are adjusted up or down automatically every January based on the company’s projections for the upcoming year, without the formal rate case hearings that most other states use to set electricity rates.
Those projections for 2027 triggered the changes, which will take effect in January.
Alabama Power also said it will comply with the commission’s request to stop billing customers for part of its advertising budget beginning in 2027. That change is expected to save the average customer about four cents per month, the company said.
Critics Say Tax Cut, Not Data Centers, Drive Decrease
Daniel Tait, executive director of clean energy advocacy group Energy Alabama, said the company should not get credit for lowering rates when the formula dictated the decrease.
“Alabama Power customers should not be fooled,” Tait said in an email. “The utility wants a public parade for handing back money it was on track to overcharge customers.”

Tait also said the company is crediting data centers for the decrease, but does not mention that a massive cut in the company’s tax bill generated even more savings.
“The company credits data centers, but its own numbers show there would be no cut without a roughly $180 million drop in its tax bill, which the company ties to nuclear tax credits from the Inflation Reduction Act,” Tait said. “Even after this action, the company’s own filing shows its return on equity, a marker for its profits, remaining above the national average.”
Relief for Customers Paying Country’s Highest Bills
Two weeks after the ICN investigation was published last November, U.S. Sen. Katie Britt said Alabama had the “highest rates in the Southeast,” amid a debate about a hyperscale data center project currently under construction in Bessemer, just west of Birmingham.
In December, the PSC approved a two-year rate freeze proposed by Alabama Power, delaying scheduled increases surrounding the purchase of a gas-fired power plant, and blocking rate increases until 2028.
Then in the spring, fierce public backlash against high electricity prices spurred state lawmakers to pass sweeping utility legislation that will dramatically reshape the PSC, but will not require the formal rate case hearings that most other states use.
The bill will expand the PSC from three members to seven next year, and create a governor-appointed secretary of energy who will set the PSC’s agenda and “have authority over personnel and administrative functions of the commission.”
The secretary can only be overruled by a vote of five of the seven commissioners.
The two incumbent PSC commissioners on the ballot this year were defeated in GOP primaries, leaving PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond as the lone returning member next year.
Britt issued a news release Friday, taking credit for next year’s decrease.
“I asked Alabama Power to find a way to lower rates—not just freeze them, but achieve lower power bills for Alabama households,” Britt said in the release. “Today, I am excited to say that is happening.
“I am proud to have successfully led this charge and that it’s resulted in putting more money back in hardworking Alabamians’ pockets.”
Tait, from Energy Alabama, said the bigger issue is the high rate of return that Alabama Power earns. The company reported $1.52 billion in profit through the first three quarters of 2026.
“Alabamians want real relief on their electric bills, and that comes from a cut to what Alabama Power is allowed to profit,” he said. “Sure, people will take the $4 per month but shuffling tax credits around doesn’t cut it.”
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. Amna Nawaz: November 22, 1963, a date forever etched in American historical memory, when President John F. Kennedy was shot and killed in his motorcade crossing Dealey Plaza in downtown Dallas. The story continues to be told and questioned. Jeffrey Brown: The setting is central to the experience, a former book depository in downtown Dallas, now the Sixth Floor Museum at Dealey Plaza. Curatorial head Stephen Fagin … Stephen Fagin: I think our job is to provide our audiences with the tools to navigate this interpretive minefield of history and culture that is the life, death, and legacy of President Kennedy. Jeffrey Brown: The youthful president who inspired millions, the challenges at home and abroad he faced in his short time in office, and inevitably and here most hauntingly the assassination of John F. Kennedy from shots investigators determined were fired from the sixth floor of this building by Lee Harvey Oswald on November 22, 1963. Museum CEO Nicola Longford … Nicola Longford: We presume that everybody has some idea of what happened here, and, actually, quite a lot of our younger generations have no idea what happened here. Darwin Payne: This is the imagined city desk. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. Darwin Payne: This is the newsroom. Jeffrey Brown: Including now 89-year-old Darwin Payne, then 26 and on the rewrite desk at the now defunct Dallas Times Herald, was quickly sent into the streets. Jeffrey Brown: Another young reporter featured of special interest to us, then 29-year-old Jim Lehrer, also with The Times Herald, who was at the airport Love Field when the president and first lady, Jackie Kennedy, arrived, and later at police headquarters where Oswald was being held. In fact, Jim's friend and "News Hour" co-founder Robert MacNeil was also in Dallas that day covering events for NBC News. Fifty years later, they spoke about it on our program. Jim Lehrer: And I was there when they brought in Oswald. And I wrote his name down. I still had the notebook. I was one of those people who asked, hey, did you shoot the president? Robert MacNeil: I was also in the police station that evening, and doing reports through NBC, and I saw Oswald paraded back and when he said, "I didn't kill anybody, I'm just a patsy." Jim Lehrer: And the guy standing next to me, who I did not know at the time, was Jack Ruby. Jeffrey Brown: The intrigue with that day lives on, outside on Dealey Plaza and the famous grassy knoll, another scene, tourists getting quick photos amid traffic on the X markings where JFK was shot, others encountering regulars at the site promoting their books and memorabilia, convinced the official story was a cover-up. Robert Wilonsky: This was never my profession. It was always my passion. Started calling witnesses out of the phone book when I was 16, and they talked to me. Jeffrey Brown: I was joined by Dallas Morning News columnist Robert Wilonsky, born and raised here, endlessly fascinated by the pull of a place, he says is still Dallas' number one tourist destination. Robert Wilonsky: Whether or not we talk about it today, whether or not we think about it today, it defined Dallas. It made us grow up, it made us look inward, and it made us think differently about who we were. Lieb, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/court-approves-7-25-billion-bayer-settlement-over-claims-roundup-weed-killer-caused-cancer Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Court approves $7.25 billion Bayer settlement over claims Roundup weed killer caused cancer Nation Nov 20, 2026 6:25 PM EST JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. (AP) — Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge. WATCH: What science tells us about the health risks of Roundup The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed and the severity of their illness. For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets. Bayer already has changed the formula for its Roundup version sold to residential users. Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don't require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements. Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing — which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling. In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are "fair and adequate" and the total dollar amount is "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements." Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is "a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation." The decision could be appealed. Roundup has been used on weeds for over 50 years Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weed killer in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weed killer's deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less. WATCH: U.S. Forest Service, timber companies spraying record amounts of glyphosate in California The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens. Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" in 2015. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it's not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed. About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets. The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion. In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court's precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence and fraud. The verdict "should send a strong signal" that plaintiffs "will face significant challenges" pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer's U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader. Attorneys disagree on whether the settlement is fair Bayer previously set aside $16 billion to cover legal costs related to Roundup cases. The new settlement, which is in addition to that, is designed to address most of the remaining lawsuits, as well as any additional cases brought in the coming years by people who were exposed to Roundup before the settlement was proposed in February. "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," said Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case. The settlement calls for Bayer to make annual payments into a special fund for up to 21 years, totaling as much as $7.25 billion. The amount of money paid out to individuals would vary. Agricultural, industrial or turf workers exposed at length to Roundup could receive an average of $165,000 if they were diagnosed with an aggressive form of the illness while younger than age 60. But anyone diagnosed at age 78 or older would get significantly less, with an average of $10,000. Some attorneys have said the individual settlement amounts are too small and the terms too restrictive. "This settlement is the scariest, worst future settlement that's ever been contemplated," attorney Gerson Smoger said during a September court hearing on whether the settlement was fair. Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.
It's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs."
"Purebreds," says the woman filming.
Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting
In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.
In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.
Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.
Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.
One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.
170 carcasses found
When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.
Chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.
On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.
Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting â taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.
"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know."
In the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.
"The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.
"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.
By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris says. "Others were liquefied."
LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.
Their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.
Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.
There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?
As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.
"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in."
'God knows what was inside those urns'
The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.
A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.
As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.
"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a big thing with the boom of the pet industry," says Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets."
These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.
Or not, as the case may be.
Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, says she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (Â£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.
Calling says Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

US declassifies more UFO footage filmed in the Middle East
The US government released an eighth tranche of records regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), marking the latest step in an effort to declassify government files on UFOs.
After US President Donald Trump called for UFO files to be released in an executive order earlier this year, the Pentagon has declassified hundreds of files. The first tranche was released 8 May 2026.
The footage in this video makes up three of the 43 files released in this tranche. All three clips were filmed from aboard US military platforms in the Middle East in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent AlpÃ¶ge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
AlpÃ¶ge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

Delgado, Associated Press By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press By — Victoria Milko, Associated Press Victoria Milko, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/activists-leaders-criticize-cop31-climate-talks-as-fossil-fuels-go-unmentioned-in-draft-deal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Activists, leaders criticize COP31 climate talks as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft deal World Nov 20, 2026 6:06 PM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — United Nations climate talks in Turkey stretched into overtime Friday and delegates put off some decisions to next year, unable to find common ground on multiple issues with mutterings and protests about failure. Still, organizers remained hopeful that they could find ways the world can work together to avert the most catastrophic effects of global warming. READ MORE: UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe "We are close to the finish line but not there yet," said Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, president of the two-week summit known as COP31. During a late-night session, delegates passed a protest banner reading "failure," while a demonstrator interrupted Kurum as he spoke, shouting, "you are killing the future, you are killing the future." "Yes, we are tired, and we have put in a great deal of effort—but we still have the capacity, right here in this hall, to convey truly meaningful messages to the world," Kurum pleaded Friday night. "By reaching a consensus, we can effect real change." The term "fossil fuels" wasn't even mentioned in the latest draft of the final agreement — meant to address how the world will deal with climate change — sending activists and country leaders into an uproar Friday. Such agreements, often adopted by nearly 200 nations and only on a near-unanimous consensus basis, are voluntary and nonbinding. Burning fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas — is the chief cause of climate change. Fossil fuels also went unmentioned in final decisions for more than 25 years until three years ago, mostly because of objections by Saudi Arabia, said Alden Meyer, a longtime analyst with the European think-tank E3G. In Dubai in 2023, however, the world agreed to "transition away from fossil fuels." "It would be a real setback if we come out of here with no signal that we were serious about what we agreed to do three years ago," Meyer said. Kurum promised that a third version of the final document will be delivered Saturday morning after overnight talks. Outstanding issues dividing nations include fossil fuel language, detailed calls for carbon capture and storage for industry, financial aid for poor countries to adapt to climate change and Europe's pseudo-tariff on carbon-intensive products, Meyer said. "Unless things change by tomorrow, we are heading for a very disappointing outcome," Meyer said Friday night. This year's talks came amid urgent warnings that the planet is sure to breach the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting long-term warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. October 2026 was 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.4 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the mid 1800s, according to Berkeley Earth. It also came after a year of climate-related disasters, including Europe's deadly heat waves and Nepal's devastating flooding. "There is nothing on the table that protects people, or addresses the priorities of the Global South," said Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International, at a Friday event, where attendees chanted and held signs that read "SHAME!" As climate talks near their end, fossil fuel debate rages One of the main goals on the table would increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% today to 35% by 2035. But the latest draft doesn't stipulate that electricity should be generated with renewable energy sources like solar and wind, leaving the door open for fossil-fueled power plants to be counted as part of an electrification push. READ MORE: At UN climate talks, 5 nations back plan to double rooftop solar panels by 2030 "At a time when the climate crisis demands decisive action, weakening commitments on fossil fuel phase-out risks undermining progress," said Ghiwa Nakat, executive director of Greenpeace in the Middle East and North Africa. The U.N. has hosted climate talks for more than 30 years, but didn't acknowledge that fossil fuels contribute to climate change until the 2021 summit in Glasgow, Scotland. Two years later in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, countries explicitly called for a transition away from fossil fuels for the first time. Turkey's Kurum said the electrification push implies a transition away from fossil fuels, adding: "We are not here to discuss decisions at previous COPs." In a rare move, Panama vowed to "formally object" if the final agreement doesn't add climate finance, cap oil production and acknowledge failing goals, among other demands. The country's Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro said the talks are being held hostage by a "petroleum mafia" and need to be reformed. Navarro reminded Kurum Friday night that he can't ram through any final decision without allowing countries to object, as has been done in previous years. "The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility," he said. "What we have here is a contest to see who speaks the most, who blows the most hot air." Vulnerable nations say climate finance is lacking The draft agreement also says a fund to compensate countries ravaged by climate change should be tripled but doesn't specify an amount. A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.
The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.
Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.
Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.
Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.
Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.
Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

Sisak, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/lawsuits-allege-corner-cutting-ignored-warnings-led-to-fatal-brooklyn-building-collapse Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lawsuits allege corner cutting, ignored warnings led to fatal Brooklyn building collapse Nation Nov 20, 2026 5:52 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — As investigators probe what caused a New York City building collapse that killed eight people, workers and residents are painting a portrait of two trouble spots side-by-side: the apartment house that fell down and the construction site being excavated next door. WATCH: Brooklyn community leaders, residents hold meeting on building collapse Lawsuits filed since the Nov. 11 disaster in Brooklyn cast blame in multiple directions: at the construction site owner and contractors; at an engineering firm that drew up the excavation plan; and at the owner of the building that collapsed. Several injured workers have also taken steps toward suing the city agency that polices construction safety. A key question for investigators is whether work underway to dig a deep pit for a new building undermined the foundation of the three-story building next door at 1321 Flatbush Ave., causing it to topple into the jobsite. A lawsuit filed by five injured construction workers said the dig at 2625 Bedford Ave. lacked adequate retaining walls, shoring and underpinning to keep the adjoining building safe, and that excavation work continued even after the building's facade began to crack. "The shoring that they were planning to keep the collapsed building up was severely insufficient," said lawyer Jonathan Damashek, who has sued on behalf of injured workers. He questioned whether the city should have approved the plans, and whether contractors' work was negligent. Damashek's lawsuits accuse defendants, including construction manager Townhouse Homes, of failing "to consider public safety above their own concern of keeping down costs." The litigation comes as families mourn the dead — among them two children. City officials said Wednesday that another building adjoining the one that crumbled will have to be demolished after the collapse peeled off an outer wall. Tenant says construction work next door led to cracks Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani vowed to do "everything we can to understand exactly how this collapse occurred, so that the responsible parties can be held to account." His department is hiring an independent engineering consultant to help. Brooklyn prosecutors also are investigating. The Buildings Department said by email Friday that it reviewed the excavation and support plans and found they complied with city requirements. As for examining what actually got installed, the agency noted that the city requires private inspectors — hired by developers — to check some stages of construction. The agency didn't answer a question about whether it responded to a preconstruction survey that found the adjoining wall of the now-collapsed building "in poor condition with noticeable cracks." That three-story brick structure, erected nearly a century ago, had its own woes — over 90 unresolved citations for exposed wiring, roof leaks, faulty doors and other alleged housing code violations. Conditions worsened once construction ramped up next door, tenant Dengane Omari Jack said in a lawsuit. Jack, who lost his extensive record collection and other personal effects, said he was rebuffed when he tried warning the landlord about cracks he noticed near the building's entrance. After providing photos of the damage, Jack was told it wasn't the landlord's fault and couldn't be fixed, the lawsuit said. Builder and excavation engineer have faced lawsuits While the investigation proceeds, the city is checking out over 160 construction sites tied to companies involved in the project at 2625 Bedford Ave., a planned apartment and commercial building. Townhouse, which also operates as Promont, has been heavily involved in New York's construction scene over the last three decades. In 2016, it was accused in lawsuits of damaging an adjacent building during a Manhattan renovation project, which it denied, and compromising the structural integrity of adjacent structures while performing excavation, pile driving and steel beam installation for a Brooklyn hotel. The company's lawyers haven't addressed the allegations in the lawsuit involving the hotel. Principals in Townhouse, other firms named in this report and the property owners haven't responded to The Associated Press' requests for comment. The Bedford Avenue project's excavation engineer, Jieming Wang, has also faced lawsuits. At least a dozen have blamed excavation plans designed by his firm, New Jersey-based LMW Engineering Group, for damage at adjacent properties, court records show. A 2015 lawsuit alleged that LMW's work on a Manhattan excavation site caused sloping floors, damaged doors and windows and destroyed utility pipes at an adjacent building. In 2016, the wall of a building next to a Queens excavation project was undermined by soil removal, another lawsuit said. A 2020 lawsuit accused the firm of skipping required testing and monitoring at another Queens project. A neighboring building's foundation was left unstable, its gas and hot water systems were damaged and an architectural arch partially separated from the structure, the lawsuit said. The company, which has worked on bridges, airports and other projects since its 1998 founding, denied the allegations in the 2015 and 2016 cases but hasn't responded to the 2020 lawsuit. Other litigation was resolved out of court. 6953481fcf20.text: By — Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press By — Samya Kullab, Associated Press Samya Kullab, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/nato-calls-russian-missiles-landing-in-poland-a-grave-violation-of-airspace Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter NATO calls Russian missiles landing in Poland a 'grave violation' of airspace World Nov 20, 2026 5:42 PM EST NOWA DEBA, Poland (AP) — Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland on Friday in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine. The incidents occurred while Russia carried out a major nighttime bombardment of neighboring Ukraine. The development stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the U.S. tries to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago. WATCH: After calling Putin his friend, Trump 'can't speak to' whether Putin is a friend to America Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared that "we are dealing with an intentional provocation" by Russia. There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the missiles and suspected drone, or on Friday's drills. One Russian missile is believed to have crashed around 35 kilometers (22 miles) from where the military exercises were taking place, officials said. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down roughly 50 kilometers (30 miles) from the Ukraine border, and what officials believe was likely a jet-powered drone hit about 30 kilometers (20 miles) from the border with Ukraine. There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage. European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia's attempts to destabilize the continent. U.S. President Donald Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff. Another envoy, Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the United States believes Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, in what could be a step toward compromise. But Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said Friday that even a quasi-membership in NATO for Ukraine would be unacceptable, Russia's Interfax news agency reported. "We discuss security guarantees primarily in terms of ensuring the security of our own country, and that's what we're talking about," Ryabkov said. Russia's nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow's war effort. NATO chief addresses a 'grave violation' by Russia Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by Poland's PAP news agency showed a large, loud explosion and a bright flash, apparently in a wooded area, in one of the crashes. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the development in Poland a "grave violation" of that country's airspace. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte wrote on X. Rutte is expected to go to Poland this weekend in response. Under NATO's collective security guarantee — Article 5 of its founding treaty — an attack on any ally should be considered an attack on all 32 members. It obliges members to provide support to that ally, most likely military backup, but does not limit them to that alone. Article 5 is not triggered automatically. Ultimately, it is a political decision that all members must agree to. Poland also has the option to enact Article 4, which it did last year. This provides for emergency consultations only. The development brought a chorus of European condemnation. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described it as "utterly unacceptable." European Council President António Costa said that Russia "continues to spread (its) threats." Germany's Foreign Ministry called it "yet another example of Russia's ongoing provocations." Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident in Poland "demonstrates the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the trans-Atlantic community." Later Friday, the chief of defense intelligence for the U.K. said he was confident that Russia "does not actively seek war with NATO." But, Lt. Gen. Matthew Jones said in a speech at a college in Cambridge, his greatest fear "is the risk of a significant miscalculation." "There are too many recent examples of reckless Russian behavior where, if the incident had been slightly different, the results could have been extremely serious," said Jones, who did not directly mention the incidents in Poland. Putin has said that Russia will not accept any European troops deployed to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal and will view them as legitimate targets. Russian attacks batter Ukraine, killing at least 8 Overnight strikes killed at least eight Ukrainian civilians and wounded more than two dozen, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic and some carrying cluster warheads that scatter dozens of smaller bomblets across a wide area, he said. The attack fit the pattern of Moscow's heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge, and added to uncertainty about the prospects for ongoing talks brokered by Washington. Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

Plans to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide at an Eastern Iowa ammunition plant are on hold after the Army postponed the operation and a federal appeals court temporarily halted an emergency permit from the Environmental Protection Agency.
Initially scheduled for Friday, the planned explosion generated immense public outcry and concern from public health experts, environmentalists and elected officials who say residents received inadequate notice and guidance regarding the impacts of lead dust on their health and the environment.
Lead azide is a common primary explosive in bombs. After decades in storage at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, 68 barrels of the compound have become dangerously unstable and require emergency disposal.
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle announced late Thursday that the detonation would be rescheduled to Monday. But hours later, a ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit placed an administrative stay on the EPA’s detonation permit, indefinitely delaying the operation.
The ruling came less than 24 hours after environmental law organization Earthjustice, representing the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, sued the EPA over its permit and filed an emergency motion asking the court to suspend it.
In their suit, the petitioners argued that the decision-making process lacked transparency and that the Army failed to adequately explore alternatives to detonation. “Within the permit, we just do not see enough things that will protect human health and the environment,” said Thien Chau, a senior attorney for Earthjustice. He described the planned detonation as “abnormal and extraordinary.”
The court could rule on the emergency motion at any point in the next few days, Chau said.
A Ticking Time Bomb
During a March safety review at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, officials discovered that stored lead azide had dissolved and reformed into irregularly shaped, highly volatile crystals. Friction, heat or shock could easily trigger spontaneous detonation.
Rather than risk an accidental explosion by leaving the barrels in storage, relocating them or chemically neutralizing the contents, all alternatives the Army considered, the department opted to conduct a controlled detonation of nearly five tons of lead azide, according to its environmental assessment. The Environmental Protection Agency granted an emergency permit for the detonation last Friday, citing an “unacceptable” risk of accidental combustion.
Even with mitigation technology like blast containment barriers and water misters in place, the explosion will generate a lead-containing dust cloud that could deposit the neurotoxin across hundreds of miles in an area where tens of thousands of Iowans live.
Residents of Middletown were informed of the planned detonation at a town hall in October. But state officials and most Iowans learned about the explosion just days before it was scheduled to take place.
Maps released by the Army in a public advisory early this week projected surface deposition of lead 50 miles northwest of Middletown, with airborne exposure as far as 100 miles afield.
A spokesperson for Gov. Kim Reynolds said that the advisory was the first she had heard of the operation.
The projected ranges for the dust cloud shrank significantly in updated maps released Wednesday, which the Army says reflect changing weather forecasts. Their most recent projections showed toxic lead dust settling on surfaces over a smaller region that extends at least 30 miles north of the plant and up to 10 miles wide.
Planning for Toxic Debris
The Army’s projections suggest outdoor lead dust levels in the plume’s path could exceed federal benchmarks for indoor lead levels in homes and childcare facilities, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa.
Still, the precise amount and location of lead that would be released by the blast is unknown and depends on weather conditions and the effectiveness of the Army’s engineered controls, O’Shaughnessy said.
According to the emergency permit issued by the Environmental Protection Agency, the Army is required to use high-end estimates to avoid underestimating the potential impact of the detonation. The Army did not respond to questions about more specific ranges of lead concentrations.
Leading up to the planned Friday detonation, the Army advised residents to stay indoors, close windows and doors, and set heating and cooling systems to “recirculate” for a few hours after the planned blast. The Army also advised residents to clean their cars and hose down play surfaces and windowsills once the cloud settled.
Any surfaces typically touched by children would be especially important to clean, said O’Shaughnessy. As a neurotoxin, lead is most harmful to small children and infants with developing brains and nervous systems.
The EPA emergency permit requires the Army to conduct monitoring before, during and after detonation. In addition, researchers at the University of Iowa scrambled to set up independent air and soil monitoring following the Army’s announcement early this week, said David Cwiertny, director of the university’s Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination.

The hat swallowed by beloved hippopotamus Fiona had become lodged in the middle of her small intestine, making removal "impossible", the Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio said.
Vets tried to save Fiona after she ingested the hat that ended up in her habitat by accident almost two weeks ago. But its location and the 2,400-pound (1,088 kg) animal's anatomy made removal unfeasible. She died on Thursday.
A necropsy, an autopsy performed on an animal, showed the hat was "located 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines", the zoo said on Friday.
Animal lovers were rooting for a recovery for Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017.
Cincinnati Zoo's director of animal health, Dr Mike Wenninger, said in a statement that an upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object.
"The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible," Wenninger added. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the woolen hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
While Fiona showed no symptoms at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system to no avail.
Christina Gorsuch, The zoo's director of animal care, Christina Gorsuch, said on Friday that the other hippos - Bibi, Tucker and Fritz - were so far eating and behaving normally after Fiona's passing.
"It's difficult to know how they're feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves, Gorsuch said.
"We have received so much love from our community and beyond," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. "We were touched when we saw stadiums, bridges, and buildings lit in purple last night" in Fiona's [honour], he added.
The US Senate even adopted a resolution on Friday to honour the beloved hippo.
Fiona first rose to fame when she was born premature at Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
"The support that we're feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," Jenike said. "She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles."
