Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the BeltrÃ¡n Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.

- Published
With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England, one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold.
Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.
Red squirrels are endangered in the UK, with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers.
There have some strongholds in England, external, particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland, external.
However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey".
He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK.
"That is actually really special for them."
Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885.
However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years.
The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey, external tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle.
The National Trust of Jersey said the island was an "important refuge" for the red squirrel, where they were "fairly widespread, external".
It said the inland valleys and woodlands were the best places to spot them.
The species is legally protected, which means it would be a criminal offence to harm them.
Nina Powell, senior animal carer at the JSPCA [Jersey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals], said Jersey has a "good population" of squirrels and that "you can see them almost anywhere".
While the primary reason for their success is the lack of grey squirrels, Powell said they also thrived "because people look out for them".
She said: "A lot of people do support them, put out feeders and stuff like that.
"Their habitats are decreasing everywhere... but we do have quite a lot of nature reserves.
"In some places, we've got rope bridges which really help them cross the roads, and our speed limits are quite low, so that helps them as well".
She said the JSPCA had handled 50 red squirrels so far this year, including hand-raising eight babies, called kits (kittens).
She said: "We want to keep all animals as wild as possible, so we try and be as hands-off as possible.
"Some of them don't like us... some of them are quite sweet. They really do vary in personality."
Glynn agreed that their success had come in part because of the efforts of islanders.
He said: "They're really beloved amongst the local community as well. A lot of people put out squirrel feeders or love to see them in the garden.
"We get lots of reports from people who just want to tell us they've seen them because they're so happy to have them around."

29f32cf5304a.text: By — Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/why-do-people-believe-recent-tech-failures-must-be-connected Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Why do people believe recent tech failures must be connected? Nation Nov 21, 2026 6:14 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. It's been one thing after another. Companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and U.S. Bank experienced technical issues and outages that caused widespread banking issues, delayed plane departures and interrupted workdays across the world. Soon after, Marriott and Apple customers also experienced digital problems, and 178 companies reported being affected by a Nov. 16 cyberattack. At the same time, various U.S. government systems — the Federal Aviation Administration, National Security Agency and National Weather Service — fell into disarray, including a rare nationwide ground stop. For many people, the pile-on of concerning news alerts had a sinister feel. WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity "We're under attack in a way we've never seen before," wrote Nalin Haley, a conservative influencer and son of Republican politician Nikki Haley, on Nov. 17. "This is an AI cyberattack." On Bluesky, Christopher Webb, a self-described "lifelong Dem" and party strategist, questioned whether the issues were connected. "Coincidence??? 4 major banks reporting outages, a massive Microsoft disruption, and a nationwide FAA ground stop, all within days of each other," he wrote Nov. 16. The best available information points to mundane explanations such as routine maintenance, one-off problems or isolated cyberattacks, rather than an imminent systemic collapse or a coordinated attack on digital systems. But why can that be hard to believe? Human brains naturally detect patterns and reject uncertainty The rapid-fire succession of events didn't help. Neither did the timing of a planned, routine Nov. 17 test of the country's Emergency Alert System. Human brains are wired to make connections and spot statistical regularities in the world. "Detecting patterns is important for perceiving the world and learning about cause and effect," said Javier Granados Samayoa, a Texas Christian University psychology professor. This tendency "can sometimes lead people to see connections where none may exist." One paper about conspiracy thinking started with a coin toss. People who reported a tendency to notice patterns in a random string of coin tosses were more likely to also endorse conspiracy theories and supernatural beliefs. WATCH: Cascade of tech outages 'separate events' and 'under control,' Trump says Research also shows that when people lack control, they're more likely to detect nonexistent patterns. For people unable to access their work platforms or stuck at airports, powerlessness and confusion were all too familiar feelings. Those feelings contribute to embracing conspiracy theories. "People are looking for ways to understand what is going on and they don't like the uncertainty that often surrounds unfolding events," said Karen Douglas, a University of Kent social psychology professor. "Also, a simple explanation is often not very appealing. People assume that there must somehow be a bigger explanation, or more going on than people know about." Human biases and social media platforms can intensify the anxieties The flurry of frustration-inducing technical issues coupled with the known negativity bias observed across social media platforms can set people up to have outsized emotional reactions when things go wrong. Negativity bias means that negative information has a stronger impact and people tend to think about it more, said Granados Samayoa. On social media, content is more likely to prompt engagement and go viral if it uses negative language or prompts a strong negative reaction. WATCH: What a string of tech problems reveals about America's digital vulnerabilities Social media algorithms have continuously circulated some of the most alarming posts and conspiracy theories — an estimated 30% of which were pushed by suspected bots, including some with potential foreign influence, Axios reported. Sharing conspiracy theories on social media is easy, fast and difficult to untangle. "Once people believe in a conspiracy theory, it is often difficult to convince them otherwise," Douglas said. The events and concerns compounded as regular people and news reporters all began paying more attention to outages that would otherwise be routine. That's commonly called frequency bias. "United's outage this afternoon is so pedestrian, it'd be a non-story if not for what's happened the last four days," Kyle Potter, an editor at Thrifty Traveler, wrote Nov. 16. 1907e33f760b.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/for-families-of-the-fallen-trumps-proposed-arch-casts-a-shadow-over-arlington-national-cemetery Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter For families of the fallen, Trump's proposed arch casts a shadow over Arlington National Cemetery Politics Nov 21, 2026 5:52 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Cpl. Spencer Collart's headstone faces the rising sun and the Lincoln Memorial to the east. The Marine Corps War Memorial is nearby. Soon, President Donald Trump's gilded, towering arch could be, too. Collart's silent stone speaks volumes in its simplicity of courage, sacrifice and loss. It stands among thousands of uniform headstones and other monuments, each telling the story of the person, or persons, beneath it. WATCH: 2nd judge blocks construction of Trump's arch in D.C. But if Trump gets his way, a different story may be told. His proposed 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) arch could cast a long shadow on Arlington National Cemetery, with the potential to literally shade gravesites, disrupt solemn visits with the noise of construction and alter the carefully designed historic landscape of the nation's capital. For many veterans and their families, and the loved ones of others buried at the cemetery, the arch has no place so close to the Arlington, Virginia, burial grounds. That opposition has sparked lawsuits by veterans groups and others, including nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty, who argue the arch, which would be built on a traffic circle about half a mile (0.8 kilometers) from Arlington's main entrance, will fundamentally change the experience of visiting the cemetery. "It's a billboard for an ego. It's a loud, boastful, gaudy piece of marketing dropped onto sacred ground," said Bart Collart, Spencer's father. His son, a young Marine who died at 21 trying to save fellow crew members in a 2023 Osprey crash in Australia, would see it as "dirtying hallowed ground." A skyline-altering arch could impact the cemetery The arch project is part of a series of renovations to Washington that Trump, a Republican, has set in motion to reimagine the city. When complete, the gold and granite arch will stretch taller than the Lincoln Memorial. Opponents say the arch would break the alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, the Memorial Bridge and Arlington House, which was formerly Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee's home, and the symbolism of a reunited North and South. But behind the fences that line Memorial Drive is an active cemetery with more than 430,000 people interred there and dozens more added each week. They include retirees and their spouses and some dependents and a few eligible dignitaries. There are two presidents, John F. Kennedy and William Howard Taft, there, along with more than a dozen Supreme Court justices. Among the dead are an untold number who died while on active duty and eligible spouses. There are more than 400 recipients of the Medal of Honor, the nation's highest honor for valor in combat. The remains of military personnel from every war, dating back to the Revolutionary War, are there. WATCH: Retired general calls Trump's proposed arch near Arlington a 'sacrilege' An estimated 3 million to 4 million people visit annually. Walking among the stones or taking the tour is a lesson in the nation's military history. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is one prominent feature, as is the grave of boxing legend Joe Louis. Audie Murphy, an actor who was one of the most decorated U.S. soldiers in World War II, is also buried there. On a recent visit, a small group of about 10 men came quietly from Section 60, an area where soldiers who died in Afghanistan and Iraq are buried. Their young ages, "PH" for Purple Heart and the inscription Afghanistan or Operation Enduring Freedom mean premature loss. What comes through is silence and distant sound, except for the passenger planes flying over from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. "I think you could, by any definition, consider it the most hallowed ground in the United States, but I think we're not even giving it credit for how hallowed, how representative, how much sacrifice and honor is there," said Micki McElya, a historian at the University of Connecticut and author of "The Politics of Mourning: Death and Honor in Arlington National Cemetery." She said the country's shifting values are represented there in all their complications, including slavery. Court battles over the arch are playing out Supporters of the arch say it completes a plan mandated by Congress in 1925 to add a monument to the circle. "It was always supposed to be a gateway to connect D.C. to Arlington," said Jared Craig, general counsel and national vice president for Veterans for America First, which joined several veteran organizations in a brief in the lawsuit supporting the arch. Craig argued the arch honors veterans and fallen service members. He said that the project does not impact the cemetery itself and requires no changes there. Jimi Shaughnessy, veterans program manager at the nonprofit National Parks Conservation Association, disagrees. A veteran, he visits his great-grandparents' resting place regularly. READ MORE: Trump says the towering arch he wants to be build might be dedicated to military veterans "The setting is open, it's quiet, it's peaceful, it is easy to navigate," he said. And there is space to transition "so I can properly acknowledge my great-grandfolks that are buried there." The sounds of major construction will intrude on that and funerals, and creating a tourist attraction at the arch will bring noise and distraction, along with a "looming dark shadow above me," he said. To the White House, the arch would serve "as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250 year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today," spokesm

A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (Â£3,058).
The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
Its new owner has not been named.
Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.
Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.
McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".
Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.
Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.
Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.
"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.
As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.
In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

f7f9724f890a.text: By — Ken Sweet, Associated Press Ken Sweet, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-vows-to-work-with-democrats-to-cap-credit-card-interest-rates-at-10 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10% Politics Nov 21, 2026 4:20 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans. "I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards. The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise. WATCH: Credit card debt surges in U.S. as high interest rates make it harder to pay off That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates. In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal. "Congress should pass my bipartisan bill to cap these rates and deliver relief right away," Hawley said at the time. READ MORE: Voters demanded economic relief. Trump and Democrats face tough choices on how to deliver Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back. About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says. Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year. Please check your inbox to confirm. The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics. The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity. The scope of the problem was not immediately clear. Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: "We just heard about it and I will say that it's not good." WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages. The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers. In September, for instance, the FBI said it was investigating a hack of its job portal website after a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed it had obtained a massive trove of data on bureau employees and applicants. And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. cdf7efb8596c.text: By — Reed Berger-Fleishman, The Conversation Reed Berger-Fleishman, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/a-doctors-guide-to-surviving-and-enjoying-holiday-feasting-while-on-glp%e2%80%911-medication Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A doctor's guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication Health Nov 21, 2026 2:46 PM EST This article originally appeared on The Conversation. Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends. But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts. For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different. WATCH: As GLP-1s reshape America, questions and new uses emerge As a physician specializing in obesity medicine, I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage. However, these medications don't eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love. Respecting fullness cues Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes, obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb. GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients feel full sooner and stay full longer. Many patients also report fewer cravings for high-calorie foods and even a reduced desire to drink alcohol. In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they're satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging. The prices of Thanksgiving staples this year won't be too much higher than in 2025. Watch the video in the player above. One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body's changing fullness signals. Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate. These symptoms can serve as reminders that you've reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving. GLP-1 medications don't make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors. A caution on alcohol Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and celebrations often revolve around drinking. Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience. Some patients report that GLP-1 medications reduce their desire for alcohol altogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment. Alcohol can worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications. If you choose to drink, consider these precautions: Limit your intake. Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication. Avoid drinking on an empty stomach. Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal. Stay hydrated. Drink water throughout the occasion. Pay attention to how you feel. Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms. The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms. Planning for travel Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment. Plan ahead for medication storage. Some injectable GLP-1 medications require refrigeration before use, while others allow room-temperature storage for a specified period after dispensing or first use. Storage requirements vary considerably by product. Check the prescribing information for your specific medication or ask your pharmacist before traveling. Don't assume that all injectable medications can remain unrefrigerated for the same length of time. If you're flying, keep your medication and supplies in your carry-on luggage. This helps protect them from extreme temperatures and prevents problems if your checked luggage gets delayed or lost. Keep in mind that you might also need to have a note from your prescribing provider to ca

a7430b200f47.text: By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-orders-federal-contractors-to-check-with-white-house-before-responding-to-congress Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress Politics Updated on Nov 21, 2026 4:02 PM EST — Published on Nov 21, 2026 2:29 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended. The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon. White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats. Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality." READ MORE: Read the full White House memo requiring agencies to get approval before testifying in front of Congress Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance. Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started." In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government." Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute. The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

5e5c12a8f2f0.text: By — Megan Janetsky, Associated Press Megan Janetsky, Associated Press By — Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press By — Martín Urista, Associated Press Martín Urista, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/mexico-detains-top-cartel-boss-el-chapo-isidro-setting-off-a-burst-of-violence-in-sinaloa Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mexico detains top cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro,' setting off a burst of violence in Sinaloa World Updated on Nov 21, 2026 5:37 PM EST — Published on Nov 21, 2026 2:13 PM EST GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico's Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in an operation that left at least 11 people dead. Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized. Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed. The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms. WATCH: Mexico's foreign secretary on Trump, cartel violence and U.S. trade talks Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores. He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state. Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups. As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions. Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violence The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city. Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders. "The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city." Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. READ MORE: Why Mexican cartels are increasingly using car bombs and other explosives Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities. Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case. "Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets. Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.
To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.
Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”
In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.
“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”
Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.
In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.
Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”
Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.
“I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.
Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”
Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.
Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.
“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.
“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.
He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.
“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”
More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.
“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.
The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.
“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”
Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?
“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”
